title: Large robust and auditable sealed-bid auctions
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can a sealed-bid auction handle a truly large market — say 100,000 bids — while remaining robust against malicious participants, publicly auditable, and able to recover from faults, all within a realistic latency budget? Formally, the target is malicious-secure, publicly correct, fault-recoverable clearing of 100,000 bids with amortized preprocessing counted against a declared latency bound.
status: This is a proposed moonshot; the closest published benchmark is Dumbo-MPC's 31-party example, which uses minutes of preparation for a 100-bidder Vickrey auction. Key works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.
solved_when: A protocol publicly and correctly clears 100,000 bids under malicious security with fault recovery, within a declared latency budget, where the accounting includes amortized preprocessing costs.
why: It would bring private, verifiable allocation to exchange or public-market scale, where today's techniques fall short by orders of magnitude.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Malicious private SQL with outsider verification
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can collaborative SQL analytics be made both maliciously secure and independently verifiable by outsiders? Concretely, the goal is a design combining maliciously secure collaborative SQL with succinct proofs that bind the query, authenticated input snapshots, and the result, while keeping intermediate relations hidden.
status: This is a design frontier. Senate (Poddar et al., 2021, *Senate: A Maliciously-Secure MPC Platform for Collaborative Analytics*, USENIX Security 2021) supplies malicious collaborative analytics, but does not automatically provide every public-audit requirement. Related directions include verifiable query processing and authenticated relational algebra.
solved_when: A construction exists that achieves maliciously secure collaborative SQL together with succinct proofs binding the query, authenticated input snapshots, and result, and hiding intermediate relations.
why: It makes private analytics independently checkable, so parties outside the computation can trust results without seeing the data.
key_works: Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate: A Maliciously-Secure MPC Platform for Collaborative Analytics*, USENIX Security 2021.

title: Private verifiable training within tenfold cost
open: Can a full machine-learning training pipeline be made private, maliciously secure, and publicly verifiable all at once, at a total cost within 10× a declared plaintext training baseline? The count includes proof generation and communication, so no cost component may be pushed off the books.
status: Proposed as a moonshot; existing specialized training proofs and secure learning systems do not establish this combined cost ratio. Key works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA*, arXiv:2508.21393.
solved_when: A complete training scheme is demonstrated that is private, secure against malicious adversaries, and publicly verifiable, with all costs — computation, proofs, and communication — within 10× the declared plaintext baseline.
why: It would make trustworthy collaborative training economically practical rather than a luxury overhead.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Large post-quantum DKG with bounded pessimistic overhead
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can a lattice-based distributed key generation protocol run asynchronously over committees of thousands of nodes while keeping its worst-case (Byzantine-path) communication and computation within a bounded factor of the optimistic case? Formally, the goal is a large-scale asynchronous DKG whose pessimistic overhead does not blow up as the committee grows.
status: This is a proposed frontier target. The current state of the art is LADKG (Yang et al. (2025), *Robust and Scalable Lattice-Based Distributed Key Generation for Asynchronous Networks*, ePrint 2025/1946), which reports optimistic completion in 45 seconds for 121 AWS nodes; related directions include approximate agreement and lattice-proof acceleration.
solved_when: A lattice-based asynchronous DKG demonstrably scales to thousands of nodes with Byzantine-path costs within a small, stated constant factor of optimistic costs — improving on the current benchmark scale of 121 nodes.
why: It would make post-quantum committees practical beyond small deployments, removing the gap between best-case performance and adversarial worst case that currently limits real-world use.
key_works: Yang et al. (2025), *Robust and Scalable Lattice-Based Distributed Key Generation for Asynchronous Networks*, ePrint 2025/1946.

title: Shared-state composition across MPC, FHE, and proofs
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can we build a practical discipline for composing services that share state — commitments, authentication keys, FHE keys, or randomness — across concurrent MPC and proof sessions, while provably preserving security? More precisely: a checked construction methodology ensuring such reuse meets shared-state and interface requirements without recompiling the whole service into generic MPC.
status: This is currently a design target. UC composition itself is established (Canetti, 2001, *Universally Composable Security: A New Paradigm for Cryptographic Protocols*, ePrint 2000/067), but any particular implementation must still satisfy its shared-state and interface requirements on its own.
solved_when: A construction discipline exists that is checked (i.e., verifiable against its security requirements), supports reuse of commitments, authentication keys, FHE keys, and randomness across concurrent MPC and proof sessions, and avoids recompiling the entire service into generic MPC; any implementation must satisfy the shared-state and interface requirements of UC composition.
why: Without it, individually secure components can yield an insecure combined service; with it, composable services with shared state can be built and audited safely.
key_works: Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security: A New Paradigm for Cryptographic Protocols*, ePrint 2000/067.

title: Security degradation with multiple corruption thresholds
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can we design protocols that guarantee different properties—privacy, public correctness, attributable abort, availability—at different corruption levels, with provably safe transitions between operating modes?
status: This is a frontier combination problem; publicly auditable MPC (Kanjalkar, Zhang, Gandlur, and Miller, 2021, *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service with succinct verification and universal setup*, arXiv:2107.04248) already separates correctness from confidentiality under stronger corruption. Related directions include graceful Byzantine degradation and fault-containment architectures.
solved_when: A protocol is specified (with a proof) whose guarantees degrade in a controlled way across multiple corruption thresholds, with formally verified transitions between the operating modes at each level.
why: It replaces a single catastrophic trust threshold with useful residual guarantees, so the system retains some security even once its main guarantee fails.
key_works: Kanjalkar, Zhang, Gandlur, and Miller (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service with succinct verification and universal setup*, arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Adaptive security for the complete service lifecycle
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can a multi-party service be proven secure against adversaries who corrupt parties adaptively at any point — not merely before startup — across its entire lifecycle, from enrollment, DKG, and preprocessing through evaluation, proving, output release, refresh, and recovery, all under a single corruption model?
status: This is currently a design target. An erasure-free adaptively secure, universally composable DKG exists (Ek, Melissaris, and Roy (2026), *Adaptively Secure, Universally Composable Distributed Generation of Discrete-Logarithm Based Keys*, ePrint 2026/457), but that result does not automatically establish adaptive security of downstream components.
solved_when: A single adaptive corruption model is formalized under which every lifecycle phase listed above carries a composable (UC-style) security proof.
why: It protects services against compromise occurring during operation rather than only before initialization, closing the gap between setup-time and runtime security guarantees.
key_works: Ek, Melissaris, and Roy (2026), *Adaptively Secure, Universally Composable Distributed Generation of Discrete-Logarithm Based Keys*, ePrint 2026/457.

title: Whole-stack post-quantum security
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can a private-computation service be built in which every layer of the stack — transport, authentication, distributed key generation, encryption, commitments, proofs, and recovery — meets a post-quantum security definition, with all of those definitions composable into a single auditable whole?
status: Currently a design target rather than a built system. Substantial components exist: post-quantum collaborative proofs are available via Pappas, Papadopoulos, and Papadopoulos (2026), *Code-based Scalable Collaborative SNARKs* (ePrint 2026/729), and lattice-based asynchronous distributed key generation via Yang et al. (2025), *Robust and Scalable Lattice-Based Distributed Key Generation for Asynchronous Networks* (ePrint 2025/1946).
solved_when: A working private-computation service exists in which each of transport, authentication, DKG, encryption, commitments, proofs, and recovery satisfies an explicitly stated post-quantum security definition, the definitions are mutually compatible (composable), and the trust assumptions across the stack are documented well enough to be audited.
why: A post-quantum claim is silently defeated when any single auxiliary primitive — a classical transport, signature, or recovery mechanism — remains breakable by a quantum adversary; closing those side doors is what makes the overall claim meaningful.
key_works: Pappas, Papadopoulos, and Papamanthou (2026), *Code-based Scalable Collaborative SNARKs*, ePrint 2026/729; Yang et al. (2025), *Robust and Scalable Lattice-Based Distributed Key Generation for Asynchronous Networks*, ePrint 2025/1946.

title: Lifetime leakage from aborts and retries
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can we build a composable privacy accountant that tracks everything a service reveals over its lifetime — successful outputs, selective aborts, rejected inputs, retries, and error messages — rather than only the outputs it returns? Formally, such an accountant should compose leakage across all of these channels throughout a service's lifetime within a unified differential-privacy accounting framework.
status: This is a frontier problem. Work by Meisingseth (2026), *On Aborts in Differential Privacy* (ePrint 2026/2059), quantifies important abort effects for differential privacy, but broader mixed-stack leakage accounting — covering the full range of channels above — remains a separate open target.
solved_when: A composable accountant exists that bounds cumulative privacy leakage from successful outputs, selective aborts, rejected inputs, retries, and error messages over a service's lifetime, so that repeated executions cannot silently exceed the budget accounted for by any single-run analysis.
why: Without such accounting, repeated execution of a service becomes an extraction oracle: each abort, retry, or error message leaks a little more, and no existing analysis bounds the total.
key_works: Meisingseth (2026), *On Aborts in Differential Privacy*, ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Correlation-aware committee security
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can committee selection for threshold schemes be optimized against realistic correlated failures — operators, clouds, software stacks, jurisdictions, and recovery paths — instead of assuming each participant is an independent trust domain? More precisely: is there a selection procedure that models these shared failure causes explicitly and yields committees with measurably better failure diversity than independence-based selection?
status: This is currently an evidence and modeling target; existing threshold specifications identify cryptographic parties but do not capture the empirical independence of their operators. Related directions include common-cause reliability modeling and correlated network interdiction. NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, NIST IR 8214C, DOI:10.6028/NIST.IR.8214C, frames the setting.
solved_when: A committee-selection method exists that takes correlated operator, cloud, software, jurisdictional, and recovery failure structure as input and demonstrably improves distributed-trust guarantees relative to treating participants as independent.
why: It makes "distributed trust" reflect actual failure diversity rather than merely counting cryptographic parties, so a threshold system's real-world compromise resistance matches its formal specification.
key_works: NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, NIST IR 8214C, DOI:10.6028/NIST.IR.8214C.

title: Semantics-preserving mixed-arithmetic compilation
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can a compiler automatically certify every conversion between modular integers, fixed-point values, approximate real arithmetic, and Boolean representations in a mixed-protocol computation, so that both the security guarantee and the application's intended semantics survive each conversion?
status: This is a design frontier; mixed-protocol frameworks exist (e.g., Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521), but numerical meaning and corruption guarantees must currently be ensured to survive every conversion.
solved_when: An automatic certification method exists that certifies such conversions across these representations while preserving both security and application semantics.
why: It prevents fast hybrid implementations from computing the wrong function securely — a silent failure mode where performance gains come at the cost of correctness.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Public auditing of private programs
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Can a committed program be executed and publicly audited while keeping its sensitive structure — branches, policy rules, model architecture, and data-dependent resource use — hidden from the auditor?
status: Public auditing of computations is established (e.g., Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service*, arXiv:2107.04248), but hiding both the program relation and its operational footprint remains a design target with separate, unmet requirements; related directions include private function evaluation and universal-circuit efficiency.
solved_when: A construction exists in which any third party can verify correct execution of a committed program, and the proof reveals nothing about the program's branching structure, policy rules, model architecture, or data-dependent resource consumption beyond what is inherently leaked.
why: It would let organizations prove they run code honestly without disclosing proprietary algorithms, opening auditing to regulated or multi-party settings where the program itself is a trade secret.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service*, arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Everlasting privacy with durable public accountability
subfield: Composable security and explicit trust assumptions
open: Construct practical distributed computation whose audit records remain statistically private even after the underlying computational assumptions fail, while still retaining useful public accountability.
status: Frontier combination; computationally private succinct audit systems provide a baseline, but do not automatically yield everlasting privacy. Related directions include long-term archival privacy and information-theoretic commitment tradeoffs; key works include Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security*, ePrint 2000/067, and Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248.
solved_when: A construction exists that achieves everlasting (statistical) privacy of audit records post-cryptographic-failure, together with meaningful public accountability, in a composable framework.
why: It protects sensitive records that must remain confidential for decades, long after today's computational assumptions may be broken.
key_works: Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security*, ePrint 2000/067; Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Proving inclusion of every accepted input
open: Can a multiparty computation service prove to the public that every input submitted and acknowledged before a cutoff was admitted into the computation exactly once, while keeping the input's value and unnecessary participant metadata private?
status: This is a design target; correctness proofs over committed inputs do not by themselves establish completeness of the admission process. Related work includes Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service*, arXiv:2107.04248, and Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648.
solved_when: A protocol exists whose public proof establishes that all inputs acknowledged before the cutoff are included exactly once, alongside privacy of values and participant metadata.
why: It prevents selective censorship that could otherwise be disguised as a valid computation over a silently filtered input set.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service*, arXiv:2107.04248; Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Authenticated inputs under dishonest-majority public blame
open: Can authenticated-input MPC be extended to work when a majority of parties are dishonest, while keeping its efficiency and producing compact public evidence that identifies invalid authentication or inconsistent sharing?
status: This is a frontier extension; the cited authenticated-input compiler of Dutta, Ganesh, Patranabis, and Singh (2024), *Compute, but Verify: Efficient Multiparty Computation over Authenticated Inputs* (ePrint 2022/1648), provides honest-majority constructions with identifiable-abort guarantees in specified thresholds.
solved_when: A compiler supports dishonest-majority computation over authenticated inputs with efficiency comparable to the honest-majority setting, and yields compact public evidence pinpointing invalid authentication or inconsistent sharing.
why: It would tie institutional credentials into stronger outsourced-computation models, letting mutually distrusting institutions verify both the authenticity of inputs and the correctness of their sharing.
key_works: Dutta, Ganesh, Patranabis, and Singh (2024), *Compute, but Verify: Efficient Multiparty Computation over Authenticated Inputs*, ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Auditable authorization-policy versions
open: Can a private computation be cryptographically bound to the exact version of the authorization policy that was in force when it was admitted — including revocations, expirations, and policy changes that occur before output release — so that the proof of correct execution also proves the execution was authorized?
status: Currently a design target; existing work on authenticated data and proofs of correct execution does not automatically establish that the execution was authorized. Key works: Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.
solved_when: A construction exists in which each private execution carries a verifiable, auditable commitment to the policy version authorized at admission, and validity fails if the policy was revoked, expired, or altered before output release.
why: Without it, stale or mismatched permissions can yield proofs that are valid yet unauthorized, so verifiable correctness alone does not imply legitimate access.
key_works: Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Incrementally auditable reactive MPC
open: Can a long-running reactive MPC service carry a single succinct public proof that its entire history — admitted inputs, state transitions, outputs, and code versions — is consistent, so that auditors never need to replay the computation?
status: Design frontier. Collaborative incremental verification exists (Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410), but a complete reactive service must additionally handle admission and state-continuity obligations, which remain unaddressed.
solved_when: A construction exists for a reactive MPC service that maintains one succinct proof binding admitted inputs, state transitions, outputs, and code versions incrementally, updating it per transition without replaying the full history.
why: It would make years of private computation publicly checkable, turning an ongoing MPC service into one whose integrity anyone can verify from a short artifact.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410.

title: Audit generation that is safe on invalid witnesses
open: Can a collaborative audit prover be designed so that malformed or adversarially crafted distributed inputs never cause it to leak honest participants' secrets before it rejects or aborts? Formally, this asks for malformed-input noninterference: privacy must hold even when the shared statement does not satisfy the intended relation.
status: This is a frontier hardening problem. 2025 work — Garg, Goel, Jain, Roberts, and Sekar (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026 — shows that collaborative proving can require more care than simply running a prover inside malicious MPC.
solved_when: A collaborative proving protocol is exhibited in which honest parties' witnesses remain hidden whenever any party supplies malformed inputs, with the prover's behavior on such inputs limited to rejection or abort — no proof obligations beyond this are required.
why: This protects privacy precisely when adversaries violate the intended relation — the case where standard zero-knowledge guarantees, which assume well-formed statements, offer no protection.
key_works: Garg, Goel, Jain, Roberts, and Sekar (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026.

title: Non-equivocating private audit histories
open: How can a service be prevented from showing different auditors mutually inconsistent but individually valid histories, while still supporting selective disclosure and intermittently connected clients? Formally, the goal is a construction in which any valid proof of a history certifies that it is the unique authoritative history.
status: Currently a design target; a valid proof of one history does not establish that it is the unique authoritative history. Related directions include fork consistency and Byzantine transparency logs; key works are Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security*, ePrint 2000/067, and Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.
solved_when: A design exists that prevents a service from presenting mutually inconsistent valid histories to different auditors, while allowing selective disclosure and intermittently connected clients; that is, validity of a proof of one history establishes it as the unique authoritative history.
why: It prevents hidden double accounting and inconsistent private ledgers, closing the gap where a valid proof of one history does not establish that it is the unique authoritative history.
key_works: Canetti (2001), *Universally Composable Security*, ePrint 2000/067; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Proof availability after computation completes
open: Can a group that has jointly completed a private computation still produce the public zero-knowledge proof of that computation after some participants drop offline, without anyone reconstructing the distributed witness?
status: This is a design target. Collaborative proving (e.g., Ozdemir and Boneh, 2022, *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs: Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Distributed Secrets*, USENIX Security 2022) supplies the privacy mechanism, but proof durability — completing the proof after participant disappearance — remains a distinct, unaddressed completion property.
solved_when: A protocol exists in which, following successful collaborative proving over a distributed secret, a public proof can be completed even after participant loss, with no party ever gaining the reconstructed witness.
why: Without it, a correct result becomes unusable because its proof is stranded — the computation succeeds but its public verifiability is lost.
key_works: Ozdemir and Boneh (2022), *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs: Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Distributed Secrets*, USENIX Security 2022.

title: Private, verifiable resource billing
open: Can a service provider produce a bill for outsourced computation — over MPC, FHE, or proof generation — that the client can verify, while the provider learns nothing about the program's structure, its inputs, or how resources were actually consumed? Formally, this asks for a billing mechanism whose correctness is publicly verifiable yet whose utilization patterns remain private.
status: Currently a design target. Existing work addresses separate pieces — proofs of computation handle verifiability, while cryptographic and financial fairness techniques (Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248; Friolo et al. (2022), *Cryptographic and Financial Fairness*, arXiv:2207.10780) address the economic side — but no approach combines them into private, verifiable billing.
solved_when: A construction exists that, for MPC, FHE, and proof-generation workloads, emits verifiable bills attesting to resource usage while hiding sensitive program structure, inputs, and utilization patterns from the billing party.
why: It makes outsourced private computation economically auditable: clients can check what they are paying for without exposing what they are computing.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248; Friolo et al. (2022), *Cryptographic and Financial Fairness*, arXiv:2207.10780.

title: Public auditing below ten-percent overhead
open: Can public auditability be made essentially free, adding less than 10% to the total cost of an otherwise identical maliciously secure MPC workload when all expenses are counted — proving, storage, communication, and verification?
status: This is a proposed moonshot, not a published record; the open problem is prompted by Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service with succinct verification and universal setup* (arXiv:2107.04248), whose succinct verification does not imply cheap proof production.
solved_when: A publicly auditable MPC system is demonstrated whose end-to-end overhead — including proof production, storage, communication, and verification — is below 10% relative to an otherwise identical maliciously secure MPC workload.
why: It would make public auditing an ordinary service feature of MPC deployments rather than a costly add-on.
key_works: Kanjalkar et al. (2021), *Publicly Auditable MPC-as-a-Service with succinct verification and universal setup*, arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Subsecond proofs of programmable bootstrapping
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can a proof that an encrypted computation was done correctly be produced as fast as the computation itself — specifically, can a representative TFHE evaluation with a programmable bootstrap be proven in under one second at matching security parameters?
status: This is a proposed performance frontier. The state of the art is HasteBoots (Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots: Proving TFHE Programmable Bootstrapping in Seconds*, USENIX Security 2026), which reports approximately ten seconds for one evaluation/bootstrap — a major improvement over the older tens-of-minutes baseline, but still an order of magnitude away from the subsecond target.
solved_when: A proof of a representative TFHE evaluation and programmable bootstrap is produced in under one second, at security parameters matching the underlying computation, with public verification and all proving costs included.
why: It would make integrity checks practical for low-latency encrypted services, where a multi-second proving overhead would dominate the service itself.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots: Proving TFHE Programmable Bootstrapping in Seconds*, USENIX Security 2026.

title: Bounded-memory proofs for long bootstrap sequences
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can a long TFHE computation involving many bootstraps be proven correct using only bounded working memory, keeping incremental checkpoints rather than materializing the full execution trace?
status: Frontier extension. HasteBoots (Liu et al., 2026, USENIX Security 2026) demonstrates batching, including sixteen operations within one minute in its configuration; see also Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.
solved_when: A proof system sustains multi-bootstrap TFHE computation with bounded memory and incremental checkpoints, never materializing the complete execution trace.
why: It would support persistent encrypted programs rather than only short benchmark circuits.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots*, USENIX Security 2026; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Simultaneously cheap RNS proving and verification
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can we build zero-knowledge proofs for RNS-based homomorphic encryption pipelines where proving time, verification time, and proof size are all simultaneously practical, instead of trading one against another?
status: The frontier is held by PRISM (Zhou et al., 2026, *PRISM: Efficient zkSNARKs for RNS-Based Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1956), which reports approximately 3.5× slower proving than ZHE while improving verification or proof size by up to 7.8×.
solved_when: A proof system for complete RNS-based HE pipelines improves the joint frontier — prover time, verifier time, and proof size together — beyond PRISM's current trade-off point (roughly 3.5× slower proving than ZHE in exchange for up to 7.8× better verification or proof size).
why: It prevents the verification bottleneck from simply being shifted onto the service provider, which is where current trade-offs land.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM: Efficient zkSNARKs for RNS-Based Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Low-cost zero knowledge for lattice-native verifiable FHE
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can a client verify that an untrusted server correctly executed a lattice-based fully homomorphic encryption scheme, without learning anything about the server's private inputs or auxiliary execution data? More precisely, can the known lattice-native approaches to verifiable FHE be extended to satisfy a complete zero-knowledge definition, at efficiency comparable to plain verifiable FHE?
status: This is a frontier combination: verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge verifiable FHE exist as separate lines and are not interchangeable guarantees. Atapoor et al. (2024), *Verifiable FHE via Lattice-based SNARKs*, DOI:10.62056/a6ksdkp10, give lattice-based SNARK-based verification; Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956, represent the more recent frontier. Related directions include lattice zero knowledge and witness-hiding algebraic proofs.
solved_when: A verifiable FHE scheme based on lattice-native techniques is given whose evaluation proofs are zero knowledge under a complete definition (hiding server-private inputs and auxiliary execution information), while matching the efficiency of existing lattice-native verifiable FHE.
why: It would allow confidential models and policies to run on untrusted encrypted-computation servers, with both correctness assurance and privacy of the server's side information.
key_works: Atapoor et al. (2024), *Verifiable FHE via Lattice-based SNARKs*, DOI:10.62056/a6ksdkp10; Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Cheaper soundness for SIMD transcript packing
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: When a verifiable-FHE computation is checked via SIMD-packed transcripts, how much extra soundness cost is truly required to guard against malformed encodings — can that cost be reduced, or shown to be necessary, without giving up the SIMD efficiency that motivates packing in the first place?
status: The frontier was sharpened by Laminate’s May 2026 correction (Peshawaria, Liu, Fisch, and Tromer, 2025/2026, ePrint 2025/2285): its repaired well-formedness test adds security-parameter-dependent ciphertext overhead, which is precisely the cost now in question.
solved_when: A proof or construction is given that either reduces the additional soundness cost of the well-formedness check for packed transcripts below the security-parameter-dependent ciphertext overhead, or proves that overhead (or comparable cost) necessary — while preserving the packed/SIMD structure of the transcript.
why: A tight answer makes transcript packing a reliable proof-compression technique rather than a newly opened attack surface in verifiable FHE.
key_works: Peshawaria, Liu, Fisch, and Tromer (2025/2026), *Laminate: Succinct SIMD-Friendly Verifiable FHE*, ePrint 2025/2285.

title: Application-level error certificates for CKKS
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can a homomorphic encryption scheme prove not only that a CKKS computation was executed correctly, but that the decrypted result is close to the real-number quantity the application intended to compute? Formally, this asks for a bound between the decrypted CKKS output and the intended real-number computation that accounts for encoding, approximation, rescaling, rounding, and accumulated error.
status: This is a frontier extension of existing work: current proofs of HE execution, such as ZHE (Zhou et al., 2025, *ZHE: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proofs for HE Evaluations*, ePrint 2025/770), do not by themselves prove application-level numerical accuracy. Related foundations come from validated numerics and formal floating-point analysis.
solved_when: A proven bound relating the decrypted CKKS result to the intended real-number computation is established, covering encoding error, approximation error, rescaling error, rounding error, and accumulated error.
why: It makes encrypted scientific and financial results interpretable — a user can trust what the number means over the reals, not merely that the ciphertext arithmetic was performed as specified.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proofs for HE Evaluations*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Proof compatibility with optimized FFT implementations
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can we formally certify that a production floating-point FFT-based FHE kernel computes the same function as the proof-friendly exact NTT representation it is claimed to instantiate, including the approximation and overflow conditions under which the equivalence holds?
status: Engineering frontier. HasteBoots (Liu et al., 2026, USENIX Security 2026) explains the arithmetic mismatch and uses proof-friendly quotient-ring representations; related directions include translation validation and certified numerical transforms.
solved_when: A certified equivalence exists between a production floating-point FFT kernel and an exact NTT representation, with explicit approximation-error and overflow conditions.
why: It removes the need to maintain a slow "provable" implementation separate from the fast production one, so proofs apply to what actually runs.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots*, USENIX Security 2026.

title: Hidden-noise decryption-reliability proofs
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can a evaluator prove to a verifier that a ciphertext will decrypt correctly — with only a negligible chance of failure — without revealing the secret key, the plaintext, or a noise trace that leaks more than necessary?
status: This remains a frontier question; execution integrity and reliable decryptability are currently distinct statements, with no unified proof known. Related directions include Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770 and Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956, alongside probabilistic program verification and certified failure bounds.
solved_when: A proof system exists that certifies a decryption-failure probability bound for a given ciphertext while exposing no keys, no plaintexts, and no unnecessarily revealing noise information; the scheme is sound and zero-knowledge with respect to those secrets.
why: It closes the gap between execution integrity and usable output: without it, an evaluator can return a ciphertext that was honestly evaluated yet fails to decrypt, and the verifier cannot tell.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770; Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Proof-bound conditional decryption
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can we build a decryption interface that hands over the plaintext only when the requester presents a valid proof that the ciphertext was evaluated correctly — and does so securely even against maliciously formed ciphertexts, replayed or repeated proof submissions, and malformed proofs?
status: This is currently a design target; the open task is to compose verifiable FHE evaluation with the real decryption security model. Related threads include threshold FHE with synchronized decryptors (Colin de Verdière, Passelègue, and Stehlé, 2026, ePrint 2026/031) and ZHE (Zhou et al., 2025), alongside work on chosen-ciphertext security and proof-carrying authorization.
solved_when: A decryption API exists that releases plaintext only for authorized evaluation proofs, with a security definition and proof covering malicious ciphertexts, proof replay, repeated requests, and errors, composing verifiable evaluation with the actual decryption security model.
why: Without such a bound, a valid-looking proof interface can be turned into a key-recovery oracle, undoing the security the underlying FHE was meant to provide.
key_works: Colin de Verdière, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *On Threshold Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Synchronized Decryptors*, ePrint 2026/031; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*.

title: Tight costs of strongly simulatable asynchronous decryption
open: What are the true communication, modulus, storage, and threshold costs of achieving strong simulatability in asynchronous threshold fully homomorphic encryption? In particular, can upper bounds be matched by provable lower bounds, pinning down which costs are inherent?
status: The frontier is the 2026 Shamir-based construction of Kim, Lee, Lee, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *Asynchronous Shamir-Based Threshold FHE: Smaller Moduli and Strong Simulation Security*, ePrint 2026/973, which substantially reduces earlier storage and modulus requirements; older large-overhead baselines are therefore stale.
solved_when: A characterization of the communication complexity, modulus size, storage overhead, and threshold-parameter tradeoffs for strongly simulatable asynchronous threshold FHE is established, ideally with upper-bound constructions matched by corresponding lower bounds where possible.
why: It identifies which threshold-FHE costs are structural rather than artifacts of current constructions, directly guiding the design of more efficient schemes.
key_works: Kim, Lee, Lee, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *Asynchronous Shamir-Based Threshold FHE: Smaller Moduli and Strong Simulation Security*, ePrint 2026/973.

title: Robust decryption without a privileged combiner
open: Can threshold fully homomorphic decryption be made robust when the party combining partial decryptions may itself be malicious? In other words, replace the semi-honest available combiner with a Byzantine-resilient combining service that still delivers output under explicitly stated honest-participation assumptions.
status: Currently a design extension; MOZI's advertised output-delivery guarantees distinguish between semi-honest and malicious combiners, indicating the gap [Chang et al. (2026), *MOZI: Threshold FHE at Scale: Efficient and Resilient, for Large-Scale MPC*, NIST TCPT3 presentation].
solved_when: A combining service tolerating Byzantine behavior is designed such that threshold decryption output is delivered whenever the stated honest-participation assumptions hold, matching the output-delivery guarantees MOZI provides only for semi-honest combiners.
why: It removes a centralized availability and honesty assumption from distributed decryption, so large-scale MPC can decrypt without trusting a single combining party.
key_works: Chang et al. (2026), *MOZI: Threshold FHE at Scale: Efficient and Resilient, for Large-Scale MPC*, NIST TCPT3 presentation.

title: Safe adaptive-query threshold-CKKS services
open: Is it possible to run a long-lived threshold-CKKS decryption service that stays secure when clients adaptively choose ciphertexts, receive repeated approximate outputs, trigger precision changes, reuse authorizations, and observe error responses? A proof would establish that the distributed decryption key remains protected across the complete query history of the API.
status: The design frontier has been sharpened by 2026 attacks and by repaired synchronized-decryptor models, notably Colin de Verdière, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *On Threshold Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Synchronized Decryptors*, ePrint 2026/031; related work concerns adaptive numerical side channels and oracle-resistant API design.
solved_when: A security proof (or repaired construction with proof) covers a threshold-CKKS service facing adaptive ciphertext queries, repeated approximate outputs, precision changes, authorization reuse, and error responses, over the full lifetime of the API.
why: Without it, each of these query behaviors is a potential side channel that leaks information about the shared decryption key; a solution makes long-lived threshold-CKKS deployments safe to expose as public services.
key_works: Colin de Verdière, Passelègue, and Stehlé (2026), *On Threshold Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Synchronized Decryptors*, ePrint 2026/031.

title: Concurrent authorization of changing decryptor sets
open: Can a threshold fully homomorphic encryption scheme handle many decryption requests at once, each bound to a different authorized subset, while cryptographically preventing shares issued under different requests, epochs, or policies from being recombined with each other?
status: This is a frontier extension of existing work. Strong designated-decryptor security is already achieved, but concurrent operational authorization remains out of reach and requires an explicit binding mechanism (Colin de Verdière et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/031).
solved_when: A scheme exists in which concurrent decryption requests assigned to distinct authorized subsets are supported, with provable security against any recombination of shares drawn from separate requests, epochs, or policies.
why: It would make decryption policy an enforced part of the cryptography itself rather than an administrative convention layered on top, closing a gap between what the policy intends and what the key shares actually permit.
key_works: Colin de Verdière et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/031.

title: Sparse threshold-CKKS DKG under WAN faults
open: Can a sparse-key distributed key generation protocol for threshold CKKS be run end-to-end among at least 1,000 parties over a realistic wide-area network, tolerating malicious behavior with public verifiability and a fully accounted setup cost?
status: Currently a design target only; Min et al. (2025/2026, *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057) report two seconds for the computational components on an RTX 4090 through 1,024 parties, but not full WAN completion.
solved_when: A sparse-threshold-CKKS DKG is demonstrated for at least 1,000 parties with malicious robustness, public verification, realistic WAN transport, and complete setup accounting — i.e., full WAN completion, not just computational components.
why: It preserves efficient CKKS bootstrapping while eliminating any central key generator, so threshold FHE deployments get strong key security without giving up performance.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Refreshable threshold evaluation keys
open: Can the set of parties holding a threshold FHE secret be refreshed or replaced — including all bootstrapping, rotation, and key-switching keys derived from it — without ever reconstructing the secret and without taking the service offline? Formally, the goal is a construction (or protocol suite) providing proactive refresh and committee change for the full evaluation-key lifecycle in threshold FHE.
status: Currently a design target. Efficient threshold key generation exists (Min et al., *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057), but it does not by itself provide lifecycle management for the derived evaluation keys. Related directions include online key rotation and key-evolving cryptography.
solved_when: A construction exists that refreshes or replaces the distributed authority and regenerates all derived evaluation keys (bootstrapping, rotation, key-switching) with no secret reconstruction, no complete service outage, and costs suitable for long-term maintenance of a live threshold-FHE deployment.
why: Without it, a threshold FHE deployment cannot be maintained over years: any change in the committee of parties effectively forces a fresh setup. With it, threshold FHE becomes operationally maintainable.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Recovery with historical ciphertext continuity
open: After a permitted operator compromise in a threshold FHE deployment, can a new committee keep its authorized access to historical ciphertexts while ensuring it does not inherit any unnecessary historical authority?
status: This is a design-combination problem: proactive sharing and threshold FHE supply the ingredients, but ciphertext continuity adds migration obligations not addressed by either alone.
solved_when: A design is given that combines proactive secret sharing with threshold FHE so that recovery from a permitted operator compromise preserves authorized access to all historical ciphertexts and provably prevents the new committee from gaining authority beyond what it is authorized to hold.
why: Without such a mechanism, an incident forces operators to abandon existing encrypted data or hand the new committee more historical authority than it should have; a solution keeps encrypted data usable across a recovery.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), *On the (Im)possibility of Asynchronous Proactive Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2026/2018; Kim et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/973.

title: Short decryption shares with public accountability
open: Can a serverless threshold fully homomorphic encryption scheme keep decryption shares compact while still letting any authorized subset detect, provably attribute, and recover from maliciously generated shares?
status: This is a frontier combination problem: serverless threshold FHE with short decryption shares already exists (Okada and Takagi, 2026, ePrint 2026/957; Rivinius, 2025, ePrint 2025/258), but not with the full accountability machinery.
solved_when: A threshold FHE scheme without a semi-trusted server achieves short decryption shares together with malicious-share rejection, transferable blame, and reconstruction for arbitrary authorized subsets.
why: It keeps publicly accountable decryption practical for bandwidth-constrained participants, where long proofs or shares would defeat the purpose of short shares.
key_works: Okada and Takagi (2026), *Threshold FHE with Short Decryption Shares without a Semi-trusted Server*, ePrint 2026/957; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

title: Threshold FHE within twice single-key lifecycle cost
open: Can a maliciously secure threshold fully homomorphic encryption scheme be run end-to-end — setup, ciphertext refresh, and decryption — at no more than twice the total amortized cost of an equivalent single-key deployment? Formally, demonstrate an auditable threshold-FHE application whose full lifecycle cost stays below a 2× overhead ratio.
status: Currently a proposed moonshot; component-level improvements exist (e.g., Min et al., 2025/2026, ePrint 2025/2057; Okada and Takagi, 2026, ePrint 2026/957), but none establish the application-level cost ratio.
solved_when: A working, auditable, maliciously secure threshold-FHE application is demonstrated with total amortized lifecycle cost — covering setup, refresh, and decryption — strictly below 2× that of an equivalent single-key implementation.
why: It makes distributed trust cheap enough that threshold FHE could be adopted routinely rather than reserved for high-stakes deployments.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057; Okada and Takagi (2026), ePrint 2026/957.

title: Concrete fully succinct multi-key FHE
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Can fully succinct multi-key FHE be implemented with concrete, defensible parameters — and when it is, does its compactness actually pay off in total memory, evaluation, and decryption cost compared to practical nonsuccinct alternatives?
status: This is an engineering frontier. Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE* (ePrint 2026/1683), already achieve leveled LWE-based succinctness of ciphertexts and individual public and secret keys, but no concrete implementation with defensible parameters exists.
solved_when: A working implementation of fully succinct multi-key FHE exists with explicitly justified concrete parameters, together with a measured comparison of total memory, evaluation, and decryption costs against practical nonsuccinct alternatives.
why: It tests whether asymptotic compactness translates into usable multi-owner computation; without concrete evidence, succinctness remains a theoretical property rather than an engineering option.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Bootstrapped fully succinct multi-key services
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Can multi-key fully homomorphic encryption remain fully succinct under unbounded-depth evaluation, once bootstrapping keys and the cost of distributed decryption are all accounted for? More precisely, is there a multi-key FHE scheme that supports arbitrary-depth circuits while keeping ciphertexts, evaluation keys, and threshold-decryption communication compact in the number of parties and the security parameter?
status: The current frontier is a leveled fully succinct construction: Afshar and Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683. Extending succinctness through bootstrapping to arbitrary depth, with all distributed-decryption costs counted, remains open.
solved_when: A construction (with proof) achieves fully succinct multi-key FHE for arbitrary-depth evaluation, with bootstrapping material included in the succinctness accounting and all distributed-decryption costs bounded; this improves on the current leveled fully succinct constructions.
why: It would extend compact multi-owner computation beyond a fixed depth budget, so jointly encrypted data can be computed on indefinitely without ciphertext or key material growing with circuit depth.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Publicly verifiable near-rate-one multi-key decryption
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Can multi-key homomorphic decryption be made publicly verifiable without giving up its communication efficiency — that is, can decryption evidence of correct, attributed behavior be produced at an amortized rate approaching the plaintext size?
status: The combination is at the frontier: rate-one simulatable partial decryption exists, but the extra material needed for verification has not yet been accounted for in the rate. Key works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Rivinius (2025), *MPC with Publicly Identifiable Abort from Pseudorandomness and Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2025/258.
solved_when: A multi-key decryption scheme exists with public correctness evidence and malicious-share accountability whose amortized decryption communication approaches the plaintext size, with the cost of any extra verification material explicitly counted toward that bound.
why: It prevents the shift from private to accountable operation from destroying the compactness that amortized decryption provides, keeping hybrid representation changes between multi-key FHE and MPC practical.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Rivinius (2025), *MPC with Publicly Identifiable Abort from Pseudorandomness and Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2025/258.

title: Owner revocation after multi-key evaluation
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: When a multi-key FHE computation involves owners who later leave the collaboration, can we revoke a departed owner's ability to influence or consume future evaluations while still letting them keep access to results they were authorized to see — all without handing the remaining owners unrestricted access to the departed owner's inputs?
status: This is currently only a design target; succinct multi-key evaluation as it exists does not determine consent or revocation semantics. Key works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.
solved_when: A specification and implementation of revocation semantics for multi-key FHE are given that block a departed owner from any future use, preserve the departed owner's access to previously authorized results, and prevent remaining owners from unrestricted access to the departed owner's inputs.
why: It makes multi-key FHE usable for collaborations whose membership changes over time, where today's designs offer no way to retire a participant cleanly.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Auditable admission of adversarial multi-key owners
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: How can a multi-key FHE system admit independently generated participant keys — verifying ownership, parameter compatibility, and any required key relations — without relying on a trusted registration authority?
status: Currently a design target; no construction exists yet beyond the requirement that a service must instantiate the key-generation and registration assumptions of its multi-key construction. Related concerns include rogue-key resistance and decentralized key registration (Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; NIST (2026), IR 8214C).
solved_when: A concrete service design exists that instantiates the key-generation and registration assumptions of the chosen multi-key construction, admitting adversarial multi-key owners with checks for ownership, parameter compatibility, and required key relations, all without a trusted registration authority.
why: It prevents malformed or misbound participant keys from breaking collaboration among independently generated key sets.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; NIST (2026), IR 8214C.

title: Public receipts for FHE-to-share conversion
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Can ciphertexts be converted into authenticated shares while producing a compact public receipt that binds the source ciphertext, the destination committee, the arithmetic interpretation, and the authorization for the conversion?
status: Currently a design target. Hybrid HE–MPC systems — e.g., Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee: Secure Two-party Inference Framework for Large Transformers*, ePrint 2023/1678, and Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ* — provide conversion precedents, but no universal publicly verifiable conversion interface exists.
solved_when: A publicly verifiable conversion interface exists that outputs authenticated shares together with compact evidence binding source ciphertext, destination committee, arithmetic interpretation, and authorization.
why: It removes the need for trusted adapters between encrypted (HE/FHE) execution and interactive (MPC) execution, letting hybrid systems switch representations without a trusted intermediary.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee: Secure Two-party Inference Framework for Large Transformers*, ePrint 2023/1678; Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*.

title: Verifiable switching between approximate, exact, and Boolean computation
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Can applications working under multi-key FHE switch a computation among CKKS approximate arithmetic, exact modular arithmetic, and Boolean circuits — while producing a verifiable proof that the conversions preserve values, respect range and rounding constraints, and no key custodian learns anything? A complete answer would give composable semantic and cryptographic preconditions for each representation change.
status: This is a design frontier. Mixed computation across these representations exists, but each conversion's semantic and cryptographic preconditions must currently be composed; key works include Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678, and Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.
solved_when: A construction exists in which CKKS–exact–Boolean conversions are accompanied by proofs of range, rounding, and value-preservation conditions, composable under distributed key custody, with the full pipeline remaining multi-key FHE-secure.
why: It lets each step of a computation run in its most efficient representation — approximate CKKS, exact modular, or Boolean — instead of forcing a single scheme throughout, which can be prohibitively expensive for mixed workloads.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Leakage-aware hybrid optimization
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: When the cost model of an optimization pass depends on secret data — as in choosing representations, batch sizes, sparsity, and precision in multi-key FHE — can the optimizer itself be made leakage-aware, so that its decisions provably stay within a declared leakage budget rather than becoming an observable side channel?
status: This is a frontier compiler target; no such leakage-aware optimizer exists, and the difficulty is that optimization decisions themselves can become observable outputs. Related directions include oblivious algorithms and information-flow-aware optimization; a natural experimental substrate is MP-SPDZ (Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521).
solved_when: A compilation/optimization method exists that selects representation choices, batch sizes, sparsity, and precision under secret-dependent costs, together with a proof of compliance with a declared leakage budget.
why: Without it, the optimization pass itself reveals exactly what the underlying protocol is designed to hide.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Portable encrypted-state exit
subfield: Multi-key FHE and hybrid representation changes
open: Can a user move encrypted private application state between providers, parameter sets, and operator committees without ever exporting it in the clear? Formally, the goal is a migration mechanism that carries a proof that the state is preserved across the transfer.
status: Currently a design target only. Existing interchangeable primitive outputs address a narrower problem than full application-state portability. Key works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Choudhuri et al. (2021), *Fluid MPC: Secure Multiparty Computation with Dynamic Participants*, ePrint 2020/754.
solved_when: A construction exists that ports complete application state (not merely interchangeable primitive outputs) across providers, parameter sets, and operator committees, produces a preservation proof, and never exposes plaintext during the migration.
why: It reduces infrastructure lock-in for encrypted-compute deployments while preserving confidentiality — today, changing provider or committee structure effectively requires giving up either security or the ability to keep running.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Choudhuri et al. (2021), *Fluid MPC: Secure Multiparty Computation with Dynamic Participants*, ePrint 2020/754.

title: General invalid-witness-safe collaborative proving
open: Can we build collaborative provers that remain private even when participants supply adversarially inconsistent shares of the witness, and characterize which broad proof-system families admit such constructions? Formally, this asks for a characterization and construction of invalid-witness-safe collaborative proving beyond specific proof systems.
status: The frontier follows the 2025 analysis of malicious collaborative-SNARK security (Garg et al. (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026), which showed that a generic wrapper must not assume the distributed witness is valid; no general invalid-witness-safe construction across broad proof-system families is known.
solved_when: A general characterization exists of which proof-system families support invalid-witness-safe collaborative proving, together with constructions (e.g., a generic wrapper) that provably preserve privacy on adversarially inconsistent witness shares without assuming the distributed witness is valid.
why: It makes proof delegation safe against malicious contributors, so a prover can distribute work without trusting that other parties hold a consistent, honest witness.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026.

title: Characterizing safe malicious-check elimination
open: Which collaborative SNARK prover computations remain secure when their expensive malicious-consistency checks are dropped, and can we give mechanically verifiable sufficient conditions that certify such check eliminations?
status: A frontier extension; 2025 work establishes useful check-elimination results for several provers in the honest-majority setting (Garg et al. (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026).
solved_when: A characterization exists of the collaborative prover computations for which malicious-consistency checks can be safely omitted, together with sufficient conditions for elimination that are mechanically verifiable.
why: It yields malicious security in distributed proving without paying unnecessary generic-MPC overhead for consistency checks that turn out to be redundant.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), *Malicious Security in Collaborative zk-SNARKs: More than Meets the Eye*, ePrint 2025/1026.

title: Adaptively secure transparent collaborative proofs
open: Can we build collaborative SNARKs that are transparent, post-quantum, and scalable, while remaining secure when the adversary adaptively corrupts witness holders, the randomness used by provers, and proof-state checkpoints? Formally, this asks for a distributed proving system secure against adaptive (rather than static) corruption of these components.
status: This is a frontier combination problem: transparent post-quantum collaborative SNARKs already exist (Pappas, Papadopoulos, and Papamanthou (2026), *Code-based Scalable Collaborative SNARKs*, ePrint 2026/729), but adaptive security across witness holders, prover randomness, and proof-state checkpoints remains unaddressed.
solved_when: A collaborative SNARK is constructed that is transparent, post-quantum, and scalable, with a proof of security against adaptive corruption of witness holders, prover randomness, and proof-state checkpoints.
why: Distributed proving jobs run long, so witnesses, randomness, and intermediate state can be compromised mid-computation; adaptive security protects against exactly this kind of during-the-attack compromise.
key_works: Pappas, Papadopoulos, and Papamanthou (2026), *Code-based Scalable Collaborative SNARKs*, ePrint 2026/729.

title: Robust distributed-witness availability
open: Can a group of provers jointly generate a SNARK so that the proof is still completed even when some participants are permitted to maliciously drop out — using explicit redundancy or honest-majority assumptions — without any party's secret witness being exposed?
status: Currently a design target; it is noted that collaborative proof generation and guaranteed proof completion are distinct properties, and no construction combining both under dropout is established. Key works: Ozdemir and Boneh (2022), *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs*; Liu et al. (2025), *Scalable Collaborative zk-SNARK and Its Application to Fully Distributed Proof Delegation*, ePrint 2024/940.
solved_when: A collaborative proving protocol exists that guarantees proof completion under malicious dropout (via explicit redundancy or an honest-majority assumption) while preserving witness privacy throughout.
why: It prevents a single prover from holding a group's completed private work hostage by refusing to finish or release their share.
key_works: Ozdemir and Boneh (2022), *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs*; Liu et al. (2025), *Scalable Collaborative zk-SNARK and Its Application to Fully Distributed Proof Delegation*, ePrint 2024/940.

title: Physical-network costs of collaborative IVC
open: Can the ideal broadcast channel assumed in collaborative incrementally verifiable computation be replaced by authenticated dissemination over a wide-area network — with failures and proof publication included — while preserving the low incremental communication the model promises? Formally, the goal is a construction whose per-party, per-step communication overhead stays close to constant even under realistic WAN dissemination.
status: This is a frontier implementation question. The 2026 collaborative-IVC result (Aldema Tshuva et al., *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410) achieves constant per-party per-step communication overhead but only under the assumption of a broadcast channel.
solved_when: An implementation of collaborative IVC is demonstrated in which the constant per-party per-step communication overhead is preserved (up to reasonable constant factors) when broadcast is replaced by authenticated WAN dissemination, tolerating failures and handling proof publication.
why: Without it, the abstract communication gains of collaborative IVC never translate into real bandwidth savings; with it, distributed proving becomes practical over actual networks.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410.

title: Private proof continuation across committees
open: Can a proving committee that is partway through an incremental proof hand off its work — including any secret shared state — to a newly selected committee, so that the proof continues correctly and only the authorized new committee can carry it forward? Formally, design a protocol for transferring a running incremental verifiable computation (IVC) across committees while preserving soundness, witness privacy, and a unique authorized continuation.
status: Currently a design target at the intersection of collaborative SNARKs and distributed proving, combining collaborative IVC with dynamic participation; no construction is known.
solved_when: A protocol exists that transfers an in-progress incremental proof and its secret state to a new committee while simultaneously preserving soundness, witness privacy, and a unique authorized continuation.
why: It would enable proving services that outlive individual operators, so long-running delegated computations do not restart or fail when the provers rotate.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410; David, Mondal, and Satish (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Assumption-diverse private MSM outsourcing
open: Can efficient private outsourcing of multi-scalar multiplication — the computational core of SNARK proving — be achieved under alternative well-studied cryptographic assumptions, rather than only LPN? Formally, this asks for encrypted-MSM protocols matching the efficiency of the LPN-based approach while keeping client work low and preserving privacy of statements, witnesses, and proofs.
status: Single-server private outsourcing already supports important SNARK families using LPN-based encrypted MSM (Abbaszadeh, Hafezi, Katz, and Meiklejohn, 2025/2026, *Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113); the extension to other assumptions remains open.
solved_when: A single-server private outsourcing scheme for encrypted MSM is constructed from a different well-studied assumption family, retaining the low client workload and the privacy guarantees for statements, witnesses, and proofs achieved by the LPN-based construction.
why: It prevents private proof delegation from resting on a single assumption family, so a break in LPN would not collapse the entire approach.
key_works: Abbaszadeh, Hafezi, Katz, and Meiklejohn (2025/2026), *Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113.

title: WAN scaling for irregular collaborative proofs
open: Can collaborative SNARK provers achieve strong distributed speedups on realistic workloads — those with irregular dependency structures, shared memory, and nonuniform witness access — rather than only on conveniently partitioned circuits?
status: This is a frontier workload extension; scalable distributed proof delegation (Liu et al. (2025), *Scalable Collaborative zk-SNARK and Its Application to Fully Distributed Proof Delegation*, ePrint 2024/940) provides the baseline.
solved_when: A distributed proving system demonstrates strong speedups on workloads exhibiting irregular dependencies, shared memory, and nonuniform witness access, improving on the scalable distributed proof delegation baseline.
why: It would extend collaborative proving from synthetic, evenly partitioned circuits to realistic software and stateful applications, where these irregularities are the norm.
key_works: Liu et al. (2025), *Scalable Collaborative zk-SNARK and Its Application to Fully Distributed Proof Delegation*, ePrint 2024/940.

title: Energy-efficient private proof delegation
open: Can a client offload private zk-SNARK proof generation to a server while consuming at least 20× less energy than proving locally — with the savings holding up under full end-to-end accounting?
status: Currently a proposed measurement target; existing single-server outsourcing work (Abbaszadeh et al. (2025/2026), *Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113) reports up to 18× client-computation reduction, but not a complete end-to-end energy result.
solved_when: A construction demonstrates at least 20× lower client energy for private proof generation, and reports the server's energy, network energy, preprocessing costs, and behavior under failure recovery.
why: It would make proof generation practical on mobile and embedded clients, where energy is the binding constraint rather than computation alone.
key_works: Abbaszadeh et al. (2025/2026), *Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113.

title: Erasure-free quadratic asynchronous DKG
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can we build an asynchronous distributed key generation protocol that achieves constant rounds and quadratic communication from plain setup, while dispensing entirely with secure erasures and retaining strong adaptive security? Formally, the target is an erasure-free, adaptively UC-secure asynchronous DKG whose communication complexity remains quadratic and whose round complexity remains constant under the plain-setup assumption.
status: This is a frontier combination problem. The 2026 quadratic plain-setup asynchronous DKG of Abraham, Bacho, and Stern (*Quadratic Asynchronous DKG from Plain Setup*, ePrint 2026/1159) assumes secure erasures, while erasure-free adaptively secure UC DKG is known in other settings (Ek et al. 2026, ePrint 2026/457); no single protocol yet combines all of these properties.
solved_when: A protocol is specified and proven that is asynchronous, uses only plain setup, runs in constant rounds with quadratic total communication, and is adaptively secure without any secure-erasures assumption.
why: Secure erasures are a demanding operational assumption in practice; removing them would let deployments adopt adaptively secure DKG without the scalability penalty of current alternatives.
key_works: Abraham, Bacho, and Stern (2026), *Quadratic Asynchronous DKG from Plain Setup*, ePrint 2026/1159; Ek et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/457.

title: One-round DKG without application-dangerous key bias
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: When can a one-round distributed key generation protocol that permits additive key-shift freedom be considered harmless, and can we achieve the stronger unbiasedness that some applications demand without falling back on expensive multi-round interaction?
status: The current frontier is a tradeoff: Janus (Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892) distinguishes a one-round key-shift-permitting variant from two-round unbiased key generation, leaving the gap between them open.
solved_when: A precise characterization exists of which applications tolerate additive key-shift freedom in one-round DKG, together with a one-round (or comparably round-efficient) protocol achieving the stronger unbiasedness where required.
why: Without this, an efficient one-round DKG variant could silently violate the security assumptions of a downstream application that depends on unbiased keys.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Erasure-free DKG with compact public blame
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can a distributed key generation protocol achieve erasure-free adaptive security with proactive refresh and compact, transferable public blame, at performance comparable to efficient erasure-assuming constructions?
status: This is a frontier combination problem. Janus reports 259-byte public blame certificates and refresh, while erasure-free UC constructions provide another frontier point; no construction is known to combine both.
solved_when: A DKG protocol is proven erasure-free and adaptively secure (in the UC sense), supports proactive refresh, produces compact transferable blame certificates, and matches the efficiency of erasure-assuming constructions (e.g., on the order of Janus's 259-byte blame certificates while remaining erasure-free).
why: It would make accountability independent of unverifiable deletion, so parties can be blamed for misbehavior without assuming anyone securely erased state.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892; Ek et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/457.

title: Thousand-party adaptive DKG under active WAN faults
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can a distributed key-generation protocol actually run at committee sizes around a thousand participants spread across wide-area networks while an adversary is actively interfering? The goal is an experimental demonstration of adaptive DKG for at least 1,000 geographically distributed participants tolerating Byzantine behavior, heterogeneous bandwidth, and node restarts, with tail latency honestly reported.
status: This is currently a proposed evidence target with no demonstration at the target scale. The closest evidence is Janus, which reports experiments through 512 nodes and approximately 310 ms for a sixteen-node intercontinental configuration (Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892).
solved_when: A working experimental system completes adaptive DKG among at least 1,000 geographically distributed participants under Byzantine faults, heterogeneous bandwidth, and restarts, and reports the resulting tail latency.
why: It tests whether large committees remain deployable under active attack — the regime where real threshold-cryptosystem deployments would have to operate, not just the small-lab setting.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Succinct VSS for changing weighted access policies
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can verifiable secret sharing be extended to weighted and general access structures whose policies change over time, so that verification remains compact and policy updates cost less than re-sharing from scratch?
status: Computational VSS for general access structures and tunable packed PVSS already exist (Atapoor et al. (2025), *On Computational VSS for General Access Structures*, ePrint 2025/2001; Atapoor et al. (2025/2026), *Batched and Packed (Publicly) Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/2018); supporting changing structures with compact verification and cheap updates remains a frontier extension.
solved_when: A VSS scheme for changing weighted/general access structures exists in which public verification is compact and each policy update is cheaper than rebuilding every share.
why: Real organizations rarely have uniform thresholds; weighted access structures model them faithfully, and cheap updates make the machinery practical when membership or weights shift.
key_works: Atapoor et al. (2025), *On Computational VSS for General Access Structures*, ePrint 2025/2001; Atapoor et al. (2025/2026), *Batched and Packed (Publicly) Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/2018.

title: Public certification of structured key distributions
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
