open: When multiple parties jointly generate an FHE secret key with sparse or other structured components, can they prove — in a way anyone can verify — that the resulting key is actually distributed according to the intended structured distribution, rather than only showing that each contribution has the right algebraic shape? Formally: construct a public, verifiable certificate that a distributedly sampled sparse/structured secret follows the target joint distribution.
status: This is a frontier extension of recent efficient sparse threshold-CKKS sampling and DKG work (Min et al., 2025/2026, *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057), which achieves efficient jointly generated sparse secrets but verifies contributions only via algebraic formatting checks, not their distribution.
solved_when: A jointly executed DKG or secret-sharing protocol for sparse/structured FHE secrets is accompanied by a publicly checkable proof that the output key's distribution matches the required (sparse/structured) distribution, with security against malicious participants who attempt to bias the distribution — beyond merely enforcing format checks on individual contributions.
why: Without distributional certification, a malicious coalition can bias the generated key toward a degenerate distribution while still passing algebraic format checks, silently degrading concrete security of the threshold-FHE deployment.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Batch DKG without cross-key compromise
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can a large batch of threshold keys be generated in an amortized protocol whose shared randomness, commitments, and preprocessing are reused across keys, with a proof that this reuse creates no exploitable correlation among the secrets and lets no compromise of some keys leak or propagate to others?
status: The area is at the design frontier: fast individual DKG and refresh protocols exist, but they do not justify arbitrary cross-key reuse of randomness or preprocessing. Key works include Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892, and Ek et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/457; related directions are multi-user security and correlated-randomness extraction.
solved_when: A batch DKG protocol exists that amortizes generation of many threshold keys, reusing randomness, commitments, and preprocessing, together with a proof that secrets remain uncorrelated and compromise of any subset of keys cannot propagate to the remaining keys.
why: Large custody and credential services need to generate many threshold keys; without cross-key security guarantees, efficiency gains from amortization would open the door to correlated-secret and cross-key compromise attacks.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892; Ek et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/457.

title: Verifiable registration for silent-setup systems
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can silent-setup threshold systems be made to tolerate realistic registration behavior — malformed keys, duplicate identities, and changing membership — with minimal, explicitly auditable registration assumptions? In other words, which registration assumptions are actually necessary, and how small can they be made while preserving security?
status: This is currently a design target. Existing silent-setup constructions remove interactive setup, but not necessarily the underlying public-key infrastructure or registration assumptions; the reference point is Bormet et al. (2025/2026), *BEAST-MEV: Batched Threshold Encryption with Silent Setup for MEV prevention*, ePrint 2025/1419.
solved_when: A silent-setup threshold system design exists in which the registration assumptions (key validity, identity uniqueness, membership churn) are formally stated, minimized, and audited, with explicit handling of malformed keys, duplicate identities, and changing membership.
why: It prevents decentralization claims from silently hiding trust in the enrollment process, which would otherwise undermine the core benefit of removing interactive setup.
key_works: Bormet et al. (2025/2026), *BEAST-MEV: Batched Threshold Encryption with Silent Setup for MEV prevention*, ePrint 2025/1419.

title: Linear-cost MPC at vanishing honest-majority gap
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: What is the true cost of secure multiparty computation that tolerates a corruption fraction arbitrarily close to one half, while keeping total arithmetic computation and communication linear in the circuit size? More precisely, can linear-cost MPC be pushed from the regime \(t<(1/2-\varepsilon)n\) with a fixed positive gap to one where the honest-majority gap vanishes?
status: Frontier refinement. The 2026 CRT construction of Bienstock, Escudero, and Polychroniadou (*Actively Secure MPC with O(|C|) Computation and Communication via CRT*, ePrint 2026/1270) achieves linear computation and communication, but only for \(t<(1/2-\varepsilon)n\) with a fixed positive gap. Whether the gap can be made to vanish at linear cost remains open.
solved_when: A construction (or a matching lower bound) is given for MPC with total computation and communication \(O(|C|)\) that remains secure for corruption thresholds approaching \(t < n/2\) with arbitrarily small (vanishing) gap \(\varepsilon\).
why: It quantifies the price of using nearly all of the available corruption tolerance: a solution tells us whether squeezing out the last bit of honest majority can be done for free, or whether linear cost is fundamentally tied to leaving a fixed slack.
key_works: Bienstock, Escudero, and Polychroniadou (2026), *Actively Secure MPC with O(|C|) Computation and Communication via CRT*, ePrint 2026/1270.

title: Practical constant-bit Boolean MPC
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: Can constant-communication Boolean MPC be turned into implementations that are actually competitive on real Boolean workloads, with explicit setup, finite-size constants, and measured behavior under malicious faults?
status: This is an engineering frontier: constant communication per Boolean gate already has a 2026 construction (Zeng, Yang, Feng, and Zhang (2026), *Unconditionally Secure MPC for Boolean Circuits with Constant Communication*, ePrint 2026/1194), but no competitive implementation with explicit setup, finite-size constants, and malicious-fault measurements exists.
solved_when: A publicly described implementation of constant-communication Boolean MPC reports explicit setup assumptions, finite-size constants, and malicious-fault measurements, and is competitive with existing practical Boolean MPC on realistic workloads.
why: It determines whether the asymptotic communication gains translate into real benefits for Boolean workloads, rather than remaining a purely theoretical improvement.
key_works: Zeng, Yang, Feng, and Zhang (2026), *Unconditionally Secure MPC for Boolean Circuits with Constant Communication*, ePrint 2026/1194.

title: Irregular workloads at optimal statistical-MPC resilience
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: Can the efficiency guarantees of statistical MPC with packed secret sharing be extended beyond regular, SIMD-style computation — achieving constant communication overhead and depth-proportional rounds at \(n=3t+1\) for sufficiently general irregular workloads, without most packed slots going to waste?
status: This is a frontier extension of known techniques. The cited statistical-MPC construction (Choudhury, Damgård, Patil, and Patra, 2025/2026, *Statistical MPC with a Constant Communication Overhead*, ePrint 2025/1555) achieves constant communication overhead and depth-proportional rounds at \(n=3t+1\) for SIMD computation; extending these properties to irregular workloads without wasting most packed slots remains open.
solved_when: A construction is given that, at \(n=3t+1\), handles sufficiently general irregular workloads with constant communication overhead and round complexity proportional to circuit depth, while maintaining nontrivial slot utilization (i.e., not wasting most packed slots).
why: It would extend the throughput benefits of packing from uniform, data-parallel batches to realistic irregular computations, where packing is currently of little use.
key_works: Choudhury, Damgård, Patil, and Patra (2025/2026), *Statistical MPC with a Constant Communication Overhead*, ePrint 2025/1555.

title: Tight subquadratic MPC startup tradeoffs
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: What is the optimal communication cost of information-theoretic MPC when measured jointly against the number of participants, the number of input owners, and the size and depth of the circuit being evaluated — specifically in the regimes where subquadratic communication is achievable?
status: Frontier problem. Bienstock, Efron, and Yeo (2026), *Breaking the n² Barrier: Information-Theoretic MPC with Sub-Quadratic Communication* (ePrint 2026/2311), breaks the \(n^2\) communication barrier under specific input-owner and circuit conditions and establishes relevant limitations.
solved_when: A characterization of optimal communication as a function of participant count, input-owner count, circuit size, and depth is established, matching the subquadratic regimes identified in the 2026 barrier-breaking work and proving the corresponding limitations tight.
why: It separates the regimes where MPC scales from those blocked by input dissemination, telling us which large-participant settings admit feasible protocols.
key_works: Bienstock, Efron, and Yeo (2026), *Breaking the n² Barrier: Information-Theoretic MPC with Sub-Quadratic Communication*, ePrint 2026/2311.

title: Total-cost YOSO MPC
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: Can "you only speak once" MPC retain its cheap online phase once every real-world cost — preprocessing, anonymous message delivery, state destruction, and recovery from failures — is charged to the same ledger?
status: This is a frontier implementation target; packed YOSO MPC already achieves online communication independent of committee size in its model (Escudero, Masserova, and Polychroniadou, 2025/2026, *Towards Scalable YOSO MPC via Packed Secret-Sharing*, ePrint 2025/635).
solved_when: A YOSO MPC construction and implementation keeps online communication independent of committee size (as packed YOSO already achieves) while its total cost, including preprocessing, anonymous delivery, state destruction, and failure handling, remains within stated budgets.
why: Without total-cost accounting, an inexpensive online phase can mask prohibitive preparation, making the efficiency claims of YOSO-style protocols misleading in practice.
key_works: Escudero, Masserova, and Polychroniadou (2025/2026), *Towards Scalable YOSO MPC via Packed Secret-Sharing*, ePrint 2025/635.

title: Packing-efficient proactive refresh
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: Can packed secret shares be refreshed proactively at a cost that scales with the portion of the underlying secrets that actually changed, rather than with the entire retained database, while still maintaining meaningful privacy and reconstruction thresholds?
status: This is a frontier combination: packed secret-sharing and proactive protocols each supply different pieces of the construction space, but no existing work combines them into packing-efficient refresh. Related directions include locally repairable codes and incremental distributed storage repair; key works are Atapoor et al. (2025/2026), *Batched and Packed (Publicly) Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/2018, and Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.
solved_when: A proactive refresh protocol for packed shares exists whose cost is proportional to the changed secret state, preserving useful privacy and reconstruction thresholds throughout.
why: It would make continuous compromise recovery affordable for large private databases, where re-refreshing all retained state on every update is the current bottleneck.
key_works: Atapoor et al. (2025/2026), *Batched and Packed (Publicly) Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/2018; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Joint packing, robustness, and public-verification frontier
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: What are the fundamental limits governing how packed secret sharing can trade off many secrets against privacy, robustness, and verifiability? Formally, characterize the optimal tradeoff surface among secrets per sharing, privacy threshold, recovery threshold, public proof size, and Byzantine reconstruction work.
status: The frontier is characterized only partially: Haven++ (Alhaddad, Varia, and Yang, 2025, DOI:10.62056/a0qj5w7sf) and tunable batched/packed PVSS (Atapoor et al., 2025/2026, ePrint 2025/2018) already provide multiple tradeoff points, but no tight joint characterization is known. Related tools include ramp-secret-sharing bounds and coding-theoretic rate regions.
solved_when: A characterization of the joint tradeoff frontier across secrets per sharing, privacy threshold, recovery threshold, public proof size, and Byzantine reconstruction work is established, showing which parameter combinations are achievable and which are impossible.
why: Applications could then select parameters against established limits rather than ad hoc heuristics, knowing exactly what efficiency, privacy, robustness, and verifiability they must give up for each gain.
key_works: Alhaddad, Varia, and Yang (2025), *Haven++*, DOI:10.62056/a0qj5w7sf; Atapoor et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2018.

title: Compact dynamic general-access VSS
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: Can a verifiable secret-sharing scheme for a general access structure be made dynamic, so that when the sharing policy changes only an update proportional to the delta between old and new policies is required, rather than a full reshare from the complete monotone representation?
status: This is a frontier extension of an active construction area: computational VSS for general access structures already has positive results, notably Atapoor, Baghery, Jadoul, and van Leeuwen (2025), *On Computational VSS for General Access Structures*, ePrint 2025/2001. Related directions include dynamic monotone circuits and span-program complexity.
solved_when: An update algorithm exists for computational VSS over general access structures whose cost is bounded by a function of the difference between the old and new policies, not of the full monotone formula/circuit representing either policy.
why: It lets organizations restructure their access policies without wholesale resharing of secrets, making general-access VSS practical under real-world policy churn.
key_works: Atapoor, Baghery, Jadoul, and van Leeuwen (2025), *On Computational VSS for General Access Structures*, ePrint 2025/2001.

title: Packed gadgets robust to probes and faults
subfield: Packed secret sharing and efficiency frontiers
open: Can we build verified gadget compilers that preserve combined probing and fault resilience when composed across realistic arithmetic kernels and hardware fault models?
status: Packed secret sharing with combined resilience already exists — an engineering frontier extension rather than a from-scratch problem — but arbitrary composition and validity under realistic hardware fault models remain open. Key work: Faust, Orlt, Wirschem, and Zhao (2025), *All-You-Can-Compute: Packed Secret Sharing for Combined Resilience*, DOI:10.46586/tches.v2025.i2.420-459.
solved_when: Gadget compilers exist that provably maintain combined probing and fault resilience under arbitrary composition over realistic arithmetic kernels and hardware fault models, with verification of that preservation.
why: It would connect distributed cryptography with implementations under physical attack, giving packed-sharing techniques a sound footing on real hardware.
key_works: Faust, Orlt, Wirschem, and Zhao (2025), *All-You-Can-Compute: Packed Secret Sharing for Combined Resilience*, DOI:10.46586/tches.v2025.i2.420-459.

title: Implementing precise asynchronous proactive models
open: Can we build an asynchronous proactive secret-sharing system whose implementation carries explicit accounting of corruptions, and verify that its runtime epoch behavior conforms to the chosen formal model?
status: This is an engineering frontier. The 2026 hierarchy (Blum et al. (2026), *On the (Im)possibility of Asynchronous Proactive Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2026/2018) supplies tight feasibility results for its models, so those bounds are not themselves open here.
solved_when: A working implementation of asynchronous proactive sharing with explicit corruption accounting exists, and testing demonstrates that runtime epoch behavior matches the selected formal model.
why: It prevents deployments from assuming a global refresh clock they do not possess, which would silently break the security guarantees of the proactive model.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), *On the (Im)possibility of Asynchronous Proactive Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Lower party-count dependence for perfect proactive MPC
open: Can perfectly secure proactive MPC, with guaranteed output delivery against the usual mobile-adversary corruption model, be achieved with a substantially smaller polynomial dependence of communication on the committee size? Formally, improve upon the current polynomial growth in n while preserving both perfect security and output delivery.
status: The frontier is set by PUFF (Li et al., 2026, *PUFF: Maximally Proactive Security for Free in Perfectly Secure MPC with Guaranteed Output Delivery*, ePrint 2026/509), which achieves O(n^6) communication per gate together with improved layer-dependent round complexity.
solved_when: A perfectly secure proactive MPC protocol with guaranteed output delivery in the same corruption model is exhibited whose per-gate communication is o(n^6), or a matching lower bound showing O(n^6) per gate is unavoidable.
why: Strong proactive guarantees are currently practical only for small committees; taming the party-count dependence would make them feasible for substantially larger committees.
key_works: Li et al. (2026), *PUFF: Maximally Proactive Security for Free in Perfectly Secure MPC with Guaranteed Output Delivery*, ePrint 2026/509.

title: Lower-cost dynamic-committee guaranteed output
open: Can multiparty computation over dynamically changing committees achieve guaranteed output delivery at materially lower communication cost than current constructions, without sacrificing constant rounds within a committee and only limited interaction between committees?
status: Frontier. Rumors MPC (David, Mondal, and Satish, 2025, *Rumors MPC: GOD for Dynamic Committees, Low Communication via Constant-Round Chat*, ePrint 2025/1464) achieves the strong guarantees — guaranteed output delivery for dynamic committees with constant intracommittee rounds and limited intercommittee interaction — but at high polynomial communication costs.
solved_when: A dynamic-committee MPC protocol with guaranteed output delivery is given whose total communication is asymptotically below the high polynomial costs of Rumors MPC, while preserving constant intracommittee round complexity and limited intercommittee interaction.
why: It would make frequent replacement of operators (committee members) affordable in practice, rather than paying the full high-polynomial communication overhead each time the committee changes.
key_works: David, Mondal, and Satish (2025), *Rumors MPC: GOD for Dynamic Committees, Low Communication via Constant-Round Chat*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Cross-protocol mobile-corruption budgets
open: Can a single, well-defined adversary corruption budget be formulated that remains meaningful when a system simultaneously runs distributed key generation, MPC, threshold decryption, and collaborative proving, each with its own refresh schedule? The goal is a formal accounting of mobile-adversary corruption across components that refresh at different times.
status: This is a frontier composition question; asynchronous proactive models show why informal global-epoch accounting is insufficient. Key works include Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018, and Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.
solved_when: A formal cross-protocol corruption-budget definition is given, covering DKG, MPC, threshold decryption, and collaborative proving under differing refresh times, together with a proof (or analysis) that the combined system is secure under this budget even when each component's refresh policy is individually valid.
why: It prevents individually valid refresh policies from failing in combination, which is the concrete failure mode of composed proactive systems.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Minimal-overlap private committee transfer
open: When can a committee running an MPC protocol hand its private state over to a replacement committee that shares almost no members with it, while still proving publicly that the transfer was done correctly and guaranteeing the outputs are delivered? More precisely, characterize and implement private state transfer between minimally overlapping committees with public correctness and explicit output-delivery conditions.
status: This is a frontier refinement of dynamic MPC; feasible overlap is understood to depend on communication, corruption, and surviving-state assumptions. Related directions include Byzantine state transfer and reconfiguration lower bounds. Key works: David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.
solved_when: A characterization exists of when such transfer is feasible — in terms of communication, corruption, and surviving-state assumptions — together with an implemented protocol meeting it, providing public correctness proofs and explicit output-delivery guarantees for minimally overlapping committees.
why: It allows genuine replacement of the original operators: a committee can retire and be succeeded by an almost entirely new set of parties without losing privacy or liveness of the ongoing computation.
key_works: David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Proactive security with imperfect cloud erasure
open: What security guarantees survive when erasure is imperfect — when shares linger in snapshots, swap space, backups, crash dumps, or caches rather than vanishing cleanly — and how can operational erasure procedures be validated against such a model?
status: No solution exists; there is an evidence gap. Secure-erasure assumptions are made explicitly in efficient adaptive DKG (Baecker et al., 2026, ePrint 2026/892; Blum et al., 2026, ePrint 2026/2018), but a malicious machine cannot cryptographically prove it retained no copy.
solved_when: A quantitative model of imperfect erasure exists, together with validated erasure procedures whose guarantees are checked against that model.
why: Without it, share refresh can provide only illusory protection: an adversary may retain stale shares that the refresh was supposed to invalidate.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Refresh while serving concurrent requests
open: Can a long-lived service refresh its private state while continuing to answer requests, so that no request ever mixes incompatible epochs or combines old and new shares unsafely?
status: Currently a design target. Existing refresh protocols lack the additional concurrency and transactional semantics needed in a continuously available service. Related work includes Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018 and Li et al. (2026), *PUFF*, ePrint 2026/509; relevant techniques include read-copy-update verification and online state migration.
solved_when: A refresh protocol exists with explicit concurrency and transactional semantics that maintains continuous availability — no service interruption — and provably prevents requests from observing or combining state across incompatible epochs, while preserving the original privacy guarantees.
why: It eliminates maintenance outages for continuously available services without weakening proactive privacy against mobile adversaries.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018; Li et al. (2026), *PUFF*, ePrint 2026/509.

title: Recovery guarantees with delayed compromise detection
open: Which secrets can still be guaranteed protected when the adversary's compromise of parties is detected — and repaired — only after a delay, rather than immediately, and how should refresh and recovery schedules be optimized to maximize protection under such delayed detection?
status: This is a frontier modeling target; existing corruption-count bounds do not directly describe real incident-detection processes. Related areas include partially observed control and incident-response reliability. Key works: Blum et al. (2026), *On the (Im)possibility of Asynchronous Proactive Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2026/2018.
solved_when: A model of proactive secret sharing with delayed compromise detection is formalized, with a characterization of which secrets remain protected as a function of the detection/repair delay and the refresh schedule, together with an optimized recovery schedule achieving the best achievable guarantee in that model.
why: It makes proactive-security parameters meaningful for operations teams, since real incident-response processes do not follow the idealized corruption-count bounds of current models.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), *On the (Im)possibility of Asynchronous Proactive Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Empirical compromise-process models
open: Can we measure how long real-world compromises last, how breaches correlate across machines, how quickly systems get repaired, and how often operators turn over — well enough to test proactive-security protocols against realistic failure distributions?
status: An evidence gap remains: existing formal mobile-adversary models yield hypotheses about attacker behavior but not empirical failure distributions. Related work includes Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018 and Li et al. (2026), *PUFF*, ePrint 2026/509, along with epidemic compromise models and common-cause reliability estimation.
solved_when: Empirical datasets or measurement studies exist that characterize compromise duration, correlated breaches, repair time, and operator churn, and these distributions are used to evaluate proactive security under realistic conditions.
why: Without such data, committee sizes and refresh frequencies are tuned against hypothetical adversaries; with it, they can be tied to actual, measured risk.
key_works: Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018; Li et al. (2026), *PUFF*, ePrint 2026/509.

title: Durable, exactly-once private admission
open: How can a client's request be bound to exactly one durable execution and one authorized result — surviving retries, coordinator crashes, and reconnection — without ever revealing its private input?
status: A design target. Dumbo-MPC (Su et al., 2024/2025, ePrint 2024/1705) already supplies robust asynchronous MPC-as-a-service foundations, but admission durability remains an application-layer obligation.
solved_when: An admission protocol exists that guarantees each client request executes at most once and returns a single authorized result across coordinator crashes and client reconnection, while leaking nothing about the private input beyond what the authorized result itself reveals.
why: Without it, MPC-as-a-service deployments either duplicate expensive private computations on retry or leave clients with ambiguous completion status; with it, exactly-once semantics carry over from the robust MPC layer to the application layer.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC: Efficient Fully Asynchronous MPC with Optimal Resilience*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Non-reusable preprocessing across crashes
open: Can a preprocessing infrastructure for MPC-as-a-service be built so that randomness material — triples, masks, nonces, and proof randomness — is never consumed twice across crashes, rollbacks, migrations, retries, and concurrent allocation, while keeping auditable allocation metadata? The goal is a construction that enforces single-use of preprocessing material as an invariant rather than relying on implementation discipline.
status: This is currently an engineering target, not a solved problem; practical concurrency vulnerabilities illustrate why protocol-state discipline matters. Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ: On the Practical Security of Malicious MPC Implementations*, ePrint 2025/789 document such weaknesses in real MPC implementations. Related directions include linear resource types and crash-consistent transactional storage.
solved_when: A preprocessing system exists in which triples, masks, nonces, and proof randomness cannot be reused after rollback, migration, retries, or concurrent allocation, and every allocation is recorded in auditable metadata.
why: It prevents recovery paths — the very mechanisms meant to make the service robust — from causing catastrophic reuse of secret-correlated randomness, which can silently break the security of the underlying MPC protocol.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ: On the Practical Security of Malicious MPC Implementations*, ePrint 2025/789.

title: Multi-provider preemptible MPC
open: Can preemption-tolerant MPC be extended so that parties may be replaced across heterogeneous cloud providers, while still preserving the original corruption assumptions during replacement and accounting for the cost of transferring private state? A full answer is a design that lets providers be swapped mid-protocol without weakening the adversary model or hiding state-migration overheads.
status: Frontier extension. ThriftyMPC (Inyangson et al. (2026), *ThriftyMPC: Reducing the Cost of Large-Scale MPC in the Cloud*, ePrint 2026/977) already studies and implements spot-instance tolerance, so basic preemption support is not the gap; the open question is heterogeneous-provider replacement with preserved corruption assumptions and state-transfer accounting.
solved_when: A working MPC design and implementation supports preemption-driven replacement of parties across heterogeneous providers, maintains the protocol's corruption assumptions under replacement, and explicitly accounts for private state-transfer costs.
why: It combines the lower infrastructure costs of preemptible/spot instances with genuine operator diversity, avoiding dependence on a single cloud provider.
key_works: Inyangson et al. (2026), *ThriftyMPC: Reducing the Cost of Large-Scale MPC in the Cloud*, ePrint 2026/977.

title: Verifiable preprocessing supply chains
open: Can we build a preprocessing supply chain in which independent producers supply correlated randomness to computation committees, with verifiable suitability and provenance, and with producer–consumer collusion assumptions made explicit?
status: This is currently a design target. Efficient preprocessing exists (e.g., Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521), but a composable outsourced supply chain is a stronger service; recent systems work such as Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705, moves in this direction.
solved_when: A composable outsourced preprocessing service exists in which committees can verify that supplied material is suitable and trace its provenance, under clearly stated producer–consumer collusion assumptions.
why: It cleanly separates expensive offline computation from online operation, letting committees run MPC-as-a-service without bearing the cost of generating their own preprocessing material.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521; Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Multi-tenant cryptographic runtime isolation
open: Can a cryptographic runtime be safely shared by multiple tenants — jobs that share committees, accelerators, caches, preprocessing pools, and proof infrastructure — with provable isolation even against concurrent malicious tenants?
status: Currently a design target; primitive-level malicious security does not automatically protect a shared runtime. Related work includes Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ*, ePrint 2025/789, and De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*; the broader context is cloud noninterference and shared-resource isolation.
solved_when: A shared-runtime design is proven to isolate tenants across all shared resources (committees, accelerators, caches, preprocessing pools, proof infrastructure), including in the presence of concurrent malicious tenants.
why: It enables economical, shared MPC-as-a-service and preprocessing infrastructure without cross-customer leakage.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ*, ePrint 2025/789; De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*.

title: Privacy-preserving operational observability
open: Can an MPC deployment be made fully observable — stalls, invalid shares, and resource exhaustion all diagnosable — without any telemetry that leaks reconstructable shares, witnesses, sensitive addresses, or private program behavior? In other words, what safe-telemetry design gives operators the diagnostics of a conventional system while the computation itself stays private?
status: This is currently an engineering target rather than a settled problem; existing runtime attacks and benchmarking tools motivate building explicit safe telemetry. Key works: Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Koch, Rotaru, and Rechberger (2025), *b4M: Holistic Benchmarking for MPC*, ePrint 2025/1106.
solved_when: An operational MPC system exposes diagnosis of stalls, invalid shares, and resource exhaustion through telemetry that provably never reveals reconstructable shares, witnesses, sensitive addresses, or private program behavior.
why: Without it, operators must either fly blind or disable privacy to debug, so real deployments become inoperable exactly when they fail; a solution makes secure systems operable without giving up their privacy guarantees during debugging.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Koch, Rotaru, and Rechberger (2025), *b4M: Holistic Benchmarking for MPC*, ePrint 2025/1106.

title: Resource-bounded private checkpointing
open: How can a long-running MPC or FHE computation be paused mid-execution and resumed later without leaking secrets or blowing up resource use? Concretely, is there a checkpointing scheme for large MPC/FHE jobs that bounds memory and storage overhead while preserving consumed-randomness state, authorization, and proof continuity?
status: The current state is a design combination: incremental proving and preemption-tolerant MPC supply components, but not arbitrary cross-stack checkpoint semantics. Key works include Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410, and Inyangson et al. (2026), *ThriftyMPC*, ePrint 2026/977.
solved_when: A checkpointing design exists for large MPC/FHE jobs that achieves bounded memory and storage overhead and preserves consumed-randomness state, authorization, and proof continuity across preemption and recovery.
why: It makes long-running private jobs recoverable on ordinary infrastructure, rather than requiring jobs to run to completion or restart from scratch after failure.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410; Inyangson et al. (2026), *ThriftyMPC*, ePrint 2026/977.

title: Private cancellation with explicit completion semantics
open: How should a multi-party-computation service define and implement client cancellation of private computations so that cancellations are both meaningful and safe? A satisfactory definition must distinguish the states not-admitted, admitted, executed, and output-released, and must show that cancellation races cannot leak secrets or undo irreversible releases.
status: This is currently a design target; no construction is known. The state of the art distinguishes cryptographic protocol abort from application cancellation but does not unify them (Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067; Appan, Heath, and Ren (2026), *Asynchronous MPC with Abort*, ePrint 2026/455).
solved_when: A formal cancellation semantics exists that separates not-admitted, admitted, executed, and output-released states, together with a realization in which cancellation races provably leak no secrets and cannot revoke outputs already released.
why: It gives clients reliable control over long-lived private work, since cryptographic protocol abort and application-level cancellation are not equivalent notions.
key_works: Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067; Appan, Heath, and Ren (2026), *Asynchronous MPC with Abort*, ePrint 2026/455.

title: Hundredfold robust preprocessing improvement
open: Can many-party asynchronous preprocessing be made roughly a hundred times faster on the adversarial path than today's reproduced baselines, while keeping setup costs counted and output guarantees intact? Formally, the target is a 100× throughput improvement over such a baseline without omitting setup or weakening output guarantees.
status: Currently a proposed moonshot with no known solution. The reproduced baseline is Dumbo-MPC (Su et al., 2024/2025, ePrint 2024/1705), which reports 94 triples/second in its pessimistic estimate and 349 optimistically for its 31-party experiment.
solved_when: A preprocessing protocol achieves at least 100× the adversarial-path many-party asynchronous throughput of the reproduced baseline (94 triples/second pessimistic, 349 optimistic, in the 31-party Dumbo-MPC experiment), with setup included in the accounting and output guarantees unchanged.
why: At current rates, preprocessing dominates the cost of useful computation in MPC-as-a-service deployments; a hundredfold gain would shift the bottleneck back to the computation itself.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Cheaper publicly identifiable abort
open: Can the cost of publicly identifiable abort be pushed further down — smaller blame evidence, cheaper verification, and negligible overhead on the normal path — for general outsourced computations, all while clients remain lightweight?
status: This is a frontier optimization problem: publicly identifiable abort for outsourced MPC already admits efficient constructions, e.g., Rivinius (2025), *MPC with Publicly Identifiable Abort from Pseudorandomness and Homomorphic Encryption* (ePrint 2025/258). Related directions include succinct accountability and distributed fraud proofs.
solved_when: A construction is given that reduces public-blame size, verification cost, and normal-path overhead relative to existing efficient constructions for publicly identifiable abort in outsourced MPC, without increasing client-side computational burden.
why: It would make accountability cheap enough that identifiable abort ships as a default in outsourced-computation deployments rather than as an expensive opt-in.
key_works: Rivinius (2025), *MPC with Publicly Identifiable Abort from Pseudorandomness and Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2025/258.

title: Minimal-leakage public blame
open: What is the least a transferable blame certificate must reveal when the offending message itself contains private credentials, secret shares, or hidden program state? More precisely, characterize and minimize the leakage inherent in publicly identifiable abort.
status: This is a frontier refinement of identifiable abort; the current state of the art is Rivinius (2025), *MPC with Publicly Identifiable Abort from Pseudorandomness and Homomorphic Encryption* (ePrint 2025/258), which achieves public identifiability but leaves open how to bound its leakage when offending messages carry secrets.
solved_when: A characterization exists of what any transferable blame certificate necessarily reveals about the offending message, together with a construction attaining that minimum while still identifying the culpable party.
why: It ensures that identification does not become an unrestricted exception to privacy, enabling public accountability without exposing protected data.
key_works: Rivinius (2025), *MPC with Publicly Identifiable Abort from Pseudorandomness and Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2025/258.

title: Blame-to-recovery without full restart
open: Can a multiparty computation protocol that has identified a cheater exclude that party and resume from authenticated private state, instead of restarting from scratch? In other words, can identification be upgraded to recovery, resuming without repeating all preprocessing and evaluation?
status: Currently a design combination question; identification and continued progress are treated as distinct guarantees. Related directions include Byzantine checkpoint repair and incremental fault recovery (Rivinius 2025, ePrint 2025/258; David et al. 2025, *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464).
solved_when: A protocol exists that, upon identifiable abort, excludes the identified cheater and resumes from authenticated private state rather than repeating all preprocessing and evaluation.
why: It stops repeated cheap aborts from forcing repeated expensive work: each malicious abort currently costs the honest parties a full re-run.
key_works: Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258; David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Tight assumptions for blaming nonresponse
open: What is the weakest set of assumptions — on timing, delivery receipts, or external witnesses — under which a protocol can soundly attribute blame for a party's nonresponse? A complete answer should characterize the minimal assumptions and derive matching bounds on the latency and evidence needed for public attribution.
status: This is a frontier classification problem; it explicitly does not ask to distinguish permanent failure from arbitrary delay without additional information. Related areas include failure-detector hierarchies and distributed fault diagnosis; see Appan, Heath, and Ren (2026), *Asynchronous MPC with Abort*, ePrint 2026/455.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the weakest timing, delivery-receipt, or external-witness assumptions that enable sound public attribution of nonresponse, together with matching latency and evidence bounds.
why: It prevents penalty mechanisms from punishing innocent participants who were merely disconnected rather than maliciously silent.
key_works: Appan, Heath, and Ren (2026), *Asynchronous MPC with Abort*, ePrint 2026/455.

title: Bounded adversarial work amplification
open: Can a protocol force an adversary to spend comparable resources to those it imposes on honest parties — bounding the computation, communication, and recovery work induced per unit of adversarial submission cost, even when the malicious traffic is cryptographically valid?
status: Currently a design target; correctness and eventual termination do not by themselves give resource-competitive behavior. Key works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.
solved_when: A protocol and analysis establish explicit bounds on honest computation, communication, and recovery work per unit of adversarial cost, covering cryptographically valid malicious submissions.
why: It would make expensive cryptography (MPC, ZK, FHE-style stacks) resistant to economical denial-of-service attacks, where correctness and termination guarantees alone leave systems exposed.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

title: Cheap admission proofs for encrypted jobs
open: Can a distributed system processing encrypted jobs be given cheap, privacy-preserving admission proofs that reject malformed ciphertexts, invalid shares, and unauthorized relations before any expensive collective computation begins?
status: The current state of the art is a design-level combination of authenticated inputs and verifiable encrypted computation, in the vein of Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648, and Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956; no realized admission-proof construction is known.
solved_when: A construction exists combining authenticated inputs with verifiable encrypted computation such that malformed ciphertexts, invalid shares, and unauthorized relations are rejected by admission checks that are substantially cheaper than the collective work they guard, while preserving privacy.
why: It keeps garbage submissions out of expensive distributed phases, so adversarial flooding cannot waste the system's collective resources.
key_works: Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648; Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Robust fallback without congestion collapse
open: Can we design the switch from an optimistic MPC path to a robust fallback path so that memory stays bounded, resources are allocated fairly, and the system keeps delivering useful throughput even when an adversary deliberately keeps triggering the fallback?
status: This is an engineering design target. Dumbo-MPC (Su et al., 2024/2025, ePrint 2024/1705) supplies both optimistic and pessimistic protocol paths, but its complete congestion behavior remains unmeasured and lacks control mechanisms.
solved_when: A transition design is given between the optimistic and pessimistic protocol paths of Dumbo-MPC that, under sustained adversarial triggering, provably maintains bounded memory, fair resource allocation, and useful throughput — with the congestion behavior validated by measurement and control.
why: Without it, the "safe" fallback becomes the attacker's preferred operating mode: forcing robust-mode operation is itself a denial-of-service.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Enforceable super-rushing runtime contracts
open: Can super-rushing security assumptions be turned into machine-checkable runtime contracts — concrete requirements for event loops, pipelining, batching, and message handlers — that an implementation can be verified against?
status: This is an engineering frontier. Round-preserving compilers for super-rushing secure MPC already exist (Ciampi, Ravi, and Zou, 2026, *Round-Preserving Compilers for Super-Rushing Secure MPC*, ePrint 2026/1745), so the generic existence of such compilers is not the open question; the gap is enforceable, machine-checkable runtime contracts. Related efforts include distributed scheduler verification and happens-before reasoning.
solved_when: A specification formalism exists that expresses super-rushing security as machine-checkable requirements covering event loops, pipelining, batching, and message handlers, together with a demonstrated enforcement (e.g., verification or runtime checking) against it.
why: It would let protocols proved secure in the ideal-round model keep that security when implemented on asynchronous, real-world runtimes.
key_works: Ciampi, Ravi, and Zou (2026), *Round-Preserving Compilers for Super-Rushing Secure MPC*, ePrint 2026/1745.

title: Anonymous, Sybil-resistant computation quotas
open: How can a service enforce per-entitlement quotas on expensive private computations while keeping legitimate requests unlinkable and refusing to treat network identities as proxies for users? Concretely, can anonymous credentials be combined with resource admission control so a user's requests stay uncorrelated, yet no adversary can multiply its quota by spinning up identities?
status: This is currently a design target connecting anonymous credentials to resource admission; related directions include anonymous rate limiting and Sybil-resistant resource allocation, with Coconut (Sonnino et al., 2019, arXiv:1802.07344) and threshold anonymous credentials with silent setup (Garg et al., 2025, ePrint 2025/2042) as key underlying works.
solved_when: A construction exists that enforces per-entitlement limits on expensive private computations without globally linking legitimate requests and without equating network identities with users.
why: It reconciles anonymity with sustainable service operation: without Sybil-resistant quotas, a provider offering anonymous expensive computation is vulnerable to resource exhaustion, while naive rate limiting destroys the privacy the service exists to provide.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Garg et al. (2025), *Threshold Anonymous Credentials with Silent Setup*, ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Lower collateral for fair-with-penalties MPC
open: Can a multiparty computation protocol with financial penalties lock up substantially less collateral, for substantially less time, than current insured-MPC constructions while still guaranteeing that each honest party either receives its authorized output or obtains enforceable compensation?
status: Insured MPC (Baum, David, and Dowsley 2020, *Insured MPC: Efficient Secure Computation with Financial Penalties*, ePrint 2018/942) provides efficient secure computation backed by financial penalties, but compensation is not the same as unconditional cryptographic fairness, and reducing the locked collateral and lock duration remains an open frontier optimization.
solved_when: A penalty-based MPC protocol is exhibited whose locked collateral and lock duration are reduced below the Baum–David–Dowsley (2020) insured MPC baseline, with proofs that every honest party gets its output or enforceable compensation.
why: Current capital requirements confine penalty-secured MPC to well-capitalized participants; cheaper collateral opens these protocols to ordinary parties and makes the fairness-with-penalties approach practical.
key_works: Baum, David, and Dowsley (2020), *Insured MPC: Efficient Secure Computation with Financial Penalties*, ePrint 2018/942.

title: Financial fairness with heterogeneous liquidity
open: Can cryptographic protocols be designed to remain fair for participants whose financial circumstances differ — for example in discount rates, collateral access, borrowing costs, and settlement delays — rather than only for parties that are financially homogeneous? In other words, is there a notion of fairness, and protocols achieving it, that provably accounts for heterogeneous liquidity rather than treating all parties symmetrically?
status: This is a frontier extension of an area where financial fairness already has formal definitions and analyses of existing penalty protocols, notably in Friolo, Massacci, Ngo, and Venturi (2022), *Cryptographic and Financial Fairness*, arXiv:2207.10780.
solved_when: A formal fairness definition is given that explicitly incorporates heterogeneous discount rates, collateral access, borrowing costs, and settlement delays, together with a protocol and proof that it satisfies this definition — so that no class of liquidity-constrained participants is systematically disadvantaged relative to financially stronger ones.
why: Without it, formally symmetric protocols can systematically disadvantage liquidity-constrained users, since equal treatment under unequal financial conditions translates into unequal real outcomes.
key_works: Friolo, Massacci, Ngo, and Venturi (2022), *Cryptographic and Financial Fairness*, arXiv:2207.10780.

title: Collusion deterrence under bounded retaliation
open: How can we deter collusion when attackers can retaliate against defectors and use side payments to hold their coalition together — and can deterrence survive when that retaliation is bounded rather than unlimited? The goal is a practically enforceable mechanism for this setting, with explicit bounds on retaliation and on the damage malicious participants can do.
status: The problem is at the frontier-refinement stage: existing analyses distinguish strong coalitions, exclusive secrets, and bounded versus unbounded retaliation (Gong et al. (2025), *Disincentivize Collusion in Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/446; Gong (2025), *A Note Comparing Three Incentive Designs Against Privacy-Targeted Collusion*, ePrint 2025/2024).
solved_when: A deterrence mechanism is constructed that remains effective against coalitions employing side payments and retaliatory contracts, with stated quantitative bounds on retaliation and malicious participation.
why: Without such mechanisms, designs that look safe because each individual participant is incentivized to behave can still collapse once participants coordinate — individual incentives get mistaken for coalition resistance.
key_works: Gong et al. (2025), *Disincentivize Collusion in Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/446; Gong (2025), *A Note Comparing Three Incentive Designs Against Privacy-Targeted Collusion*, ePrint 2025/2024.

title: Optimal trackable access structures
open: How much robustness against colluding coalitions can a trackable access structure buy for a given size budget? More precisely, determine exact or asymptotically tight size–robustness tradeoffs for trackable access structures beyond the parameter regimes where constructions are currently known.
status: A 2025 frontier combinatorial problem: Gong, Kate, Maji, and Nguyen (2025), *Disincentivize Collusion in Verifiable Secret Sharing* (ePrint 2025/446), connect constructions and bounds to Steiner systems, restricted intersections, and binary codes, via partial Steiner-system packing and extremal constant-weight codes.
solved_when: Matching (or asymptotically tight) upper and lower bounds on the size of trackable access structures are established for parameter regimes outside those covered by existing constructions.
why: It characterizes which coalitions can be disincentivized without inflating the system, telling designers the true cost of collusion deterrence in verifiable secret sharing.
key_works: Gong, Kate, Maji, and Nguyen (2025), *Disincentivize Collusion in Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/446.

title: Efficient secret sharing for near-optimal trackability
open: Can we build secret-sharing schemes for near-optimal trackable access structures that are both compact and efficiently updatable across broad parameter ranges?
status: This is a frontier extension; existing work supplies efficient schemes only for selected close-to-optimal constructions (Gong et al. 2025, *Disincentivize Collusion in Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/446). Related directions include monotone span-program complexity and hypergraph vertex-cover approximation.
solved_when: A construction exists that achieves compact shares and efficient updates for near-optimal trackable access structures over broader parameter ranges than existing selected constructions.
why: It converts combinatorial deterrence guarantees into practical protocols usable in real deployments.
key_works: Gong et al. (2025), *Disincentivize Collusion in Verifiable Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2025/446.

title: Bounding economically useful early-output advantage
open: How much advantage can a party gain by learning an output before honest participants when the value of that output depends on timing and cannot necessarily be restored by later payment? The goal is to quantify — and then minimize — this early-output advantage.
status: This is a frontier fairness refinement; current work distinguishes financial compensation from simultaneous information release as distinct guarantees (Friolo et al. (2022), *Cryptographic and Financial Fairness*, arXiv:2207.10780).
solved_when: A bound on the early-output advantage is established, together with a protocol or mechanism achieving that bound for outputs whose value is time-sensitive.
why: It yields meaningful fairness guarantees for auctions, trading, and other time-sensitive decisions, where late financial compensation is not an adequate remedy.
key_works: Friolo et al. (2022), *Cryptographic and Financial Fairness*, arXiv:2207.10780.

title: Confidential penalty adjudication
open: Can a party prove it is owed a penalty or compensation — without revealing the computation's inputs, its outputs, or any unrelated execution history — in a way that still deters parties from fabricating disputes? Formally, this asks for an adjudication mechanism that is confidential, sound against fabricated claims, and composable with the underlying secure computation.
status: No such mechanism is fully realized; the current state of the art is a design-level combination of publicly identifiable abort and insured computation, drawing on Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258, and Baum et al. (2020), *Insured MPC*, ePrint 2018/942.
solved_when: A construction exists that combines publicly identifiable abort with insured computation, achieving verifiable penalty entitlement while revealing nothing beyond the validity of the claim — no inputs, no sensitive outputs, no unrelated execution history — and preventing fabricated disputes.
why: Without it, dispute resolution forces parties to expose exactly the confidential data the secure computation was designed to protect, so any cheating party can undo confidentiality by simply raising a dispute.
key_works: Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258; Baum et al. (2020), *Insured MPC*, ePrint 2018/942.

title: Penalty guarantees under imperfect settlement
open: Can a ledger-backed penalty mechanism be designed and implemented so that compensation of honest parties still functions when the underlying payment rail misbehaves — under transaction censorship, fee spikes, probabilistic finality, and chain reorganizations — with the residual risks made explicit rather than hidden?
status: Currently a design target. Ledger-backed penalty protocols are known to require a settlement model rather than assumed instant payment, but no such analysis or implementation exists yet. Key works: Baum et al. (2020), *Insured MPC*, ePrint 2018/942; Friolo et al. (2022), arXiv:2207.10780.
solved_when: A compensation scheme is analyzed and implemented under transaction censorship, fee spikes, probabilistic finality, and reorganizations, with an explicit accounting of residual risks; the design rests on a settlement model of the ledger rather than an assumption of instant payment.
why: Without it, fairness guarantees collapse exactly when the payment infrastructure misbehaves; with it, penalties and compensation remain meaningful in realistic ledger conditions.
key_works: Baum et al. (2020), *Insured MPC*, ePrint 2018/942; Friolo et al. (2022), arXiv:2207.10780.

title: Efficient partial fairness for private statistical services
open: Can multiparty computation protocols deliver practical partial fairness — with tolerable latency and abort behavior — for realistic statistical workloads, while realizing the stronger privacy guarantees that partial fairness has been shown to offer?
status: This is a frontier application area. A 2026 analysis by Meisingseth (*On Aborts in Differential Privacy*, ePrint 2026/2059) shows that partial fairness can yield privacy guarantees close to those of full fairness in relevant settings, but no practical construction for statistical workloads with explicit latency and abort bounds yet exists.
solved_when: A partially fair MPC protocol for statistical workloads is constructed with explicit, quantified latency and abort bounds, and it provably achieves the privacy guarantees identified for partial fairness in the 2026 analysis.
why: Full fairness is often unattainable in practice; a solution here would let statistical services achieve privacy close to the full-fairness baseline in exactly those settings, rather than settling for no fairness guarantee at all.
key_works: Meisingseth (2026), *On Aborts in Differential Privacy*, ePrint 2026/2059.

title: End-to-end TLS-to-result provenance
open: Can the entire path from encrypted web data to delivered answer be made verifiable as one chain — so that TLS-origin data, the extraction semantics applied to it, the user's authorization, the private computation over it, and the final output are all bound together cryptographically, with no trusted conversion service bridging the steps?
status: Currently a design extension. TLShare (Santos, Mouris, Xie, de Vega, and Lapets, 2025, *TLShare: Private Authenticated MPC and FHE Inputs Over TLS*, ePrint 2025/1434) already delivers authenticated MPC and FHE inputs over TLS, providing a foundation for this end-to-end chain.
solved_when: A construction exists in which TLS-origin data, extraction semantics, authorization, private computation, and the final output are bound into a single verifiable chain, without reliance on trusted conversion services.
why: It eliminates the manual trust currently required between data provenance and computation, so a verifier need not separately attest the integrity of each hand-off.
key_works: Santos, Mouris, Xie, de Vega, and Lapets (2025), *TLShare: Private Authenticated MPC and FHE Inputs Over TLS*, ePrint 2025/1434.

title: Unambiguous semantic extraction
open: How can a system prove not merely that a TLS-authenticated response contains certain bytes, but that those bytes establish the intended application-level claim? A satisfactory design extracts the intended interpretation of authenticated HTML, JSON, compressed data, localized values, and schema changes, together with whatever context is needed to rule out misleading readings.
status: Currently a design target; it is recognized that authentic bytes do not automatically establish an application-level proposition. Relevant work includes Zhang et al. (2020), *DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS*, arXiv:1909.00938, and Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*; related lines include verified parsers and parser-differential attacks.
solved_when: There exists a construction for which, given an authentic TLS response, the prover commits to a single unambiguous semantic interpretation covering HTML, JSON, compressed data, localized values, and schema changes, and any selective or ambiguous parsing of a genuine response is detected or prevented.
why: Without this, a party holding a genuinely authenticated response can still cherry-pick how it is parsed, making proofs of authenticity compatible with misleading claims about what the data says.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2020), *DECO: Liberating Web Data Using Decentralized Oracles for TLS*, arXiv:1909.00938; Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*.

title: Complete authenticated pagination
open: When a computation runs over a paginated, filtered API response, how can we prove that it consumed every record matching the query rather than a favorable subset? The goal is a completeness proof — under explicit source-completeness assumptions — that covers all relevant pages and filters.
status: Currently a design target; existing response-provenance mechanisms (as in DECO, Zhang et al. 2020, arXiv:1909.00938, and TLShare, Santos et al. 2025, ePrint 2025/1434) authenticate what was returned but do not establish dataset completeness.
solved_when: A proof system exists that authenticates both the provenance of each record and the completeness of the consumed dataset across all pages and filters, so that omitting any matching record is detectable; the source-completeness assumptions under which this holds are explicitly stated.
why: It secures claims about totals — liabilities, holdings, income, eligibility — where proving a cherry-picked subset is not merely weaker but entirely misleading.
key_works: Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434; Zhang et al. (2020), *DECO*, arXiv:1909.00938.

title: Freshness across TLS resumption and replay
open: Can an attestation of a TLS-held web secret be bound not just to the secret itself, but to when and how it was obtained — so that a proof tied to an application challenge, a permitted time window, and the requester's account state cannot be replayed via TLS session resumption or favorable historical responses?
status: This is a design-extension stage problem. Existing TLS provenance constructions, including Little, Roche, and Varia (2026), *Ticket to Hide: Private, Practical Proofs of Provenance for TLS*, ePrint 2026/540, provide authentication of the underlying communication, but application-level freshness is not automatic and must be explicitly enforced. Related threads include replay-resistant authentication and authenticated time.
solved_when: A design exists that binds attestations to application challenges, permitted time windows, and account state, and demonstrably handles TLS resumption, retries, and replay of favorable historical responses without allowing stale attestations to pass as fresh.
why: Without freshness, a web attestation only certifies that something was true at some point in the past, so it cannot support live decisions such as authorization or real-time verification; with it, proofs of provenance become usable for decisions at the moment of presentation.
key_works: Little, Roche, and Varia (2026), *Ticket to Hide: Private, Practical Proofs of Provenance for TLS*, ePrint 2026/540.

title: Robust threshold TLS notaries
open: Can a threshold TLS notary system be built that distributes attestation across committees whose membership changes over time, while still preserving session privacy against the notaries, allowing public blame for misbehaving participants, keeping online interaction efficient, and recovering cleanly when individual notaries fail?
status: This is currently a design-combination problem: existing TLS-oracle protocols do not automatically supply a complete notary lifecycle. The relevant building blocks are Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434, and Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation*, ePrint 2026/892.
solved_when: A complete notary protocol design is specified that simultaneously supports changing committees, session privacy, public blame, efficient online interaction, and recovery from failed notaries — covering the full notary lifecycle rather than isolated components.
why: It removes a single attestation provider as an availability and trust bottleneck for TLS-based oracles.
key_works: Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434; Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Post-quantum hidden-source attestation with public accountability
open: Can a TLS attestation system simultaneously hide which server produced the evidence, survive post-quantum adversaries, aggregate attestations under a robust threshold, and let accountability transfer publicly — all at practical wide-area-network latency?
status: This is a frontier combination not yet achieved. Ticket to Hide (Little, Roche, and Varia, 2026, ePrint 2026/540) already supports post-quantum TLS components and reports under three seconds for a hundred-server anonymity set.
solved_when: A single system combines post-quantum-compatible TLS provenance, hidden source identity, robust threshold attestation, and transferable public accountability while operating at practical WAN latency, matching or beating the reported baseline of under three seconds for a hundred-server anonymity set.
why: It protects both the privacy of the source server and the long-term authenticity of the evidence, so neither anonymity nor accountability has to be sacrificed.
key_works: Little, Roche, and Varia (2026), *Ticket to Hide*, ePrint 2026/540.

title: Mechanically checked TLS-oracle context assumptions
open: Can we mechanically verify that deployed TLS protocol variants actually satisfy the message-format, padding, and AEAD context conditions assumed by their provenance proofs — rather than trusting that they do?
status: This is a frontier implementation target; proxy-oracle security has positive results under specific conditions, not unconditional security for arbitrary application protocols (Luo, Jia, Shen, and Kate (2025), *Proxying Is Enough: Security of Proxying in TLS Oracles and AEAD Context Unforgeability*, ePrint 2024/733).
solved_when: A mechanical verification exists covering the message-format, padding, and AEAD context conditions for deployed protocol variants against the requirements of their provenance proofs.
why: It prevents a sound abstraction from being instantiated unsafely, so zkTLS provenance guarantees hold for real deployments.
key_works: Luo, Jia, Shen, and Kate (2025), *Proxying Is Enough: Security of Proxying in TLS Oracles and AEAD Context Unforgeability*, ePrint 2024/733.

title: Minimal additional trust for real-world truth
open: How can many authenticated but possibly false or correlated statements about the real world be aggregated into claims we can actually trust, under explicitly stated assumptions about source honesty and independence?
status: This remains a frontier systems question; current provenance techniques establish what a source said, not that the statement is true. Key works include Zhang et al. (2020), *DECO*, arXiv:1909.00938, and Luo et al. (2025), ePrint 2024/733; related directions include Byzantine sensor fusion and robust estimation with correlated sources.
solved_when: A framework exists that takes provenance-authenticated source statements as input and produces aggregated real-world claims with explicit, formalized honesty and independence assumptions — not merely transport authenticity.
why: It addresses the actual oracle problem: zkTLS systems like DECO prove what a source said, not that the statement was true, so without this aggregation layer real-world claims rest on unexamined trust in sources.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2020), *DECO*, arXiv:1909.00938; Luo et al. (2025), ePrint 2024/733.

title: Ten-percent-overhead private web attestations
open: Can a TLS-based web oracle add privacy while costing an ordinary page load less than ten percent in median overhead? Formally, achieve <10% median overhead on a declared representative web workload while preserving privacy through authentication, large responses, retries, and unsupported-feature handling.
status: Proposed as a moonshot; modern TLS-oracle protocols already have useful WAN benchmarks, but not against this broad joint target. Key works include Little et al. (2026), *Ticket to Hide*, ePrint 2026/540, and Celi et al. (2025/2026), *DiStefano*, ePrint 2023/1063.
solved_when: A protocol is demonstrated on a declared representative web workload with median overhead below 10%, while privacy is maintained across authentication, large responses, retries, and unsupported-feature handling.
why: It would make authenticated private inputs usable in ordinary browsing rather than only in specialized deployments.
key_works: Little et al. (2026), *Ticket to Hide*, ePrint 2026/540; Celi et al. (2025/2026), *DiStefano*, ePrint 2023/1063.

title: End-to-end adaptively secure FROST custody
open: Can the components of threshold-signature custody — adaptively secure FROST, distributed key generation, durable nonce management, policy authorization, key refresh, and recovery — be composed into a single custody service with one audited security boundary?
status: This is currently a design target. Fully adaptive FROST with identifiable aborts already exists (Baecker et al. (2025/2026), *Fully Adaptive FROST with Identifiable Aborts from AOMDL*, ePrint 2025/1950; Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892), so the core signing primitive is available, but the full composed custody service has not been built.
solved_when: A working custody service exists that integrates adaptive FROST, DKG, durable nonce management, policy authorization, refresh, and recovery within one audited service boundary, with an end-to-end security argument covering the composed system.
why: A secure signing protocol alone is not a custody product; this integration is what converts one into the other.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2025/2026), *Fully Adaptive FROST with Identifiable Aborts from AOMDL*, ePrint 2025/1950; Baecker et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/892.

title: Rollback-safe threshold nonces
open: Can threshold-signing infrastructure be engineered so that nonces and presignatures are never consumed twice, even when processes crash, databases roll back, signers run concurrently, or backups are restored?
status: This is currently an engineering target rather than a solved problem: threshold-signature security assumes correctly maintained protocol state, and no construction meeting the goal is recorded. Related directions include rollback-resistant storage and one-time resource verification; see Baecker et al. (2025/2026), *Fully Adaptive FROST with Identifiable Aborts from AOMDL*, ePrint 2025/1950.
solved_when: A deployment design exists in which, across process crashes, database rollbacks, concurrent signing, and backup restoration, no nonce or presignature is ever reused; every scenario listed in the record is addressed.
why: Operational recovery — a crash, rollback, or backup restore — must not expose the signing key through accidental nonce reuse; threshold-signature security only holds if protocol state is maintained correctly.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2025/2026), *Fully Adaptive FROST with Identifiable Aborts from AOMDL*, ePrint 2025/1950.

title: Private proofs of signing-policy compliance
open: Can a threshold-signature custodian prove that a given signature was produced in compliance with a committed authorization policy — such as who must approve, under what limits, and under what counterparty rules — without revealing those confidential policy details or any unnecessary transaction information?
status: Currently a design-combination problem: existing key protection mechanisms do not establish application-level authorization correctness. Related work includes Baecker et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1950, and Ozdemir and Boneh (2022), *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs*; adjacent directions are proof-carrying authorization and confidential policy evaluation.
solved_when: A construction exists in which a verifier can check compliance of a threshold signature with a committed policy, while the policy's limits, approvers, counterparty rules, and unnecessary transaction details remain hidden; the construction combines threshold signing with a privacy-preserving proof system.
why: It removes the need for trusted policy middleware in custody, so application-level authorization correctness no longer depends on an honest intermediary.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1950; Ozdemir and Boneh (2022), *Experimenting with Collaborative zk-SNARKs*.

title: Lower-bandwidth standard-compatible threshold ML-DSA
open: Can a threshold ML-DSA scheme cut its online communication cost dramatically below the current baseline of roughly 100 KB per party per rejection round, without altering the standard signature format that ordinary verifiers already accept?
status: The state of the art is frontier optimization: Quorus (Bienstock et al., 2025/2026, ePrint 2025/1163) already produces standard-compatible ML-DSA signatures via MPC without changing public-key or signature sizes, but its online communication sits near the cited 100 KB-per-party-per-rejection-round baseline.
solved_when: A multiparty, standard-compatible threshold ML-DSA signing protocol exists whose online communication is substantially below 100 KB per party per rejection round, while still producing signatures that verify under the standard ML-DSA public key and signature sizes and scaling to large parties sets.
why: Bandwidth, not computation, is what makes post-quantum custody impractical on constrained networks; cutting per-party communication brings threshold ML-DSA within reach of real deployments.
key_works: Bienstock et al. (2025/2026), *Quorus: Efficient, Scalable Threshold ML-DSA Signatures from MPC*, ePrint 2025/1163.

title: Standard compatibility plus proactive low-round signing
open: Can a threshold signing scheme verify under the standard, unmodified ML-DSA verification algorithm while still offering efficient proactive key refresh, low online interaction (FROST-like round complexity), public accountability, and finite-party costs competitive with purely lattice-native designs?
status: This is a frontier combination problem: standard-compatible threshold ML-DSA and FROST-like lattice constructions currently represent different design points, with no construction known to unify them. Key works include Bienstock et al. (2025/2026), *Quorus*, ePrint 2025/1163, and Borin et al. (2026), *Hermine: An Efficient Lattice-based FROST-like Threshold Signature*, ePrint 2026/419.
solved_when: A construction exists whose signatures verify under standard ML-DSA verification, supports efficient proactive refresh, achieves low-round online signing with public accountability, and has competitive concrete costs for finite numbers of parties.
why: It removes the current forced trade-off between ecosystem interoperability with the deployed ML-DSA standard and operationally useful threshold-custody features.
key_works: Bienstock et al. (2025/2026), *Quorus*, ePrint 2025/1163; Borin et al. (2026), *Hermine: An Efficient Lattice-based FROST-like Threshold Signature*, ePrint 2026/419.

title: Recovery without a custody superuser
open: Can a threshold custody service replace a lost device or a lost operator through distributed recovery that verifiably cannot bypass ordinary authorization, leaving tamper-evident evidence of what was recovered and by whom? In other words, recovery should require the same distributed authorization as any other operation, plus produce verifiable recovery evidence.
status: Currently a design target; no such construction is known. Any recovery authority must today be included in the threshold service's trust model, which is precisely the gap. Key works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation*, ePrint 2026/892.
solved_when: A recovery design exists in which no recovery authority — or any superuser it controls — can act outside the ordinary threshold authorization policy, and every recovery event yields verifiable evidence of the recovery action.
why: Without it, emergency recovery becomes the easiest takeover path: an attacker who controls the recovery mechanism bypasses the entire threshold custody model.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Cross-domain authorization binding
open: Can we make authorization and signing shares unusable outside the context they were issued for, so that shares minted for one tenant, chain, protocol version, or transaction class cannot be replayed against another?
status: Currently an engineering target rather than a settled construction: the requirement is that the application context be completely bound into signing and approval semantics. Related concerns include cross-protocol attacks and typed authorization tokens; see Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067, and Baecker et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1950.
solved_when: A construction exists in which the full application context (tenant, chain, protocol version, transaction class) is cryptographically bound into the signing and approval semantics, so that no authorization or share validates outside its intended context.
why: Without domain binding, perfectly valid cryptography ends up authorizing the wrong action — e.g., a share approving a benign transaction on one chain being replayed to approve a different action elsewhere.
key_works: Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067; Baecker et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1950.

title: Censorship-resistant signing coordinators
