open: Can a threshold-signing system route authorized signing requests around malicious coordinators, so that a legitimate request is served even when the coordinator tries to suppress it? The goal is robust request routing that avoids duplicate execution, nonce reuse, and leakage of private transaction metadata.
status: Currently a design target; efficient signing with identifiable aborts (e.g., Baecker et al. (2025/2026), *Fully Adaptive FROST with Identifiable Aborts from AOMDL*, ePrint 2025/1950) does not by itself provide robust request routing.
solved_when: A coordinator design exists that routes authorized signing requests despite malicious coordinators, with identifiable aborts, no duplicate execution, no nonce misuse, and no disclosure of private transaction metadata.
why: It removes the coordinator as a centralized availability point in distributed custody, so an attacker cannot censor transactions by attacking coordination alone.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2025/2026), *Fully Adaptive FROST with Identifiable Aborts from AOMDL*, ePrint 2025/1950.

title: Evidence of independent share control
open: How can a threshold-custody deployment demonstrate — without leaking sensitive operational details — that its signing shares and its recovery authority actually live under separate administrative control?
status: Currently an evidence target only; no method exists, and it is recognized that a cryptographic threshold does not by itself prove independent ownership or infrastructure. Related directions include organizational attestation and correlated-failure measurement; see NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, IR 8214C.
solved_when: A reproducible experimental method exists that yields useful, verifiable evidence that signing shares and recovery authority occupy genuinely distinct administrative domains, going beyond the mere presence of a cryptographic threshold.
why: It makes custody decentralization measurable rather than nominal, since a cryptographic threshold alone is not proof of independent ownership or infrastructure.
key_works: NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, IR 8214C.

title: Censorship-auditable sealed-bid clearing
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can a sealed-bid auction be cleared so that every timely accepted bid is provably included in the computation, while losing bids remain hidden and the declared output-delivery guarantee still holds? Formally, the task is to prove correct clearing over the full set of accepted bids, not merely over whatever subset a operator chooses to present.
status: This is currently a design combination of existing primitives: robust MPC and private auctions exist separately, but their correctness guarantees cover only a selectively chosen bid set, which is insufficient for censorship auditability. Key works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705; Baum, David, and Frederiksen (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283.
solved_when: A clearing protocol exists that simultaneously proves correct clearing and inclusion of all timely accepted bids, hides losing bids, and preserves the declared output-delivery guarantee.
why: It prevents invisible bid suppression, where an operator silently excludes bids and no participant can detect the omission.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705; Baum, David, and Frederiksen (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283.

title: Post-quantum weighted, label-free batch decryption
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can weighted batch threshold encryption be built with post-quantum security while dispensing with epoch labels and encryption-time indices, and keeping communication compact for each party? In other words, is there a labeling-free weighted batching scheme whose per-party communication stays small under post-quantum assumptions?
status: The combination is a frontier target: the 2026 weighted constructions of Frolov, Partap, Resnick, and Tas (*Weighted Batch Threshold Encryption with Efficient DKG*, ePrint 2026/2053) achieve strong compactness, but rely on bilinear-group assumptions, leaving the post-quantum, label-free regime open.
solved_when: A weighted batch threshold encryption scheme is constructed that (i) uses no epoch labels or encryption-time indices, (ii) achieves compact per-party communication, and (iii) is proven secure against post-quantum adversaries.
why: It would support private transaction ordering, as in auctions and dark pools, without relying on classical pairing-based cryptography that quantum attackers can break.
key_works: Frolov, Partap, Resnick, and Tas (2026), *Weighted Batch Threshold Encryption with Efficient DKG*, ePrint 2026/2053.

title: Small batch-decryption keys without positional restrictions
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can a batched threshold encryption scheme give committee members small decryption keys while still allowing pending ciphertexts to sit anywhere in the batch and decryption to remain efficiently verifiable? In other words, is the key-size savings of Simple BTE achievable without its restriction on permissible ciphertext positions?
status: The state of the art is a frontier tradeoff: Simple BTE (Polichina 2026) reduces key size, but only via a variant that restricts which positions pending ciphertexts may occupy. No scheme is known that achieves small keys with unrestricted placement; the question sits amid broader work on encryption compactness and storage–flexibility lower bounds.
solved_when: A scheme is exhibited whose committee secret-key storage is reduced (matching, or approaching, the reduction achieved by Simple BTE) while ciphertexts may be placed in unrestricted positions within a batch and verifiable batch decryption remains efficient.
why: A solution removes the current forced choice between censorship resistance (unrestricted ciphertext placement) and storage efficiency, so committees with limited key storage need not accept positional restrictions that enable censorship.
key_works: Policharla (2026), *A Simple Batched Threshold Encryption Scheme*, ePrint 2026/760.

title: Provable private order cancellation
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can a market operator accept, cancel, and replace encrypted orders in a way that preserves confidentiality while making the ordering of each cancellation unambiguous with respect to admission and clearing? Concretely, the design must prevent retroactive cancellation and never reveal order content.
status: This is currently a design target. Existing private matching approaches (e.g., Baum, David, and Frederiksen (2021), *P2DEX: Privacy-Preserving Decentralized Cryptocurrency Exchange*, ePrint 2021/283) do not automatically establish cancellation semantics.
solved_when: A mechanism exists that supports encrypted-order cancellation and replacement with a well-defined ordering relative to admission and clearing, hides order content, and rules out retroactive cancellation.
why: Without sound cancellation semantics, confidential markets cannot be operated in practice; this makes private matching engines operationally usable.
key_works: Baum, David, and Frederiksen (2021), *P2DEX: Privacy-Preserving Decentralized Cryptocurrency Exchange*, ePrint 2021/283.

title: Private cross-venue atomic settlement
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can trades matched privately on one venue be settled atomically across heterogeneous ledgers or custody systems, without exposing the orders to any single settlement agent and without assuming the ledgers reach finality in lockstep?
status: Current designs are combinations of separate pieces: private matching and confidential transfers each solve different parts of settlement, but no unified design handles the cross-venue, heterogeneous-finality setting. Key works include Baum et al. (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283, and Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; related directions are Byzantine atomic commit and heterogeneous finality.
solved_when: A construction exists that privately matches trades and completes confidential cross-venue settlement atomically under heterogeneous finality, with no single settlement agent seeing the orders.
why: It extends private markets beyond isolated venues, allowing confidential trading to operate across the heterogeneous ledgers and custody systems used in practice.
key_works: Baum et al. (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283; Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850.

title: Private collateral without double commitment
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can a party prove that its hidden order is backed by real collateral that has not been pledged anywhere else, without disclosing its total holdings or its trading strategy? Formally, this asks for a proof of global exclusivity of a commitment on top of confidential balances and valid-transfer proofs.
status: Currently a design target. Known techniques for confidential balances and valid transfers do not automatically establish global exclusivity of commitments. Related directions include proofs of liabilities and distributed resource reservation; see Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces: Confidential Token Transfers via MPC and CoSNARKs*, ePrint 2026/850.
solved_when: A construction exists in which hidden orders are verifiably collateralized and demonstrably not simultaneously pledged elsewhere, while revealing neither total holdings nor trading strategy.
why: It would let private markets verify solvency of hidden orders cryptographically, rather than depending on trusted credit exposure.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces: Confidential Token Transfers via MPC and CoSNARKs*, ePrint 2026/850.

title: Residual manipulation after encrypted ordering
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Once transaction contents are encrypted, how much profitable manipulation — through selective release of decrypted transactions, inclusion timing, post-decryption ordering, or coalitions — can still be extracted, and can it be characterized and reduced?
status: This is a frontier mechanism-design question: encrypted mempools protect specified transaction information, but they do not automatically establish complete market fairness. Key works include Bormet et al. (2025/2026), *BEAST-MEV*, ePrint 2025/1419, and Frolov et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2053.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the manipulation strategies that remain feasible for proposers, sequencers, or coalitions despite encrypted ordering, together with a mechanism that measurably reduces the profit available from those strategies.
why: It measures the economic protection encrypted mempools actually deliver, rather than assuming that cryptographic privacy of transaction contents implies market fairness.
key_works: Bormet et al. (2025/2026), *BEAST-MEV*, ePrint 2025/1419; Frolov et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2053.

title: Repeated-market output privacy
subfield: Auctions, dark pools, and encrypted transaction ordering
open: Can a market be run repeatedly so that its legitimate outputs — allocations and prices — leak acceptably little about losing bids, inventory, reserve prices, and participant strategies? Formally, design matching and pricing rules for which the transcript of repeated play remains informative about little beyond the outcomes themselves.
status: This is a frontier mechanism-design question: existing cryptographic approaches, such as Baum et al. (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283, and Friolo et al. (2022), arXiv:2207.10780, hide the execution of the market but not information intentionally released by the market rule. Related work includes differententially private mechanism design and strategic inference.
solved_when: Matching and pricing rules are constructed whose repeated outputs provably reveal acceptably little about losing bids, inventory, reserve prices, and strategies, with an explicit notion of "acceptably little" (e.g., a formal privacy guarantee) satisfied across repeated executions.
why: Cryptographic execution privacy does not help once the market rule itself publishes information; solving this extends economic privacy beyond merely encrypting the order book, protecting participants from strategic inference in repeated interaction.
key_works: Baum et al. (2021), *P2DEX*, ePrint 2021/283; Friolo et al. (2022), arXiv:2207.10780.

title: Fast general private execution without hardware trust
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can general, EVM-compatible confidential smart-contract execution be made fast enough for real use without relying on trusted hardware? Concretely, the goal is publicly auditable, shared-private-state execution sustaining at least 500 transactions per second on declared workloads, with no TEEs.
status: This is a proposed performance target rather than an achieved result. The gcVM system (Yana et al., 2026, *gcVM: Publicly Auditable MPC via Garbled Circuits with Applications to Private EVM-Compatible Computation*, ePrint 2026/170) reports 83 confidential transactions per second; the 500 transactions/second figure is a projection, not a measured result.
solved_when: A publicly auditable, EVM-compatible confidential execution system without TEEs sustains at least 500 transactions per second on the declared workloads.
why: Achieving this would make general private applications practical beyond simple transfers.
key_works: Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM: Publicly Auditable MPC via Garbled Circuits with Applications to Private EVM-Compatible Computation*, ePrint 2026/170.

title: Private-state data availability
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: When a private smart contract's state is secret-shared across parties, how can we ensure that enough valid shares of that state remain recoverable so authorized parties can continue executing the contract — without ever publishing the private state or trusting a single archive to hold it?
status: Currently a design target only; it is known that a valid state-transition proof does not establish continued availability of the state it commits to. Related directions include data-availability sampling and verifiable distributed storage. Key works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Alhaddad et al. (2025), *Haven++*, DOI:10.62056/a0qj5w7sf.
solved_when: A scheme exists in which, even if some shares or holders fail or withhold, authorized parties can always recover sufficiently many valid shares to continue the contract, with no single trusted archive and no exposure of private state beyond authorized shares.
why: It prevents valid private contracts from becoming permanently frozen simply because their state, while correctly committed by a valid state-transition proof, is no longer available to continue execution.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Alhaddad et al. (2025), *Haven++*, DOI:10.62056/a0qj5w7sf.

title: Recovering the unique finalized private state
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: After a crash or committee reconfiguration, how can a private smart contract system restore exactly the last finalized private state — with proof that the recovered commitment is consistent and immunity to stale or forked recovery snapshots?
status: Currently a design target; confidential-state commitments and committee reconfiguration are in place, but an explicit recovery composition has yet to be specified.
solved_when: An explicit recovery composition exists that restores the unique last finalized private state from confidential-state commitments under committee reconfiguration, with verifiable commitment consistency and protection against stale or forked snapshots.
why: Without it, private contracts lose durability across operational incidents; with it, confidential state survives failures and committee changes.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Atomic private calls across committees
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can transactions that read and write private state controlled by different committees be executed atomically, without leaking intermediate values, weakening either committee's trust policy, or leaving partial commits?
status: The problem is a frontier system combination; a secure single-committee private state machine does not supply arbitrary cross-committee atomicity. Related threads include Byzantine atomic commit and distributed serializability. Key works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.
solved_when: A protocol exists that executes cross-committee transactions on shared private state with atomic all-or-nothing commits, privacy of intermediate values, and preservation of each committee's existing trust assumptions.
why: It turns isolated single-committee private applications into composable ones, allowing private smart contracts to span jurisdictions or trust domains instead of remaining silos.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Conflict-private transaction concurrency
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can transactions operating on secret shared state be executed in parallel while preserving serializability and keeping the underlying conflict structure — which records, accounts, or contracts touch each other — hidden from all observers?
status: The current frontier is designs that go beyond correct but strictly sequential private execution; cited works are Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM*, ePrint 2026/170, and Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039; related directions include oblivious concurrency control and private conflict graphs.
solved_when: A concrete scheme exists that executes private transactions concurrently, proves serializability of the resulting schedule, and reveals no information about which transactions conflict or on which shared objects, with throughput exceeding sequential private execution.
why: It raises throughput of private smart contracts without leaking the application’s access graph, which is itself sensitive metadata in a conflict-private system.
key_works: Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM*, ePrint 2026/170; Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039.

title: Verifiable private upgrades
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can a private smart-contract system be upgraded — new code, new representations of shared private state — while users can verify that the change was authorized, that the contract's invariants still hold, and that their existing rights survive the migration? In other words, can we produce proofs not merely that fixed code executed correctly, but that a change to that code is safe?
status: Currently a design target. State of the art supports proving correct execution of fixed code (e.g., Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM*, ePrint 2026/170; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410), but proving that a change to that code is safe remains strictly harder and unsolved.
solved_when: An upgrade mechanism exists that carries machine-checkable proofs of authorization, invariant preservation across the new code and state representation, and preservation of every existing user's rights through the migration.
why: It allows contracts to be repaired and evolved without granting administrators unrestricted power over private state, so upgrades stop being an all-or-nothing trust decision.
key_works: Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM*, ePrint 2026/170; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410.

title: Thin-client private applications without trusted gateways
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can a resource-constrained client — a phone or browser — participate in a general private-state application without downloading the private state, building large witnesses itself, or trusting a privileged gateway to relay and verify on its behalf? In other words, is there a design in which thin clients can authenticate their inputs and verify arbitrary private-state transitions, not just specialized ones, with no trusted intermediary?
status: This is a design-extension problem. Lightweight clients exist today only for specialized confidential-transfer protocols; support for general private-state applications remains broader and open. Key works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434.
solved_when: A construction exists in which constrained clients authenticate inputs and verify general private-state transitions while neither downloading private state, constructing large witnesses, nor relying on a trusted privileged relay.
why: It would make private applications usable from ordinary devices, rather than requiring powerful machines or a trusted operator at the network's edge.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces*, ePrint 2026/850; Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434.

title: Ten-thousand-transition private-state services
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can a private-state service sustain 10,000 publicly verifiable private state transitions per second on a specified WAN committee, with proof generation included and active-fault recovery measured as part of the evaluation?
status: This is a proposed moonshot with no known system achieving the target; the closest reported result is Merces (Escudero et al., 2026, *Merces: Confidential Token Transfers via MPC and CoSNARKs*, ePrint 2026/850), which achieves over 300 confidential transfers per second in its benchmark configuration.
solved_when: A system demonstrates 10,000 publicly verifiable private state transitions per second on a specified WAN committee, counting proof generation time, and reports measurements of recovery from active faults.
why: Meeting this target would establish that shared private state can support high-volume applications rather than only low-rate confidential transfers.
key_works: Escudero et al. (2026), *Merces: Confidential Token Transfers via MPC and CoSNARKs*, ePrint 2026/850.

title: Bounded emergency governance for private services
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can a private smart-contract system constrain its own administrators — so that committee replacement, fee changes, policy updates, and emergency interventions are verifiably authorized and bounded in what they may reveal or override?
status: Currently a design target. Cryptographic execution by itself does not automatically constrain governance, so no existing mechanism is known to provide these verifiable, bounded emergency powers.
solved_when: A design exists in which every governance action (committee replacement, fee change, policy update, emergency action) carries verifiable authorization and explicit, enforced limits on what emergency powers can reveal or override.
why: Without bounded governance, administrators can simply undo the trust minimization the cryptography provides, collapsing the system's privacy guarantees back to trust in operators.
key_works: Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067; Garg et al. (2025), *Threshold Anonymous Credentials with Silent Setup*, ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Compact post-quantum verifiable shuffles
open: Can a verifiable shuffle of ElGamal ciphertexts be proven under post-quantum assumptions with proof sizes and prover costs comparable to the best modern compact constructions? Formally, the goal is a shuffle argument whose proof size and prover time match the compact ElGamal-shuffle regime without relying on quantum-broken assumptions.
status: Frontier. The 2026 ElGamal construction of Xue, Lu, and Au (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles for ElGamal Ciphertexts*, ePrint 2026/805, reports a 2.6 KiB proof for \(2^{20}\) ciphertexts, but under its structured-setup model and not post-quantum assumptions.
solved_when: A post-quantum verifiable shuffle exists whose proof size and prover performance match modern compact ElGamal-shuffle proofs — the benchmark being a roughly 2.6 KiB proof for \(2^{20}\) ciphertexts.
why: Without it, publicly auditable mixing breaks the moment anonymous-communication infrastructure migrates to post-quantum assumptions and loses today's compact proofs.
key_works: Xue, Lu, and Au (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles for ElGamal Ciphertexts*, ePrint 2026/805.

title: Transparent compact shuffle proofs
open: Can a compact verifiable shuffle of, say, ElGamal ciphertexts be proved with small proofs and near-linear practical proving work, yet with no structured setup at all? More precisely, can the known logarithmic-size shuffle arguments be made fully transparent, with no trusted or updatable structured reference string?
status: The current frontier is a tradeoff: the logarithmic-size shuffle of Xue, Lu, and Au (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles for ElGamal Ciphertexts* (ePrint 2026/805), relies on an updatable structured reference string; no construction removes structured setup at comparable proof size and proving cost. Related directions include transparent polynomial commitments and proof-size lower bounds.
solved_when: A transparent (setup-free) verifiable shuffle proof is constructed whose proof size remains compact — matching the logarithmic size of the structured-reference-string constructions — with proving work that is practical and near-linear.
why: It removes setup dependencies from auditable mixnets, so anonymity systems can be deployed and verified without establishing or updating a structured common reference string.
key_works: Xue, Lu, and Au (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles for ElGamal Ciphertexts*, ePrint 2026/805.

title: Auditable mixing with traffic-analysis guarantees
open: Can we build a mixing system whose shuffle is verifiably correct while also carrying a quantified anonymity guarantee against traffic analysis under realistic conditions — variable timing, uneven volumes, message retries, and an observer who sees part of the network?
status: Currently a design-combination problem: verified shuffling addresses shuffle correctness, while Loopix-style traffic defenses (Piotrowska et al., 2017, *The Loopix Anonymity System*, arXiv:1703.00536) address traffic analysis, and these strands tackle different attack surfaces (see also Xue et al., 2026, ePrint 2026/805).
solved_when: A combined design exists in which shuffle correctness is proven/verified and the anonymity loss from timing, volume, retry behavior, and partial network observation is quantified within stated budgets.
why: A correct permutation does not hide correlations in surrounding traffic, so verification alone leaves the dominant traffic-analysis attack surface unprotected.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *The Loopix Anonymity System*, arXiv:1703.00536; Xue et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/805.

title: Anonymous accountability for dropped packets
open: Can messages dropped or malformed by malicious mixnet relays be attributed to those relays without exposing who is communicating with whom? In other words, can public blame coexist with sender–receiver unlinkability, under explicit assumptions that separate malicious dropping from ordinary network loss?
status: This is a frontier combination that remains open: existing mixing and public-blame techniques lack a shared leakage and delivery model under which both anonymity and accountability can be reasoned about simultaneously. Key works include Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536, and Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.
solved_when: A scheme (with security proof) exists that attributes maliciously dropped or malformed-forwarded packets to the responsible relay, while preserving sender–receiver anonymity against an adversary within the stated leakage and delivery model that distinguishes relay misbehavior from network loss.
why: It would let mixnets improve availability and hold relays accountable during disputes without sacrificing the anonymity guarantees users rely on.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

title: Proactive mixnet keys with historical anonymity
open: Can the distributed authority running a mixnet refresh its keys proactively, so that an adversary who gradually compromises operators learns nothing about historical communication links beyond an explicitly defined leakage model?
status: This is a frontier problem combining the lifecycle of anonymous communication systems with proactive secret sharing; no construction currently achieves it. Related work includes Loopix (Piotrowska et al., 2017, arXiv:1703.00536) for mixnet-based anonymous communication and Blum et al. (2026, ePrint 2026/2018).
solved_when: A proactive key-refresh protocol for mixnet relay authorities is given, together with a proof that gradual (mobile-adversary) compromise reveals no historical communication patterns except what the stated leakage model permits.
why: It protects archived traffic metadata against sequential compromise of operators, so past anonymity does not decay as machines are breached over time.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Fast robust mixing including preparation
open: Can total maliciously secure asynchronous mixing be made two orders of magnitude faster on a reproduced workload, with the preprocessing on the adverse path included in the accounting rather than treated as free?
status: This is a proposed moonshot with no known progress beyond the target itself; the state of the art is Dumbo-MPC (Su et al., 2024/2025, ePrint 2024/1705), which reports 10–36 minutes of preparation for its 31-party, \(2^{10}\)-input mixing example.
solved_when: On a reproduced workload comparable to Dumbo-MPC's 31-party, \(2^{10}\)-input mixing example, total cost — including adverse-path preprocessing — is reduced by two orders of magnitude relative to the reported 10–36 minutes of preparation.
why: Robust private communication that currently takes tens of minutes to prepare would become responsive enough for interactive use.
key_works: Su et al. (2024/2025), *Dumbo-MPC*, ePrint 2024/1705.

title: Adaptive cover traffic with certified leakage
open: Can cover traffic in a mixnet adapt in real time to load, battery, bandwidth, and latency constraints without leaking enough information through the adaptation itself to undo the anonymity it protects? Formally, the goal is an adaptive traffic-shaping policy whose induced information leakage about user behavior is provably bounded.
status: Fixed traffic-shaping mechanisms, such as those in the Loopix anonymity system (Piotrowska et al. 2017, arXiv:1703.00536), provide a baseline; this is a frontier extension, as adaptive optimization of cover traffic is not free — the adaptation itself can leak information.
solved_when: An adaptive cover-traffic scheme exists that responds to load, battery, bandwidth, and latency constraints and carries a certified bound on the information revealed by the adaptation itself.
why: It would let systems lower the cost of anonymity — in bandwidth, energy, and delay — without silently discarding the anonymity guarantees that cover traffic exists to provide.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *The Loopix Anonymity System*, arXiv:1703.00536.

title: Anonymous authenticated private RPC
open: Can users invoke MPC or FHE services anonymously while still authenticating themselves to those services — hiding which user called which service even though the service enforces credentials, quotas, and abuse controls and returns reliable responses?
status: This remains a design-combination challenge: mixnets, credential systems, and private computation each exist, but their metadata interfaces differ and no integrated construction is on record. Key works include Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536, and Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344.
solved_when: A working design combines mixnet-style transport with anonymous credentials and private computation such that user–service linkage is hidden, credentials and quotas are enforced, responses are delivered reliably, and abuse can be handled — with the metadata interfaces of these components reconciled.
why: It protects service-use metadata — who invoked which computation, when, how often — not just the content of inputs, closing a privacy gap left by encrypted computation alone.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344.

title: Adversarial mixnet replay datasets
open: Can the community obtain public, privacy-respecting trace datasets and replay tools that exercise mixnets under realistic adversarial conditions? Concretely, these should cover churn, congestion, heterogeneous clients, packet dropping, and adaptive observation.
status: No common adversarial benchmark exists; evidence is limited to individual system evaluations, such as those accompanying systems like Loopix (Piotrowska et al. (2017), arXiv:1703.00536) and Compact Verifiable Shuffles (Xue et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/805).
solved_when: A published dataset and replay tooling exist that encompass churn, congestion, heterogeneous clients, packet dropping, and adaptive observation, released in a privacy-respecting form usable as a common adversarial benchmark.
why: It makes availability and anonymity claims from individual system evaluations comparable against a shared adversarial benchmark, closing the current evidence gap.
key_works: Piotrowska et al. (2017), *Loopix*, arXiv:1703.00536; Xue et al. (2026), *Compact Verifiable Shuffles*, ePrint 2026/805.

title: Malicious updatable multiparty PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can multiparty private set intersection support dynamically updated sets with malicious security, while keeping computation proportional to the size of the update and online interaction as low as in the semi-honest setting?
status: The frontier is the 2026 one-pass construction of Zhang et al. (*Multi-Party Private Set Intersection with Optimal Online Round Complexity and Updatability*, ePrint 2026/1774), which achieves optimal online round complexity and updatability but only semi-honest security, with collusion guarantees that depend on the leader.
solved_when: A multiparty updatable PSI protocol is proven maliciously secure and, after a set update, incurs computation proportional to the update size and retains the low (one-pass) online round complexity of the 2026 construction, without its leader-dependent collusion guarantees.
why: It would let mutually distrusting organizations keep collaborating on jointly maintained datasets, since today a malicious leader (or colluding parties) can break privacy of the semi-honest protocol.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), *Multi-Party Private Set Intersection with Optimal Online Round Complexity and Updatability*, ePrint 2026/1774.

title: Leader-independent update-efficient PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can update-efficient multiparty private set intersection be achieved without any privileged leader party, while preserving its favorable communication complexity and resistance to large coalitions? In other words, can the coordinator's special role in updatable PSI be replaced by a leaderless or threshold-style protocol without sacrificing the guarantees that make it useful?
status: The frontier is a refinement question: the cited updatable construction (Zhang et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1774) achieves its strongest collusion guarantee only under the assumption of an honest leader.
solved_when: An update-efficient multiparty PSI construction is given in which no party holds a privileged-leader role, and which retains favorable communication and resistance to large coalitions (matching the collusion guarantees currently achieved only under an honest leader).
why: It removes the need to concentrate trust in the intersection coordinator, so no single coordinating party must be assumed honest for the protocol's strongest collusion guarantees to hold.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1774.

title: Fast PSI updates secure against adaptive input selection
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can a private set intersection scheme support efficient updates — built largely from symmetric-key techniques — that remains secure when the adversary adaptively chooses future updates based on what it has already observed? The goal is a single construction combining malicious security, deletion support, and safety against such adaptively selected updates.
status: This combination is a frontier; adaptive safety is not wholly unconstructed, since Liu et al. (Liu, Miao, Rosulek, Shi, and Wang (2026), *Updatable Private Set Intersection from Symmetric-Key Techniques*, ePrint 2026/438) identify adaptive-update attacks and provide secure variants.
solved_when: A construction exists that simultaneously achieves symmetric-key-heavy update efficiency, malicious security, deletion support, and security against adaptively chosen future updates, with a proof of the combined guarantee.
why: A long-lived PSI service leaks through its update history unless updates are protected against adaptive input selection; without it, clients of a persistent service effectively sacrifice the privacy the base PSI scheme was meant to provide.
key_works: Liu, Miao, Rosulek, Shi, and Wang (2026), *Updatable Private Set Intersection from Symmetric-Key Techniques*, ePrint 2026/438.

title: Enriched PSI without additional cardinality leakage
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can we build maliciously secure enriched private set operations — PSI-sum, circuit-PSI, and set-union — whose communication and computation remain efficient, while leaking nothing about the intersection size beyond what the authorized output already implies?
status: This is a frontier refinement problem: the 2026 shuffled-DOPRF approach of van Baarsen et al. (2026), *Maliciously Secure Shuffled Distributed OPRF with Applications to Private Set Operations* (ePrint 2026/2035), explicitly permits additional intersection-cardinality leakage, leaving the cardinality-hiding variant open.
solved_when: A maliciously secure protocol realizes PSI-sum, circuit-PSI, and set-union functionality with no additional intersection-cardinality leakage beyond what is implied by the authorized output, at efficiency comparable to current malicious PSI constructions.
why: Intersection cardinalities are themselves sensitive relationship counts; hiding them protects participants in applications where the size of the overlap, not just its contents, reveals sensitive information.
key_works: van Baarsen et al. (2026), *Maliciously Secure Shuffled Distributed OPRF with Applications to Private Set Operations*, ePrint 2026/2035.

title: Assumption-conservative post-quantum enriched PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can we build enriched private set operations that remain secure against malicious adversaries while resting only on well-studied post-quantum assumptions? In other words, can the current constructions be instantiated with carefully analyzed post-quantum primitives, together with concrete security reductions and practical parameter sets?
status: This remains a frontier target. The 2026 shuffled-DOPRF work of van Baarsen et al. (ePrint 2026/2035) offers a DDH-based construction and a plausibly post-quantum variant built on Dark-Matter assumptions; relatedly, Liu, Rosulek, and Trieu (2026), *Post-Quantum Private Set Intersection for Small Sets* (ePrint 2026/1985), pursue post-quantum PSI for small sets.
solved_when: An efficient malicious-secure enriched set-operation protocol is given that relies solely on well-analyzed post-quantum primitives, accompanied by concrete reductions and explicit parameter choices.
why: It would give durable, long-term privacy for sensitive institutional data linkage — record matching whose confidentiality survives future quantum adversaries.
key_works: van Baarsen et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2035; Liu, Rosulek, and Trieu (2026), *Post-Quantum Private Set Intersection for Small Sets*, ePrint 2026/1985.

title: Low-bandwidth post-quantum small-set PSI
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can a post-quantum private set intersection protocol for small sets achieve communication within a factor of two of a comparable classical baseline, without weakening the security model? Formally, the target is a 2× communication bound relative to a matched classical PSI scheme.
status: This is a proposed moonshot. Liu, Rosulek, and Trieu (2026) (*Post-Quantum Private Set Intersection for Small Sets*, ePrint 2026/1985) report communication as low as 1.67 KiB per item, with a 16.7× communication penalty in their comparison against classical baselines.
solved_when: A post-quantum small-set PSI protocol is described and its communication cost is shown to be at most 2× that of a matched classical baseline, while retaining the stated security model.
why: Such a protocol would make private contact and credential matching practical on mobile links, where bandwidth is the binding constraint.
key_works: Liu, Rosulek, and Trieu (2026), *Post-Quantum Private Set Intersection for Small Sets*, ePrint 2026/1985.

title: Output-sensitive fuzzy PSI on dense datasets
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can fuzzy private set intersection be computed efficiently on arbitrary dense datasets, with communication and computation that scale with the unavoidable output size and an explicit dependence on the dimension? A satisfactory protocol would remove the structural assumptions — separability or density restrictions — currently needed for efficiency.
status: Frontier. Paik and Seo (2026), *Fuzzy Private Set Intersection from Density-Bounded Assumptions* (ePrint 2026/262), replace separation assumptions with a bounded-collision condition rather than eliminating all structural assumptions.
solved_when: A fuzzy PSI protocol exists for dense, non-separated datasets whose cost is output-sensitive (proportional to the true output size) with explicitly stated dimensional dependence, and which relies on no restrictive separation or density assumption.
why: Real-world inputs such as clustered identifiers and high-dimensional embeddings are dense and poorly separated, so current fuzzy PSI assumptions exclude exactly the datasets practitioners need to match on.
key_works: Paik and Seo (2026), *Fuzzy Private Set Intersection from Density-Bounded Assumptions*, ePrint 2026/262.

title: Publicly auditable authenticated set operations
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can a private set-operation protocol be made publicly auditable, so that anyone can confirm the output was computed from authenticated, committed snapshots and only permitted updates — without learning anything about nonmatching elements?
status: The current state of the art is a design-level combination of malicious set operations and authenticated-input computation; no full construction is established. Key works: van Baarsen et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2035; Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648.
solved_when: A construction exists combining malicious-secure private set operations with authenticated-input computation, such that a public verifier can check provenance and correctness of a result while nonmatching elements remain hidden.
why: It would let outside parties verify private linkage results rather than trusting the computation, enabling auditable record linkage built on authenticated set commitments.
key_works: van Baarsen et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2035; Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Billion-record private linkage under churn
subfield: Private set intersection and enriched private set operations
open: Can we build private set-intersection and enriched set-operation protocols that remain authenticated and maliciously secure while being updated continuously, even at the scale of a billion records? The goal is an updateable design with recovery from churn and explicit, justified budgets for leakage, storage, and network communication.
status: This is a proposed moonshot with no existing construction at the target scale; the cited multiparty baseline (Zhang et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1774) evaluates sets only through \(2^{20}\) items and under a weaker threat model. Related updatable techniques exist (Liu et al. (2026), *Updatable Private Set Intersection from Symmetric-Key Techniques*, ePrint 2026/438), and adjacent work includes external-memory joins and fault-tolerant data processing.
solved_when: A demonstrated protocol supports billion-record datasets with all of the following: malicious security with authentication, updateability (recovery from churn), and explicit leakage, storage, and network budgets.
why: Such a protocol would make industry-wide or national-scale private linkage practical, where current techniques cannot cope with the scale or the churn.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1774; Liu et al. (2026), *Updatable Private Set Intersection from Symmetric-Key Techniques*, ePrint 2026/438.

title: Private query planning without selectivity leakage
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can a query optimizer choose join orders, indexes, partitioning, and predicate pushdown without revealing sensitive cardinalities or selectivities beyond what a negotiated leakage policy permits?
status: This is a frontier compiler target; Conclave (Volgushev et al., 2019, arXiv:1902.06288) demonstrates the benefits of hybrid optimization, but private cost estimation still needs its own leakage guarantees.
solved_when: An optimizer demonstrates hybrid optimization of joins, indexes, partitioning, and pushdown while provably restricting all leakage of cardinalities and selectivities to the agreed leakage policy.
why: Without such guarantees, the cost estimation at the heart of query planning becomes a channel through which protected data leaks.
key_works: Volgushev et al. (2019), *Conclave: Secure Multi-Party Computation on Big Data*, arXiv:1902.06288.

title: Incrementally verifiable private materialized views
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can a secret-shared materialized view be maintained so that each small update — including deletions and ownership changes — costs work proportional to the update and yields an incrementally updatable public proof of correctness?
status: The problem is viewed as a design combination: collaborative incremental verifiable computation (IVC) already supplies the incremental proof machinery, but database-style update semantics — deletions and ownership changes in particular — still need to be integrated on top of it. Key works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410; Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*.
solved_when: A construction is given in which view updates (insertions, deletions, and ownership changes) require update-proportional work rather than full recomputation, with the public proof updated incrementally via collaborative IVC and verified without redoing prior computation.
why: It removes the need to recompute and re-prove an entire shared view after every small change, making verifiable collaborative analytics practical under frequent updates.
key_works: Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/410; Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*.

title: Private streaming joins with bounded state
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can a system execute joins and windowed aggregates over authenticated data streams while keeping its secret state bounded as the stream grows, with well-defined semantics for late-arriving data and proofs that no valid input was silently dropped?
status: Existing work extends private analytics and incremental verification to these settings, but static-query correctness does not specify continuing stream semantics; designs build on systems such as Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*, and Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410.
solved_when: An engineering design exists that performs authenticated streaming joins and windowed aggregates with bounded secret state, explicit late-data semantics, and verifiable completeness.
why: It would enable private monitoring and operational analytics over streams, where unbounded state growth or ambiguous late-data handling makes current approaches impractical.
key_works: Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*; Aldema Tshuva et al. (2026), *Collaborative Incrementally Verifiable Computation*, ePrint 2026/410.

title: Hardware-independent horizontal private analytics
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can private analytics over large data reach the scale that hardware-assisted systems achieve today, without trusting a TEE — or with substantially weakened hardware trust assumptions?
status: This is a frontier, moonshot-level target; the current state of the art, CoVault (De Viti et al., 2025, USENIX Security 2025), explicitly combines server-aided MPC with TEEs to scale analytics within a datacenter — i.e., it still leans on hardware trust.
solved_when: A private analytics system matches the useful scale of hardware-assisted private analytics (e.g., datacenter-scale analysis of personal data) while eliminating or substantially weakening reliance on TEEs.
why: It would reduce dependence on a small set of hardware trust roots, removing a concentrated point of failure and trust from confidential analytics deployments.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data*, USENIX Security 2025.

title: Malicious analytics under heterogeneous trust policies
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can several data owners jointly run an analysis when each trusts a different subset of the operators, with a protocol that simultaneously satisfies every owner's policy instead of degrading to the weakest common one? Formally, this asks for a maliciously secure construction whose security holds with respect to each owner's individual corruption threshold and trusted-set assumption.
status: A frontier extension: heterogeneous-trust optimization already has precedents (Volgushev et al., 2019, *Conclave*, arXiv:1902.06288; Poddar et al., 2021, *Senate*), but combining this with the stronger malicious-security requirement still lacks an explicit construction.
solved_when: An explicit protocol is given that executes joint analytics over owners with heterogeneous trust policies and provably preserves each owner's distinct operator subset and corruption threshold under malicious adversaries, rather than collapsing to the weakest policy.
why: It would let institutions with incompatible governance and compliance requirements — e.g., different regulators or trust domains — still participate in the same collaborative analysis.
key_works: Volgushev et al. (2019), *Conclave*, arXiv:1902.06288; Poddar et al. (2021), *Senate*.

title: Enforceable future-use restrictions after deletion
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can a system enforce that, once a user deletes their data or withdraws consent, all future computation genuinely excludes it — while the design explicitly disclaims impossible promises such as erasing outputs already learned or plaintext maliciously retained out-of-protocol?
status: Currently a design target. It is recognized that meaningful deletion depends on key management, storage, and erasure assumptions. Key works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.
solved_when: An engineered construction is given in which deletion or consent withdrawal provably constrains all subsequent computation under stated key-management, storage, and erasure assumptions, with the excluded guarantees (already-learned outputs, maliciously retained plaintext) explicitly scoped out.
why: It turns data-lifecycle privacy promises into operationally precise, checkable properties rather than aspirational policy language.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*; Blum et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/2018.

title: Crash-consistent private database recovery
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can a large shared database be recovered after a crash without rolling back its privacy-critical metadata — so that access-control state, remaining privacy budgets, consumed randomness, and key epochs are all consistent with the restored data snapshot rather than stale or replayed?
status: This is currently a design target; data confidentiality alone does not establish consistency of all recovery metadata. Key works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*; Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ*, ePrint 2025/789.
solved_when: A recovery procedure exists that restores the database together with access control, privacy budgets, consumed randomness, and key epochs in a mutually consistent state, with no component rolled back relative to the restored snapshot.
why: Without it, restoring from backup silently invalidates the privacy guarantees — e.g., replayed randomness or refreshed budgets let queries exceed their intended privacy limits.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault*; Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ*, ePrint 2025/789.

title: Churn-tolerant publicly verifiable distributed RAM
subfield: Private databases, RAM, and collaborative analytics
open: Can a publicly verifiable, distributed oblivious RAM be made to survive realistic operation — committees being replaced, clients acting concurrently, and machines crashing and recovering — without revealing which addresses are being accessed?
status: The frontier is VDORAM (Qi, Xu, Jia, and Cheng, 2025/2026, ePrint 2025/039), which constructs and implements public verifiability together with distributed obliviousness; churn, concurrency, and recovery remain open.
solved_when: A construction and implementation extends VDORAM-style publicly verifiable distributed ORAM with efficient committee replacement, concurrency, and recovery, while preserving distributed obliviousness of addresses.
why: It would let long-lived private programs actually run in production settings where membership and faults are the norm, rather than only in static, failure-free deployments.
key_works: Qi, Xu, Jia, and Cheng (2025/2026), *VDORAM: Towards a Random Access Machine with Both Public Verifiability and Distributed Obliviousness*, ePrint 2025/039.

title: Proactive private revocation with intermittent clients
open: Can an anonymous-credential system support large-scale private revocation, changing authorities, proactive recovery, and intermittently connected holders all at once, while still bounding how long stale credentials remain acceptable?
status: This is a frontier extension of decentralized real-time private revocation, which already reports subsecond operation over more than one billion credentials (Edalatnejad et al. (2026), *Do You Need a Receipt? Anonymous Credential Revocation at Continental Scale via Private Record Certification*, ePrint 2026/1189); no construction yet handles changing authorities, proactive recovery, and intermittently connected holders with a bound on stale-credential acceptance.
solved_when: A construction combining large-scale private revocation, changing authorities, proactive recovery, and intermittent client connectivity exists, with a proven bound on stale-credential acceptance; the natural performance bar is the subsecond operation over more than one billion credentials already reported for decentralized real-time private revocation.
why: It would make anonymous authorization robust over long lifetimes, where authorities churn, corruptions must be proactively healed, and holders cannot be assumed to be always online.
key_works: Edalatnejad et al. (2026), *Do You Need a Receipt? Anonymous Credential Revocation at Continental Scale via Private Record Certification*, ePrint 2026/1189.

title: Silent-setup credentials beyond generic-group analysis
open: Can the silent-setup paradigm for anonymous credentials — threshold issuance, issuer hiding, constant-size showing, and dynamic verifier policies — be realized under standard, falsifiable assumptions with concrete, non-generic-group security reductions?
status: The current frontier is the cited silent-setup construction of Garg, Garg, Policharla, and Roberts (2025), *Threshold Anonymous Credentials with Silent Setup* (ePrint 2025/2042), which proves security in the generic group model; extending it beyond generic-group analysis remains open.
solved_when: A construction achieving threshold issuance, issuer hiding, constant-size credential showing, and dynamic verifier policies is proved secure under explicit alternative assumptions (beyond the generic group model) with concrete reductions.
why: It removes the reliance of silent-setup credentials on generic-group heuristics, diversifying the foundations of decentralized identity.
key_works: Garg, Garg, Policharla, and Roberts (2025), *Threshold Anonymous Credentials with Silent Setup*, ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Practical post-quantum threshold issuer-hiding credentials
open: Can an anonymous credential system achieve all of post-quantum security, threshold issuance, issuer hiding, and flexible attribute policies, at showing costs a phone can afford?
status: This is a frontier combination problem: no construction delivers the complete post-quantum package. Strong classical threshold-credential constructions, notably Coconut (Sonnino et al., 2019, arXiv:1802.07344), establish useful baselines, and recent work (Garg et al., 2025, ePrint 2025/2042) pushes toward the post-quantum setting; related efforts include lattice-based anonymous credentials and mobile-scale post-quantum proofs.
solved_when: A single construction simultaneously provides post-quantum security, threshold issuance, issuer hiding, and support for flexible policies, with mobile-scale showing costs.
why: Credentials issued today may need to guarantee both identity privacy and authenticity for decades, outlasting the classical hardness assumptions behind current threshold credential systems.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Unlinkable stateful entitlements
open: Can users hold credentials whose rights — spending limits, one-time uses, or per-user quotas — are correctly enforced across multiple independent verifiers, without any globally linkable identifier tying their interactions together?
status: The design frontier; authenticating an unlinkable credential does not itself synchronize consumption of its rights. Key works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189. Related areas include offline electronic cash and anonymous double-use prevention.
solved_when: A scheme exists in which stateful entitlement consumption is synchronized or otherwise correctly enforced across multiple verifiers while preserving unlinkability, i.e., verifiers cannot correlate a user's presentations into a global identity.
why: It enables genuinely anonymous access to scarce or rationed services, where today enforcing quotas seems to force exactly the linkability anonymous credentials are meant to eliminate.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189.

title: Credential issuance from authenticated private evidence
open: Can a credential be issued on the basis of TLS-derived or jointly computed evidence in a way that the issuer learns nothing beyond what the credential attests, while the provenance of that evidence remains verifiable whenever the credential is later shown? The goal is a single construction combining authenticated input transfer with credential issuance, rather than composing them ad hoc.
status: No unified construction exists; the state of the art is a design combination in which authenticated input transfer and threshold credentials supply separate components (Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434; Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042).
solved_when: A construction exists that issues credentials from authenticated private evidence, hides all unnecessary source data from the issuer during issuance, and preserves provenance into later showings, with the construction realized as a working design rather than merely separate components.
why: Today a user must disclose a complete record to obtain a credential asserting a small fact; solving this means minimal credentials without wholesale disclosure of the underlying data.
key_works: Santos et al. (2025), *TLShare*, ePrint 2025/1434; Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Anonymous migration across issuer committees
open: Can an anonymous-credential system replace the set of issuers (rotate an issuer committee) without holders having to reveal who they are, give up unlinkability across the transition, or re-derive their credentials from scratch with the original underlying evidence?
status: This is a design target; nothing deployed achieves it. Threshold issuance schemes such as Coconut (Sonnino et al., 2019, arXiv:1802.07344) and dynamic-participation MPC such as Rumors MPC (David et al., 2025, ePrint 2025/1464) supply building blocks, but neither threshold issuance nor dynamic participation automatically provides holder-preserving migration.
solved_when: A concrete protocol exists in which credential issuance is threshold-based across a committee that can be reconfigured, and holders migrate credentials to the new committee preserving anonymity and unlinkability and without reissuance from original evidence.
why: Without it, users remain permanently dependent on the initial issuer set — a committee that disappears, is compromised, or must be rotated effectively strands every credential it issued.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; David et al. (2025), *Rumors MPC*, ePrint 2025/1464.

title: Non-linkable evidence of issuer misconduct
open: Can a credential holder prove that an issuer has misbehaved — issuing unauthorized, conflicting, or malformed credentials — without revealing which honest holders are involved or exposing anything about their past authentications?
status: This is a frontier combination of anonymous credentials and public accountability; recent work includes Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042, and Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.
solved_when: A construction (with proof of security) exists that publicly demonstrates issuer misconduct while preserving holder anonymity and unlinkability of authentication histories for honest users.
why: It makes credential issuers publicly answerable for abuse without turning honest users into traceable parties, resolving the core tension between accountability and privacy in anonymous credential systems.
key_works: Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042; Rivinius (2025), ePrint 2025/258.

title: Credential recovery without universal impersonation
open: Can we design a credential recovery mechanism that lets holders restore lost credentials through distributed authorities without granting those authorities the power to silently impersonate every holder or link identities across services?
status: Currently a design target; no scheme is known. The core difficulty is that holder recovery inherently introduces authority beyond ordinary issuance and showing. Related efforts include Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344, and NIST (2026), IR 8214C.
solved_when: A concrete credential scheme exists in which distributed recovery restores a holder's credential while introducing no authority capability beyond ordinary issuance and showing — in particular, no universal impersonation and no cross-service identity linking.
why: It reconciles usable identity management with resistance to centralized takeover, so account recovery does not become the backdoor that undoes the privacy guarantees of anonymous credentials.
key_works: Sonnino et al. (2019), *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; NIST (2026), IR 8214C.

title: Adversarial credential-lifecycle benchmarks
open: Can we construct a benchmark suite that evaluates an anonymous-credential ecosystem under adversarial pressure — simultaneous issuance, revocation bursts, authority churn, mobile-holder constraints, and longitudinal linkage attacks — at large population scale? Formally, the goal is a unified dataset and measurement methodology covering all of these dimensions together rather than each in isolation.
status: The field has an evidence gap: billion-credential revocation performance already exists (Edalatnejad et al., 2026, ePrint 2026/1189; Garg et al., 2025, ePrint 2025/2042), but it does not certify an entire credential ecosystem. Related threads include longitudinal reidentification testing and identity workload modeling.
solved_when: A benchmark exists that exercises issuance, revocation bursts, authority churn, mobile constraints, and longitudinal linkage attacks jointly, at population scale large enough to certify the behavior of a full credential ecosystem rather than a single subsystem.
why: It measures the actual privacy and availability that credential holders experience, closing an evidence gap that currently leaves whole-ecosystem guarantees uncertified.
key_works: Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189; Garg et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/2042.

title: Distributed-witness proofs of private training
open: Prove an agreed training procedure over multiple private datasets without centralizing either the data or the complete training witness.
status: Frontier combination: zkDL proves training, while collaborative proving protects distributed witnesses. Key works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Deep Learning Training*, ePrint 2023/1174; Pappas et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/729.
solved_when: A working system jointly proves a training procedure across multiple private datasets such that no single party holds the full witness or the raw data, and any verifier can independently check the resulting proof.
why: It makes collaborative model production independently auditable, so parties who never see each other's data can still certify what was trained and how.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Deep Learning Training*, ePrint 2023/1174; Pappas et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/729.

title: Verifiable private federated LoRA
open: Can efficient zero-knowledge proofs of LoRA fine-tuning be extended to a federated setting where contributors hold private datasets, some may act maliciously, aggregation is authenticated, and distributed proving can recover from participants dropping out?
status: This is a frontier extension of existing work. VeriLoRA (Liao et al., 2025/2026, *VeriLoRA: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models with Verifiable Security via Zero-Knowledge Proofs*, arXiv:2508.21393) already proves LoRA fine-tuning, so basic verifiable fine-tuning is not open.
solved_when: A proof system exists that verifies LoRA fine-tuning across federated private datasets while handling malicious contributors, authenticated aggregation, and recoverable distributed proving.
why: It would allow auditable adaptation of shared models without any participant pooling sensitive data.
key_works: Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models with Verifiable Security via Zero-Knowledge Proofs*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Poisoning resistance beyond valid update constraints
open: Can we bound the damage a malicious participant can cause with training updates that pass every enforced norm, range, and formatting check, without weakening the privacy protections applied to honest updates? Formally, this asks for a guarantee against semantically harmful updates in settings where integrity predicates are satisfied.
status: The frontier is represented by RoFL (Lycklama et al., 2023, arXiv:2107.03311) and EIFFeL (Roy Chowdhury et al., 2022, arXiv:2112.12727), which enforce integrity predicates on updates; however, satisfying a predicate is not equivalent to semantic harmlessness.
solved_when: A proof (or construction with analysis) exists that bounds the damage achievable by any update satisfying all enforced norm, range, and formatting constraints, while preserving the privacy guarantees given to honest updates.
why: Without such a bound, privacy protections can serve as cover for effective model poisoning: a malicious update is hidden by the same mechanisms that protect honest ones.
key_works: Lycklama et al. (2023), *RoFL: Robustness of Secure Federated Learning*, arXiv:2107.03311; Roy Chowdhury et al. (2022), *EIFFeL*, arXiv:2112.12727.

title: Authenticated private training examples
open: Can a training pipeline verify that every training example comes from an authorized source and meets its provenance requirements, without revealing the examples themselves — and while keeping authenticity of data separate from correctness of labels?
status: The state of the art is a design-combination problem: authenticated MPC and training proofs supply different, non-overlapping guarantees. Key works: Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648; Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174.
solved_when: A design exists that jointly provides authentication of training-example origins (authorized sources, provenance requirements satisfied) under privacy of the examples, without conflating authenticity with label correctness; the existing tools (authenticated MPC and training proofs) supply these guarantees only separately, so the criterion is a combination achieving them together.
why: It reduces fabricated-data and unauthorized-data attacks on training pipelines, which current single-guarantee designs cannot block.
key_works: Dutta et al. (2024), *Compute, but Verify*, ePrint 2022/1648; Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174.

title: Verifiable training under numerical nondeterminism
open: Can we formally certify that a training run followed its intended behavior even when it executes on accelerators whose floating-point results are not bit-reproducible? The task is to define and prove a suitable relaxed execution relation that permits numerically nondeterministic steps while still ruling out arbitrary drift in the trained model.
status: This is a frontier extension of existing exact-execution proofs: zkDL (Sun et al., 2025, ePrint 2023/1174) and VeriLoRA (Liao et al., 2025/2026, arXiv:2508.21393) establish verifiable training, but exact execution proofs need a carefully specified relation when production training is numerically nondeterministic. Related directions include numerical reproducibility and approximate program equivalence.
solved_when: A precisely specified execution relation for numerically nondeterministic training exists, together with a verification scheme that certifies compliance with allowed training behavior without requiring bit-identical execution and without permitting unbounded model drift.
why: It would make training verification compatible with real distributed ML, where exact numerical reproducibility across accelerators and schedules is unattainable.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Dropout-robust aggregation with honest privacy accounting
open: Can we build a distributed training aggregation scheme that simultaneously tolerates malicious updates and participant dropouts while still providing a rigorous differential-privacy guarantee whose accounting holds even when participants strategically abort?
status: Currently a frontier combination problem: robust private aggregation and abort-aware differential privacy each address separate portions of the requirement, but no unified treatment is known. Related work includes Roy Chowdhury et al. (2022), *EIFFeL*, arXiv:2112.12727, and Meisingseth (2026), ePrint 2026/2059.
solved_when: A single aggregation protocol is proven to (i) validate/reject malicious updates, (ii) recover from participant dropouts without biasing the privacy noise, and (iii) retain a valid end-to-end privacy bound under strategic aborts, with the accounting stated formally.
why: Without it, privacy accounting in federated training silently breaks under the participation failures and adversarial behavior that occur in practice, so real deployments cannot trust their privacy claims.
key_works: Roy Chowdhury et al. (2022), *EIFFeL*, arXiv:2112.12727; Meisingseth (2026), ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Proving training-data inclusion without revealing records
open: Can a trainer cryptographically prove that every record the training policy required was actually included in training, without exposing the underlying records themselves? In other words, prove completeness of the used dataset with respect to the accepted contribution set, not merely valid execution on whatever subset the operator chose.
status: Currently a design target; existing verifiable-training approaches establish valid training execution but do not establish completeness of the selected dataset. Key works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Dutta et al. (2024), ePrint 2022/1648.
solved_when: A proof system exists that simultaneously verifies (i) valid training execution and (ii) that all required accepted records or contributions were used according to the training policy, while keeping individual records hidden.
why: It closes the gap that allows silent omission of inconvenient data and selective model construction dressed up as compliant training.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Dutta et al. (2024), ePrint 2022/1648.

title: Private model-update ratchets
open: Can we cryptographically bind each deployed model to its authorized training or fine-tuning history, so that rolling back to a disallowed version is impossible — without exposing the model's private parameters?
status: Currently this is a design-combination problem: existing proof systems for training and inference (e.g., Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Sun, Li, and Zhang (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109) do not automatically enforce deployment history, so ratchet-style deployment binding remains unrealized.
solved_when: A deployment scheme exists in which every released model carries an efficiently verifiable proof of its authorized lineage, rollback to unauthorized versions is prevented, and the model parameters remain private throughout.
why: It turns model governance from a discretionary promise into an auditable, mechanically enforced property — training and inference proofs alone do not enforce deployment history.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), *zkDL*, ePrint 2023/1174; Sun, Li, and Zhang (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Both-sided malicious security for verifiable large-model inference
open: Can we build a verifiable inference system for large transformer models that simultaneously protects the client's input, keeps the model itself private, and remains secure even when either the client or the model operator is malicious, while proving that only an authorized model was executed at practical latency?
status: This is a frontier combination problem; private inference, malicious-client protection, and large-model proofs each have strong separate results — e.g., BumbleBee (Lu et al., 2025, ePrint 2023/1678), MUSE (Lehmkuhl et al., 2021, ePrint 2021/1040), and zkLLM (Sun et al., 2024) — but no system unifies all properties.
solved_when: A system exists achieving client-input privacy, model privacy, malicious security against both parties, and proofs of authorized-model execution, all at latency suitable for large transformer inference.
why: It removes the need to trust either party: clients cannot abuse the service or learn the model, and operators cannot deviate from the authorized model or peek at inputs.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE*, ePrint 2021/1040; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*.

title: Inference proofs with numerical fidelity
open: When a private-inference pipeline replaces exact arithmetic with quantization, truncation, polynomial approximations, and encrypted computation, does the resulting model still honor the accuracy or error guarantee promised for the authorized reference model? Formally, show that these transformations jointly preserve a stated error or task-quality bound relative to the reference model.
status: The frontier is that correct cryptographic execution and acceptable model approximation remain separate claims; no existing result combines them. Key works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.
solved_when: A proof establishes that the composition of quantization, truncation, polynomial approximation, and encrypted arithmetic preserves the stated error or task-quality guarantee relative to the authorized reference model.
why: Without such a proof, performance optimizations can silently change the service the client is paying to verify — correct cryptographic execution of a degraded model would still pass.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Private, verifiable autoregressive state
open: Can we build a long-conversation assistant in which the user's prompts, the evolving generated-token state, and internal caches remain private across the whole session, while every continuation is accompanied by a proof of correctness and the system survives crashes mid-conversation?
status: The problem is currently a design extension: private transformer inference and large-model proofs do not automatically provide durable conversational state. Related efforts include Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678, and Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.
solved_when: A working design or implementation provides (i) privacy of prompts, autoregressive token state, and caches across multi-turn conversations, (ii) a verifiable proof for every generated continuation, and (iii) recovery of authenticated conversational state after a crash.
why: Existing private transformer inference and large-model proof systems handle isolated forward passes; without durable, private, verifiable conversational state, they cannot support practical private assistants.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Hiding adaptive model routing and sequence structure
open: When a machine-learning inference is verified privately, how much can an observer learn from the *shape* of the computation itself — sequence lengths, early exits, mixture-of-experts routing, sparsity patterns, and adaptive batching — even when the numerical inputs are hidden? The goal is a theory of leakage from execution structure in private verifiable inference, with bounds on what such metadata reveals.
status: This is a frontier deployment target; it is known that hiding numerical inputs does not automatically hide execution structure.
