Related directions include oblivious sparse computation and traffic-analysis-resistant inference. Key works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.
solved_when: Formal leakage bounds (or obliviousness guarantees) exist for sequence lengths, early exits, mixture-of-experts routing, sparsity, and adaptive batching in private verifiable inference, ideally with constructions achieving those bounds.
why: Execution metadata can reveal user intent or content even when the data itself is protected, so without such bounds private inference leaks exactly the information an adversary wants.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Verifiable private retrieval-augmented generation
open: Can a retrieval-augmented generation system prove to a client that the answers it produces genuinely rest on authorized records from a committed private corpus and on faithful model inference, while hiding the queries, the access patterns, and the confidential model parameters from everyone involved? Formally, this asks for a combined protocol that simultaneously realizes verifiable retrieval from a committed corpus, oblivious access, and verifiable inference over the retrieved records.
status: No unified construction exists; the problem is currently approached as a design combination. Distributed oblivious RAM and model-inference proofs each exist as separate building blocks, via Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039, and Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109, but composing them remains open.
solved_when: A working construction exists that proves authorized retrieval from the committed private corpus and correct use of the retrieved records in inference, while hiding queries, access patterns, and confidential model parameters.
why: It would extend private-inference techniques from closed models to systems grounded in private databases, the setting real RAG deployments actually face.
key_works: Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Private inference bound to live model policy
open: Can a verifiable-inference scheme guarantee that every proof it accepts was produced by an authorized model version, under the currently permitted adapter set and access policy, even while the model is being updated or retried concurrently? Formally, this asks for a binding between each inference result and a freshness- and authorization-attested live model state.
status: Currently a design target. The state of the art is that a valid inference proof does not by itself establish freshness or authorization of the model; relevant systems include Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM* (arXiv:2404.16109) and Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA* (arXiv:2508.21393), with adjacent work in versioned authorization and confidential software supply chains.
solved_when: A design exists in which each accepted inference result provably corresponds to an authorized model version, the permitted adapter set, and the current access policy at execution time, correctly handling concurrent updates and retries; a valid inference proof alone must not suffice when freshness or authorization is absent.
why: It closes the gap that lets a served model be substituted or run stale while clients still verify proofs, which is the remaining trust hole in private inference pipelines.
key_works: Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109; Liao et al. (2025/2026), *VeriLoRA*, arXiv:2508.21393.

title: Output-policy defenses against model extraction
open: Can a model-serving system enforce private query policies that limit how much any client can extract from a model — including model extraction and membership inference — using only the legitimate outputs the client already receives, and without revealing user queries to a trusted monitor?
status: This remains a frontier service problem. Existing malicious-client secure inference (e.g., Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE: Secure Inference Resilient to Malicious Clients*, ePrint 2021/1040) prevents protocol deviations, but does not eliminate all black-box extraction through legitimate outputs. Related directions include black-box model extraction attacks and adaptive query auditing.
solved_when: A defense exists that provably mitigates black-box model extraction and membership inference through legitimate outputs alone, while keeping user queries hidden from any trusted monitor.
why: It protects both the provider's model as an asset and the privacy of the training data behind it.
key_works: Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE: Secure Inference Resilient to Malicious Clients*, ePrint 2021/1040.

title: Jointly private and verifiable inference within tenfold cost
open: Can a large-model inference workload be served with input privacy, model privacy, malicious security, and verifiable execution all at once, while keeping total overhead below ten times the cost of the unprotected computation? Formally, the target is a jointly private and verifiable inference system whose end-to-end cost for a declared large-model workload stays within a 10× factor.
status: This is a proposed moonshot with no system yet meeting the joint-property benchmark; existing results such as Lu et al. (2025) *BumbleBee*, Lehmkuhl et al. (2021) *MUSE*, and Sun et al. (2024) *zkLLM* report isolated inference or proof-kernel timings, which do not establish the combined target. Related directions include accelerator co-design and encrypted numerical optimization.
solved_when: A system demonstrates, for a declared large-model workload, input privacy, model privacy, malicious security, and verifiable execution simultaneously, with total overhead strictly below 10× (measured end-to-end, not from isolated component timings).
why: It would make trust-minimized machine learning competitive as a routine service rather than a premium add-on, since today's compositional costs push such guarantees far out of practical reach.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*; Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE*; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*.

title: Selective-failure-resistant hybrid inference
open: Can a hybrid HE–MPC inference protocol be made resistant to malicious clients who craft ciphertexts, malformed intermediates, or manipulate client-controlled nonlinear steps to induce selective failures? Formally, the goal is a construction whose leakage about the model and input is independent of whether and where such active manipulations cause the computation to abort or deviate.
status: This is a frontier hardening target; malicious-client inference attacks have shown that semi-honest hybrid reasoning is insufficient. Key works include Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE*, ePrint 2021/1040, and Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.
solved_when: A hybrid inference construction exists that withstands malicious ciphertexts, malformed intermediate values, and adversarial client-controlled nonlinear steps without selective-failure leakage — i.e., an explicit protocol with a proof that abort behavior reveals nothing beyond what honest execution reveals.
why: Without it, a malicious client can extract model or input information by observing which malformed inputs make the protocol fail, undermining the privacy guarantees that hybrid inference is supposed to provide.
key_works: Lehmkuhl et al. (2021), *MUSE*, ePrint 2021/1040; Zhou et al. (2025), *ZHE*, ePrint 2025/770.

title: Certified noise under changing distributed authority
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can a long-lived distributed system keep its certified differential-privacy noise guarantees intact as the parties and parameters around it change — through threshold generation, committee refresh, malicious dropout, and private output release?
status: This is a frontier combination problem; no existing work addresses the full setting. Noisette (Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette: Certifying Differential Privacy Mechanisms Efficiently*, ePrint 2026/074) already certifies broad discrete and continuous noise mechanisms, including floating-point privacy effects, but not under changing distributed authority.
solved_when: There exists a construction (with proof) in which the certified noise distribution is preserved across threshold generation, committee refresh, malicious dropout, and private output release.
why: It removes the need for a trusted noise generator in long-lived private services, so no single party must be trusted with the randomness that protects privacy.
key_works: Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette: Certifying Differential Privacy Mechanisms Efficiently*, ePrint 2026/074.

title: Tight privacy composition under adaptive abort-and-retry
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: What is the tight privacy cost of running a differentially private mechanism many times when the adversary may adaptively abort executions, retry them, and choose which outputs are ever observed? A satisfying answer gives lifetime privacy bounds for such adaptive abort-and-retry processes that match what is achievable.
status: This is a frontier extension of known composition results; a 2026 abort analysis (Meisingseth, *On Aborts in Differential Privacy*, ePrint 2026/2059) established important single-execution and functionality-level distinctions, but the repeated, adaptive setting remains open.
solved_when: Tight lifetime privacy bounds are derived for repeated executions under adversarial abort, retry, and output selection — no quantitative budget is specified in the record, so tightness is the criterion.
why: Without such bounds, repeated rejection can bias private releases and the cumulative leakage of adaptive retrying remains unaccounted for.
key_works: Meisingseth (2026), *On Aborts in Differential Privacy*, ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Fork-resistant distributed privacy budgets
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can a distributed system maintain a single, coherent privacy accountant across the whole lifecycle of its query workload — concurrent queries, retries, committee replacement, and restored backups — so that no failure or reconfiguration event resets the budget or spends it twice?
status: Currently a design target. Secure aggregation (e.g., Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio: Private, Robust, and Scalable Computation of Aggregate Statistics*, NSDI 2017) does not automatically provide durable global release governance; related directions include privacy odometers and fork-resistant accounting (Meisingseth (2026), ePrint 2026/2059).
solved_when: A concrete design exists that enforces one global privacy accountant under concurrent queries, retries, committee replacement, and backup restoration, provably preventing any budget reset or double spending.
why: It keeps lifetime privacy promises to data subjects valid even after system failures; without fork-resistance, a restored backup or replaced committee silently reopens spent budget and over-releases.
key_works: Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio: Private, Robust, and Scalable Computation of Aggregate Statistics*, NSDI 2017; Meisingseth (2026), ePrint 2026/2059.

title: Private heterogeneous privacy accounting
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can a privacy-accounting system enforce each contributor's own privacy budget without the system itself learning any contributor's limit, who participated, or whose budget was exhausted when a query is denied? Formally, this asks for mechanisms combining distributed aggregation with private policy enforcement such that heterogeneous per-contributor privacy parameters and rejection events reveal nothing beyond the released output.
status: The current frontier combines distributed aggregation with private policy enforcement; the closest system building blocks are Prio (Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh, 2017) for distributed aggregation and Noisette (Pang et al., 2026, ePrint 2026/074) for private policy enforcement, but their combination into heterogeneous privacy accounting remains open.
solved_when: A construction exists that enforces contributor-specific privacy limits while hiding the limits, participation patterns, and the identity of any contributor whose limit caused a rejection, with a formal proof of both the privacy guarantee and the hiding properties.
why: It would enable collaborations — federated analytics, cross-institution data sharing — where members legitimately demand different protection levels but cannot disclose those levels or their participation to any central party.
key_works: Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio*; Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074.

title: Hidden sensitivity and cohort certificates
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can a privacy mechanism prove that its sensitivity bounds, clipping rules, cohort sizes, and accounting parameters were chosen correctly, without revealing the population statistics those parameters depend on?
status: This is a frontier problem; it is known that correct noise sampling does not justify every parameter supplied to the mechanism. Key works: Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074; Bontekoe, Asghar, and Turkmen (2024), ePrint 2024/1042.
solved_when: There exists a construction that certifies sensitivity bounds, clipping rules, cohort sizes, and accounting parameters while hiding the protected population statistics, with a formal proof that the certification neither leaks those statistics nor validates incorrectly parameterized privacy claims.
why: Correct noise sampling alone does not justify every parameter supplied to a mechanism; without such certificates, proofs can bless privacy claims built on wrong parameters.
key_works: Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074; Bontekoe, Asghar, and Turkmen (2024), ePrint 2024/1042.

title: Authenticated sampling against Sybil participants
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can differential privacy guarantees survive a population of contributors who strategically manipulate participation — duplicating identities, joining and leaving adaptively, or submitting correlated records — and can private eligibility evidence be used to authenticate who counts without erasing utility?
status: This is a frontier combination: authenticated-input verifiable differential privacy exists (Bontekoe, Asghar, and Turkmen (2024), *Efficient Verifiable Differential Privacy with Input Authenticity in the Local and Shuffle Model*, ePrint 2024/1042), but strategic manipulation of participation has yet to be treated explicitly.
solved_when: A privacy mechanism and analysis are given that maintain meaningful privacy and utility under participation manipulation (duplicate identities, adaptive join/leave, correlated submissions), with private eligibility evidence incorporated where appropriate.
why: It prevents privacy guarantees from resting on an unrealistically honest population; without it, real deployments can be undermined by Sybil-style manipulation of the data contributors themselves.
key_works: Bontekoe, Asghar, and Turkmen (2024), *Efficient Verifiable Differential Privacy with Input Authenticity in the Local and Shuffle Model*, ePrint 2024/1042.

title: Auditable robust statistics without exposing outliers
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can a private statistical service prove it computed a robust estimate honestly — including its rejection rules, noise, and approximation error — without revealing which contributors were flagged as outliers or rejected?
status: Currently a design-combination problem: robust private aggregation and certified noise mechanisms each address different layers, but no combined system is known. Key works include Lycklama et al. (2023), *RoFL*, arXiv:2107.03311, and Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074.
solved_when: A working design combines robust private aggregation with certified noise mechanisms so that robustness, rejection, randomness, and approximation error are all auditable while outlier and rejected-contributor identities remain hidden.
why: It makes private statistical services resilient to bad data, so clients can trust aggregate outputs even when some inputs are malicious or corrupted.
key_works: Lycklama et al. (2023), *RoFL*, arXiv:2107.03311; Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074.

title: Public auditing without participation leakage
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can a system publish verifiable aggregate statistics while keeping secret the mere fact of which individuals participated, against leakage through proofs, timing, batch failures, and admission records alike?
status: Remains a design target; what is missing is one unified participation-leakage definition under which public auditability and private aggregation can coexist. Key works: Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio*; Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248.
solved_when: A single formal definition of participation leakage covers all of these channels, together with a construction that achieves public auditability and private aggregation under it.
why: Current protections cover submitted values but not the fact of participation, which traffic analysis or public audit artifacts can expose even when the data itself is private.
key_works: Corrigan-Gibbs and Boneh (2017), *Prio*; Kanjalkar et al. (2021), arXiv:2107.04248.

title: Joint privacy–utility–trust–cost frontiers
subfield: Differential privacy, statistics, and output leakage
open: Can we map, in a reproducible way, the trade-off surface that privacy-preserving systems actually face across privacy loss, statistical accuracy, corruption assumptions, latency, communication, and energy? Concretely, this asks for measured Pareto frontiers over these objectives for representative workloads, rather than isolated single-objective results.
status: This is currently an evidence gap: privacy mechanisms and cryptographic benchmarks typically optimize different objective sets, so no joint frontier exists.
solved_when: Published, reproducible Pareto frontiers covering privacy loss, statistical accuracy, corruption assumptions, latency, communication, and energy for representative workloads.
why: It lets users choose meaningful, jointly achievable guarantees instead of comparing systems on isolated metrics.
key_works: Pang et al. (2026), *Noisette*, ePrint 2026/074; Koch et al. (2025), *b4M*, ePrint 2025/1106.

title: Mechanically verified concurrent MPC runtimes
open: Can we build a concurrent MPC runtime whose message scheduling, MAC checking, shared-state access, and parallel job execution are mechanically verified against the malicious-security proof?
status: Engineering frontier; practical SPDZ attacks (Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ: On the Practical Security of Malicious MPC Implementations*, ePrint 2025/789) demonstrate vulnerabilities at the concurrency boundary.
solved_when: A mechanically verified implementation exists whose concurrency behavior — scheduling, MAC checks, shared state, and concurrent jobs — is proved to refine the malicious-security specification.
why: It makes protocol security survive parallel execution; without it, practical SPDZ attacks demonstrate that the concurrency boundary is exactly where malicious-security guarantees break down in real implementations.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), *Rushing at SPDZ: On the Practical Security of Malicious MPC Implementations*, ePrint 2025/789.

title: Verified delayed-consistency-check optimization
open: Can we build a compiler or verification tool that automatically repositions, batches, or delays consistency checks — using proved dependency conditions — while refusing any transformation that would expose an unchecked adversarial value unsafely?
status: The frontier is the 2026 attacks and fixes of Brüggemann and Schneider (*When Trying to Catch Cheaters Breaks the MPC: Breaking and Fixing Delayed Consistency Checks in Trident, Fantastic Four, SWIFT, and Quad*, ePrint 2026/234); the repaired instances themselves are not listed as still broken.
solved_when: A verified tool exists that performs these check-scheduling transformations automatically and provably rejects any transformation that exposes unchecked adversarial values unsafely.
why: It preserves the performance benefits of delayed and batched checks without reintroducing the security flaws of the kind demonstrated in the 2026 attacks.
key_works: Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), *When Trying to Catch Cheaters Breaks the MPC: Breaking and Fixing Delayed Consistency Checks in Trident, Fantastic Four, SWIFT, and Quad*, ePrint 2026/234.

title: Proof-carrying cryptographic parameters
open: Can every cryptographic parameter choice in a stack carry machine-checkable evidence that it is safe — its security level, noise budget, proof soundness, packing, and allowed conversions — so that a compiled configuration is correct by construction?
status: Currently a design target; no existing mechanism is reported. Independently plausible defaults need not form a safe combined configuration. Related directions include certified configuration synthesis and automated parameter optimization (Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956; Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057).
solved_when: A mechanism exists that attaches machine-checkable evidence to each parameter choice covering security level, noise, proof soundness, packing, and allowed conversions across the stack, and rejects configurations whose individually plausible defaults do not combine safely.
why: It prevents configuration errors from silently invalidating the mathematical guarantees the parameters were chosen for, which is the realistic failure mode when safe-looking defaults are combined across a stack.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956; Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Leakage-certified accelerator kernels
open: Can we validate MPC, FHE, and proof-system accelerators against explicit side-channel models — cache, memory access, contention, and multi-tenant — so that cryptographic privacy survives the hardware layer? Formally, does an accelerator kernel executing privacy-preserving cryptographic workloads satisfy noninterference under these leakage models?
status: This is an experimental frontier; cryptographic privacy does not automatically imply accelerator-level noninterference. Key works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.
solved_when: A validation method exists that checks MPC, FHE, and proof accelerators against explicit cache, memory-access, contention, and multi-tenant side-channel models and establishes accelerator-level noninterference (experimentally, given the problem type).
why: Without it, hardware speedups reopen plaintext leakage channels that the cryptography was designed to close.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), *BumbleBee*, ePrint 2023/1678; Sun et al. (2024), *zkLLM*, arXiv:2404.16109.

title: Cross-platform arithmetic equivalence
open: Can we automatically prove that a cryptographic kernel compiled for an accelerator computes exactly the same function as its CPU counterpart — including lazy reduction, vectorization, overflow, decomposition, and exceptional inputs?
status: Currently an engineering target; proof-friendly arithmetic representations are known to expose specific translation obligations. Related directions include translation validation and verified SIMD compilation (Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956; Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots*).
solved_when: An automated verifier establishes equivalence between CPU and accelerator implementations of cryptographic kernels, covering lazy reduction, vectorization, overflow, decomposition, and exceptional-input behaviors.
why: It would let implementations be ported across hardware platforms without changing ciphertext semantics, so the same cryptographic guarantees hold everywhere.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956; Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots*.

title: Leakage-certified data-dependent control flow
open: Can a compiler automatically choose among oblivious execution, padding, private branching, or explicit declassification — and prove that the result satisfies a user-declared confidentiality contract on leakage?
status: This is a frontier compiler target; general MPC frameworks such as MP-SPDZ (Keller 2020, ePrint 2020/521) provide programming support, but no system automatically certifies the leakage choices of every application. Related directions include information-flow type systems and oblivious compilation.
solved_when: A tool exists that, given a program with data-dependent control flow and a declared confidentiality contract, automatically selects the leakage-mitigation strategy (oblivious execution, padding, private branching, or declassification) and discharges a machine-checkable proof that the contract holds.
why: It removes reliance on manual cryptographic code review, which is the current bottleneck and a recurring source of leakage in MPC applications.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ: A Versatile Framework for Multi-Party Computation*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Adversarial cross-library interoperability
open: Can independent implementations of MPC, FHE, and proof systems interoperate correctly when faced with malformed messages, version mismatches, aborted sessions, and incompatible parameters? The goal is an engineering design achieving robust cross-library interoperability along these adversarial or degenerate paths.
status: Currently an engineering target; successful primitive test vectors are narrower in scope than malicious-path interoperability. Key works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521.
solved_when: Independent MPC, FHE, and proof implementations successfully interoperate under malformed messages, version mismatch, aborted sessions, and incompatible parameters.
why: It enables implementation diversity without creating new protocol seams.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521.

title: Safe fallback when hardware trust fails
open: Can a hybrid TEE–MPC service be designed so that when one hardware trust root fails, the system degrades to an explicitly characterized residual guarantee instead of collapsing? Formalizing what "residual guarantee" and "recovery path" mean in this hybrid setting is itself part of the problem.
status: This remains a frontier architecture question; current hardware-assisted scalability results, including De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data*, USENIX Security 2025, do not by themselves provide assumption-failure recovery.
solved_when: A hybrid TEE–MPC construction is given whose security statement explicitly quantifies the guarantees that survive the failure of one hardware trust root, together with a demonstrated recovery path in that event.
why: It lets systems exploit hardware performance for secure computation without treating hardware trust as an absolute, so compromise of the TEE does not silently void the whole protocol's security.
key_works: De Viti et al. (2025), *CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data*, USENIX Security 2025.

title: Source-to-proof semantic binding
open: How can we establish that the binary actually deployed, the MPC circuit actually evaluated, the relation actually proven, and the program version the user believes they are running all encode the same authorized computation?
status: Currently a design target only. Verifying a circuit does not establish that it faithfully implements the intended source program. Related efforts include Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521; Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039; adjacent areas are verified compilation, reproducible builds, and proof-carrying software.
solved_when: A verified chain exists binding source programs to deployed binaries, compiled MPC circuits, and proof relations, so that verifying the circuit entails verifying faithful implementation of the intended source program.
why: Closes the major gap between cryptographic correctness and application correctness: today a verified proof or circuit says nothing about whether it represents what users authorized.
key_works: Keller (2020), *MP-SPDZ*, ePrint 2020/521; Qi et al. (2025/2026), *VDORAM*, ePrint 2025/039.

title: Security-normalized cross-stack benchmarks
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Can we build benchmarks that let cryptographically dissimilar systems — say MPC, ZK, and FHE stacks — be compared on performance only after their security-relevant parameters have been normalized to a common footing?
status: This is currently an evidence-infrastructure target. The b4M framework of Koch, Rotaru, and Rechberger (2025), *b4M: Holistic Benchmarking for MPC* (ePrint 2025/1106), supplies benchmarking machinery, but cross-paradigm security normalization is broader than what it covers.
solved_when: A benchmark suite or dataset exists that compares systems across paradigms while explicitly normalizing corruption model, output guarantee, setup, quantum assumptions, leakage, precision, and included lifecycle costs.
why: Without such normalization, weaker security guarantees can masquerade as unexplained performance superiority, misleading practitioners choosing between stacks.
key_works: Koch, Rotaru, and Rechberger (2025), *b4M: Holistic Benchmarking for MPC*, ePrint 2025/1106.

title: Shared adversarial lifecycle test suite
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Can the community converge on a shared, reusable test suite for adversarial lifecycle events in secure-computation systems — malformed inputs, malicious shares, selective aborts, super-rushing, coordinator loss, rollback, churn, and recovery — so that security claims can be checked against a common battery rather than bespoke experiments?
status: Currently an evidence gap: published attacks and repairs — e.g., Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), ePrint 2026/234; Ciampi et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1745 — provide concrete regression seeds, but no complete cross-system suite exists.
solved_when: A cross-system test suite exists that covers all listed lifecycle events (malformed inputs, malicious shares, selective aborts, super-rushing, coordinator loss, rollback, churn, and recovery), is reusable across systems, and incorporates published attacks and repairs as regression seeds.
why: It makes security claims experimentally falsifiable, replacing an evidence gap with concrete, repeatable checks.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), ePrint 2026/234; Ciampi et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1745.

title: Reproducible total energy and cost accounting
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Can we produce a fully reproducible accounting of what it actually costs — in energy and money — to run a cryptographic service end to end, rather than just its computation kernel? Ideally, this covers setup, refresh, preprocessing, computation, proving, communication, storage, and recovery, measured on published hardware under published workloads.
status: Currently only an evidence target; existing selected online-phase or kernel measurements do not establish service economics. Key works: Koch et al. (2025), *b4m*, ePrint 2025/1106; Inyangson et al. (2026), *ThriftyMPC*, ePrint 2026/977. Related efforts include green-computing measurement and total-cost-of-ownership modeling.
solved_when: A complete cost accounting exists that measures all phases (setup, refresh, preprocessing, computation, proving, communication, storage, recovery) on publicly specified hardware and workloads, with results reproducible by third parties.
why: Such accounting is the evidence base for identifying which trust-minimization technology combinations are economically sustainable; without it, selected online-phase or kernel measurements cannot establish real service economics.
key_works: Koch et al. (2025), *b4M*, ePrint 2025/1106; Inyangson et al. (2026), *ThriftyMPC*, ePrint 2026/977.

title: Corpus of cryptographic integration failures
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Can we build a structured corpus of cryptographic integration failures that links each failure to the assumptions it violated, the interfaces it exposed, its exploit prerequisites, the repairs applied, and an executable regression capturing it?
status: A data target with no corpus yet; recent implementation attacks and proof corrections (e.g., work by Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), ePrint 2026/234; Peshawaria et al. (2025/2026), *Laminate*, ePrint 2025/2285) supply the initial cases.
solved_when: A public, structured corpus exists in which recorded failure cases are linked to violated assumptions, vulnerable interfaces, exploit prerequisites, repairs, and executable regression tests, seeded with initial cases drawn from recent implementation attacks and proof corrections.
why: Such a corpus lets systems learn from recurring cryptographic failures instead of rediscovering them independently.
key_works: Kyster et al. (2025), ePrint 2025/789; Brüggemann and Schneider (2026), ePrint 2026/234; Peshawaria et al. (2025/2026), *Laminate*, ePrint 2025/2285.

title: Independent replication of frontier systems
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Can the major benchmarks for DKG, threshold-FHE, collaborative proofs, and private-state systems be reproduced on independently operated infrastructure while still preserving each benchmark's original security model?
status: This is currently an evidence target only; the publication of results and availability of code do not yet establish independent replication.
solved_when: The major DKG, threshold-FHE, collaborative-proof, and private-state benchmarks have been run on infrastructure operated independently of the original authors, with results matching under the same security models.
why: Independent replication produces reliable records on which future research and real-world deployment decisions can be grounded.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057; Pappas et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/729; Escudero et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/850.

title: Machine-readable trust and guarantee manifests
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Can the field agree on a standardized, machine-checkable manifest that captures a cryptographic component's trust assumptions and guarantees — its setup authorities, thresholds, leakage bounds, failure semantics, parameter dependencies, and permitted compositions — with each manifest linked to a concrete implementation?
status: This is an engineering infrastructure target; NIST's reference-material process (NIST 2026, IR 8214C) provides a foundation, but does not automatically validate the whole stack. Canetti (2001, ePrint 2000/067) is a key reference. Related directions include software bills of materials and proof-carrying component contracts.
solved_when: A working manifest standard exists that covers setup authorities, thresholds, leakage, failure semantics, parameter dependencies, and permitted compositions, is machine-checkable, and is linked to concrete implementations.
why: Such manifests would let practitioners select actual deployed systems from a cross-linked problem census based on verifiable properties rather than prose claims.
key_works: NIST (2026), IR 8214C; Canetti (2001), ePrint 2000/067.

title: Sustainable maintenance and replication funding
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: How much does it actually cost to keep foundational cryptographic software maintained — multiyear compatibility, security fixes, and independent replication — and which funding mechanisms can sustainably cover those costs rather than only the initial construction?
status: This is a funding hypothesis, not a claim that funding is absent; the VERIFHE project is one documented funded effort (European Commission (2026), *VERIFHE: An Open-Source Library for Verifiable Fully Homomorphic Encryption for Trustworthy Machine Learning*, grant 101287502, DOI:10.3030/101287502).
solved_when: A credible measurement of maintenance and independent-audit needs is produced, together with an evaluation of funding mechanisms shown to support multiyear compatibility, security fixes, and replication beyond initial constructions.
why: Without sustained maintenance funding, foundational software stops being trustworthy after its initial research release, undermining everything built on top of it.
key_works: European Commission (2026), *VERIFHE: An Open-Source Library for Verifiable Fully Homomorphic Encryption for Trustworthy Machine Learning*, grant 101287502, DOI:10.3030/101287502.

title: Procurement evidence for actual trust reduction
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Can we formulate procurement criteria that let an institution test whether a cryptographic system actually reduces the trust it must place in operators — separating genuine mathematical threshold guarantees from reliance on operator independence, centralized recovery, hardware assumptions, or unverified availability claims?
status: This is a governance and evidence target rather than a solved technical problem. NIST's threshold call (NIST, 2026, *NIST First for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, IR 8214C) collects reference material and does not certify every deployment.
solved_when: A set of testable procurement criteria exists that distinguishes mathematical threshold properties from operator independence, centralized recovery mechanisms, hardware assumptions, and unverified availability claims, and that an institution can apply to a candidate deployment to determine what trust reduction is actually demonstrated.
why: Institutions currently buy labels rather than demonstrated trust reduction; such criteria would let them procure cryptographic systems on the basis of evidence.
key_works: NIST (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, IR 8214C.

title: Continuously corrected open-problem registry
subfield: Benchmarks, evidence infrastructure, funding, and governance
open: Build a continuously updated, versioned registry of open problems in this area that tracks the full life cycle of each question — which variants are established open problems, which are proposed targets, which have been solved, which are impossible, which claims remain unverified, and which results supersede earlier ones.
status: Currently an infrastructure target; no such registry exists yet. Recent results (e.g., Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Abraham et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1159; Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189) have repeatedly invalidated broad older labels such as "compact multi-key FHE" or "private large-scale revocation is missing," underscoring the need.
solved_when: A versioned registry exists that distinguishes established open questions, proposed targets, solved variants, impossibility boundaries, unverified claims, and superseding results, and is maintained through continuous correction as new findings arrive.
why: It makes a million-problem census cumulative rather than duplicative or stale, so researchers and funders act on the current state of knowledge instead of invalidated labels.
key_works: Afshar and Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683; Abraham et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1159; Edalatnejad et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1189.

title: Energy-efficient private proof delegation
open: Can a client offload private zk-SNARK proof generation to a server while consuming at least 20× less energy than proving locally — with the full energy picture, including server-side energy, network energy, preprocessing, and failure recovery, measured and reported end to end?
status: Currently a proposed measurement target. Existing single-server outsourcing work (Abbaszadeh et al., 2025/2026, *Single-Server Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113) reports up to 18× reduction in client computation, but no complete end-to-end energy result of this kind exists.
solved_when: A demonstrated private proof-delegation system achieves at least a 20× reduction in client energy for proof generation, with accompanying measurements of server energy, network energy, preprocessing cost, and failure-recovery behavior.
why: Proof generation on mobile and embedded clients is currently out of reach; hitting this target would make verifiable computation practical on battery-constrained devices.
key_works: Abbaszadeh et al. (2025/2026), *Single-Server Private Outsourcing of zk-SNARKs*, ePrint 2025/2113.

title: Thousand-party adaptive DKG under active WAN faults
subfield: Distributed key generation and verifiable secret sharing
open: Can a distributed key-generation protocol actually hold together with a thousand geographically scattered participants while an adversary actively disrupts it? Demonstrate adaptive DKG for at least 1,000 geographically distributed participants under Byzantine behavior, heterogeneous bandwidth, and restarts, reporting tail latency.
status: This is currently a proposed evidence target. Janus reports experiments through 512 nodes, and approximately 310 ms for a sixteen-node intercontinental configuration (Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892).
solved_when: An experimental deployment of adaptive DKG runs with at least 1,000 geographically distributed participants, tolerating Byzantine behavior, heterogeneous bandwidth, and restarts, and reports tail latency.
why: It tests whether large committees remain deployable under active attack — the regime real WAN deployments face but current experiments have not reached.
key_works: Baecker et al. (2026), *Adaptive Distributed Key Generation for Discrete-Log Cryptosystems*, ePrint 2026/892.

title: Fast general private execution without hardware trust
subfield: Private smart contracts and shared private state
open: Can general-purpose confidential smart-contract execution — publicly auditable, EVM-compatible, and free of any trusted hardware — run fast enough for real applications? The goal is to sustain at least 500 transactions per second on declared workloads without TEEs.
status: The 500 transactions/second figure is a proposed performance target, not a measured result. The closest reported system is gcVM (Yana et al., 2026, *gcVM: Publicly Auditable MPC via Garbled Circuits with Applications to Private EVM-Compatible Computation*, ePrint 2026/170), which achieves 83 confidential transactions per second; the 500 target is a projection beyond its measured performance.
solved_when: A system achieves sustained, publicly auditable, EVM-compatible confidential execution at 500 or more transactions per second on declared workloads, with no trusted execution environment in the design.
why: Without such performance, private smart contracts remain limited to simple transfers; achieving it would make general private applications practical on-chain.
key_works: Yana et al. (2026), *gcVM: Publicly Auditable MPC via Garbled Circuits with Applications to Private EVM-Compatible Computation*, ePrint 2026/170.

title: Sparse threshold-CKKS DKG under WAN faults
open: Can a sparse-key distributed key generation protocol for threshold CKKS actually be run end-to-end at the 1,000-party scale, withstanding malicious participants, publicly verifiable shares, and realistic WAN network conditions including the full setup cost?
status: This is a design target. Min et al. (2025/2026) (*Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057) report two seconds for the computational components on an RTX 4090 through 1,024 parties, but this is not full WAN completion.
solved_when: A demonstration of sparse-key DKG for at least 1,000 parties is shown to complete over a realistic WAN transport with malicious robustness, public verification, and a complete accounting of setup; reported timings distinguish full WAN completion from computational components alone.
why: It preserves the efficient CKKS bootstrapping that sparse threshold keys provide while removing reliance on a trusted central key generator, which is the main obstacle to deploying threshold CKKS in real multi-party settings.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), *Distributed Key Generation for Efficient Threshold-CKKS*, ePrint 2025/2057.

title: Threshold FHE within twice single-key lifecycle cost
open: Can a maliciously secure threshold fully homomorphic encryption system be run end-to-end at a total cost less than twice that of an equivalent single-key implementation? The ratio is amortized over the whole lifecycle — setup, ciphertext refresh, and decryption — at the application level, not per component.
status: Proposed as a moonshot; existing component-level improvements do not establish the application-level cost ratio. Key works: Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057; Okada and Takagi (2026), ePrint 2026/957.
solved_when: An auditable, maliciously secure threshold-FHE application is demonstrated whose total amortized lifecycle cost (setup, refresh, and decryption combined) is below 2× that of an equivalent single-key implementation.
why: It would make distributed trust inexpensive enough to be adopted routinely rather than treated as a costly special case.
key_works: Min et al. (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/2057; Okada and Takagi (2026), ePrint 2026/957.

title: Subsecond proofs of programmable bootstrapping
subfield: Verifiable FHE and zero-knowledge evaluation proofs
open: Can a cryptographic proof that an encrypted computation — a representative TFHE evaluation with a programmable bootstrap — was carried out correctly be generated in under one second? The target is a proving system at matching security parameters, with public verification and all proving costs counted toward the budget.
status: This is a proposed performance frontier. The state of the art is HasteBoots (Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots: Proving TFHE Programmable Bootstrapping in Seconds*, USENIX Security 2026), which reports approximately ten seconds for one evaluation/bootstrap — a major improvement over the older tens-of-minutes baseline, but still an order of magnitude away from the subsecond goal.
solved_when: A proof of a representative TFHE evaluation including a programmable bootstrap is produced in under one second, at security parameters matching the underlying scheme, with public verifiability and all proving costs included in the timing.
why: It would make integrity checks practical for low-latency encrypted services, where multi-second or multi-minute proving overhead is currently disqualifying.
key_works: Liu et al. (2026), *HasteBoots: Proving TFHE Programmable Bootstrapping in Seconds*, USENIX Security 2026.

title: Ten-percent-overhead private web attestations
open: Can a private TLS oracle system carry real web traffic — authentication, large responses, retries, and unsupported features included — with less than 10% median overhead on a declared representative web workload?
status: A proposed moonshot. Modern TLS-oracle protocols already have useful WAN benchmarks, but none has been evaluated against this broad joint target.
solved_when: A protocol and implementation is demonstrated whose median overhead on the declared representative workload is below 10%, while preserving privacy through authentication, large responses, retries, and unsupported-feature handling.
why: It would make authenticated private inputs usable in ordinary browsing, moving privacy-preserving web attestations from demos to deployable defaults.
key_works: Little et al. (2026), *Ticket to Hide*, ePrint 2026/540; Celi et al. (2025/2026), *DiStefano*, ePrint 2023/1063.
